article_title: Connect Science
citation: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://www.connectscience.org
title: Service-learning integrated elementary science unit pattern combining NGSS practices, collaborative skills, and a service project
description: This pattern organizes an elementary science unit around three integrated strands: standards-aligned science instruction, explicit social and collaborative skills teaching, and a facilitated service-learning experience. The article describes Connect Science as designed "to prepare teachers to use Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) instructional practices, teach social and collaborative skills, and facilitate a service-learning experience in their science class." The sequence of 31 lessons runs 14 weeks or more and can be integrated with other content instruction.
requirements: Teacher professional development prior to implementation
science materials kit and trade books accompanying the lessons
constraints: Designed for fourth grade; lessons replace existing science units
examples: The evaluation implemented the pattern as 30 lessons of 30-50 minutes each over 14-22 weeks, compared against business-as-usual science instruction.
key_sources: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/connect-science/

article_title: Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools
citation: Agodini, R., Harris, B., Atkins-Burnett, S., Heaviside, S., Novak, T., & Murphy, R. (2009). Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/achievement-effects-of-four-early-elementary-school-math-curricula-findings-from-first-graders-in-39-schools
title: Choose early elementary math curricula based on rigorous experimental evidence of achievement effects, since textbook-based programs differ in impact
description: The report addresses a long-standing debate among educators and policymakers over "which textbooks and their associated instructional approaches have the greatest impact on student learning in key subjects." Its experimental evidence shows measurable achievement differences among four widely used first-grade math curricula, supporting curriculum selection informed by rigorous comparative effectiveness evidence rather than by adoption defaults.
requirements: Comparative experimental evidence of the kind produced by the federal evaluation, in which schools are assigned to curricula and achievement outcomes are compared.
constraints: The evidence reported here covers first graders in 39 schools in the 2006-2007 cohort; effects for other grades and later cohorts are not reported on this page.
examples: Mathematica's large-scale federal study assigned 39 first-grade schools to four math programs and found significantly higher achievement under Math Expressions and Saxon Math.
key_sources: Agodini, R., Harris, B., Atkins-Burnett, S., Heaviside, S., Novak, T., & Murphy, R. (2009). Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/achievement-effects-of-four-early-elementary-school-math-curricula-findings-from-first-graders-in-39-schools

article_title: Sharing Study Data: A Guide for Education Researchers
citation: Neild, R., Robinson, D., & Agufa, J. (2022). Sharing Study Data: A Guide for Education Researchers (NCEE 2022-004). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/NCEE2022004
title: Pair each guidance section with a checklist and supply templates and samples in appendices
description: The guide's support structure pairs each topical section with a checklist and backs the guidance with appendices containing templates and samples, plus links to other resources. The guide "includes links to other resources, a checklist aligned to each section, and appendices that contain templates and samples." This structure lets researchers verify coverage of each data-sharing decision as they complete it.
requirements: Checklists must be aligned to each section of guidance so researchers can track completion of each data-sharing step
target_learners: education researchers using the guide while preparing datasets
target_learning_goals: completing data-sharing steps accurately and completely
examples: Appendices contain templates and samples that researchers can adapt when documenting shared datasets
key_sources: Neild, R., Robinson, D., & Agufa, J. (2022). Sharing Study Data: A Guide for Education Researchers (NCEE 2022-004). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/NCEE2022004

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research
citation: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research
title: Select the research design that fits the intervention and evaluation setting
description: The article recommends that school health researchers take practical steps to ensure high-quality evidence, beginning with design choice. Among the steps it names are "selecting the right research design for the intervention and evaluation setting, identifying appropriate sample definitions and analysis methods." The principle holds that design selection should be driven by the characteristics of the intervention being evaluated and the setting in which the evaluation takes place, rather than applied uniformly.
requirements: Researchers must consider the characteristics of the intervention and the evaluation setting when choosing a design
target_learners: school health researchers evaluating school-based programs
target_learning_goals: producing high-quality evidence on program effectiveness
examples: The guide frames this as one of several practical steps researchers can take to meet growing demands for evidence and accountability in education policy and programming.
key_sources: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research

article_title: Examining the State-Trait Composition of Social-Emotional Learning Constructs: Implications for Practice, Policy, and Evaluation
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld, Emily Wolk, Sharon Bi. (2019). Examining the state-trait composition of social-emotional learning constructs: Implications for practice, policy, and evaluation. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness 12(3), 550-557. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Treat SEL measures cautiously in school accountability systems because SEL constructs are more context-dependent than achievement
description: Because the study finds SEL domains "seem to be more strongly influenced by contextual factors" than the highly stable rank ordering of math and reading skills, the authors argue that SEL measures should be interpreted differently from achievement measures in evaluation and policy settings. The abstract states that "Implications for school accountability systems and intervention approaches are discussed," positioning state-trait composition as a consideration when using SEL scores for accountability or judging intervention effects.
requirements: Awareness of the state-trait composition of the specific SEL construct being used in evaluation or accountability
constraints: The article's evidence base covers four SEL domains and math/reading achievement; the text provided does not print specific accountability recommendations
target_learners: K-12 students in accountability and evaluation systems
target_learning_goals: Appropriate interpretation of SEL measures in policy and evaluation
key_sources: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld, Emily Wolk, Sharon Bi. (2019). Examining the state-trait composition of social-emotional learning constructs: Implications for practice, policy, and evaluation. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness 12(3), 550-557. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/examining-the-state-trait-composition-of-social-emotional-learning-constructs-implications-for-practice-policy-and-evaluation/

article_title: Robust IRT scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years
citation: Jungnam Kim, Furong Gao, & Dong-In Kim. (2017). Robust IRT Scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, San Antonio, TX.
title: When test design changes may introduce multidimensionality, prefer separate calibration with as few equating transformations as possible over concurrent calibration
description: The article recommends considering separate calibration with minimal equating transformations when accumulated tests share overlapping items but blueprint or item-type changes may violate IRT assumptions. It notes that "concurrent calibration is more accurate when the data fit the IRT model" but is "less robust to violations of the IRT assumptions due to multidimensionality," and its results showed the separate-calibration transformations (CH and SM) agreed closely while concurrent calibration diverged. The study operationalized this by transforming multiple tests simultaneously (SM) to minimize equating steps.
requirements: Overlapping common items between tests to anchor transformations
At least 20 common items per test for grouping tests into a simultaneous transformation
constraints: The article's support is one licensure exam context; a single concurrent calibration failed to run for the second block and had to be split into sub-blocks
The authors state a study to investigate why concurrent calibration produced such different results would be necessary
target_learning_goals: stable item parameters and comparable scores across years of test administrations
examples: In the study, chain equating added tests one at a time starting from 2014F, choosing at each step the test sharing the highest number of common items with the bank; simultaneous equating equated 19 second-block tests together in a first step and the remaining 15 in a second step
key_sources: Jungnam Kim, Furong Gao, & Dong-In Kim. (2017). Robust IRT Scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, San Antonio, TX. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/robust-irt-scaling-considerations-in-constructing-item-bank-from-tests-across-years/

article_title: Practitioners at the Center: Catalyzing Research on Problems of Practice in Realistic Settings
citation: Pautz Stephenson, S., Banks, R., & Pakhira D. (2022, December). Practitioners at the center: Catalyzing research on problems of practice in realistic settings. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/164
title: Center practitioners in research via six guiding principles spanning inclusion, power-shifting, lived experience, problems of practice, feedback loops, and dissemination
description: Based on interviews with three SEERNet digital learning platform teams, the report identifies six principles to guide strategies for centering practitioners: include practitioners with diverse backgrounds; "Empower practitioners and intentionally shift power dynamics so that they have a voice, especially in research questions"; value practitioners' lived experiences as content and context experts; surface problems of practice and connect them to research goals; structure feedback loops that transform knowledge, actions, or goals of all involved; and disseminate findings so platforms are widely used, used well, and have positive impact.
requirements: Practitioners should help define research questions and objectives for the end result to be useful in practice
constraints: The models work well for iterative, agile, comparative improvement research; practitioner involvement could look different in effectiveness or scale-up studies or fundamental scientific research; equity in how partnership districts are selected must be addressed so partnerships broaden rather than perpetuate inequities
target_learners: K-12 educators, instructional and technology coaches, school administrators, and district-level staff
target_learning_goals: Research that impacts educational decision making and addresses consequential problems of practice
examples: SEERNet's Office Hours initiative was the network's first endeavor to apply these guiding principles, strategically advertising to K-12 Title I school districts
key_sources: Pautz Stephenson, S., Banks, R., & Pakhira D. (2022, December). Practitioners at the center: Catalyzing research on problems of practice in realistic settings. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/164

article_title: Classroom-Based Experimentation in a Digital Learning Platform
citation: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306
title: Embed experiments seamlessly into the natural flow of platform instruction
description: The report's first emerging insight is that classroom-embedded experiments "can and should be seamless and non-disruptive, requiring minimal, if any, burden on the part of the instructor." Embedded manipulations operate naturalistically within the existing flow of instruction, preserving the integrity of students' learning experiences without requiring teachers to modify practice or manage groups. Group random assignment keeps students in the same class or school in the same condition, avoiding perceived unfairness and visible differences, and supports ecological validity and generalizability.
requirements: UpGrade's flexible randomization schemes, including group random assignment, to preserve consistency of learning experiences across groups.
constraints: Particularly important in school settings where maintaining coherence within classroom structures has practical and pedagogical importance.
target_learners: K-12 students and their classroom teachers
target_learning_goals: Rigorous experimental evidence generated without disrupting everyday instruction
examples: Metacognitive prompts and self-efficacy surveys were embedded fully in the MATHia instructional flow, with interventions randomized by classroom.
key_sources: Murphy, A. (2026, July). Classroom-Based experimentation in a digital learning platform. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/306

article_title: Designing an App to Support Families’ Joint Engagement with Media: Design Principles and Lessons from Research
citation: Digital Promise, The Jim Henson Company, Concord Evaluation Group, & Curious Media. (2021). Designing an app to support families' joint engagement with media: Design principles and lessons from research. [White Paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/121
title: Second-screen app structure with episode-synced conversation starters, hands-on activities, and a topical guide
description: A reusable design pattern for family joint media engagement apps: a second-screen resource that syncs to episode content and organizes support into a Dive In section with per-episode conversation starters, science themes, characters, and clips; hands-on Activities connecting science ideas to everyday experiences; and an Ocean Guide with environments, topics, and clips. The app "includes detailed information about the science concepts in the show, allows parents to easily access ideas for conversation during or after they watch the show with their children, and provides hands-on activities."
requirements: Content tied to a media program with identifiable science themes
Conversation starters accessible via sync or episode search
constraints: Component usefulness varies with the child's interest or age
target_learners: Families with young children watching educational media together
target_learning_goals: Science talk and connecting show science ideas to everyday life
examples: The Splash and Bubbles for Parents app implements this pattern with Dive In, Activities, Ocean Guide, My Favorites, and a microphone-icon sync feature
key_sources: Digital Promise, The Jim Henson Company, Concord Evaluation Group, & Curious Media. (2021). Designing an app to support families' joint engagement with media: Design principles and lessons from research. [White Paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/121

article_title: Preparing Young Children for School
citation: Burchinal, M., Krowka, S., Newman-Gonchar, R., Jayanthi, M., Gersten, R., Wavell, S., Lyskawa, J., Haymond, K., Bierman, K., Gonzalez, J. E., McClelland, M. M., Nelson, K., Pentimonti, J., Purpura, D. J., Sachs, J., Sarama, J., Schlesinger-Devlin, E., Washington, J., & Rosen, E. (2022). Preparing Young Children for School (WWC 2022009). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov/
title: Build lessons sequentially with an evidence-based curriculum rather than pieced-together activities
description: Each learning area should proceed deliberately and systematically, with new teaching building on what children know and adding challenge toward kindergarten-ready skills. The guide states: "New learning should proceed in a sequenced order, from easy to more difficult skills and concepts, and be based on knowledge of young children's natural development." The panel recommends choosing an evidence-based program or curriculum developed by content experts rather than piecing together a variety of activities, and scheduling consistent intentional instruction time in each domain.
requirements: An evidence-based program or curriculum with a sequence of topics in social-emotional, executive function, mathematics, and literacy
A schedule devoting consistent intentional instruction time to each area, fitting the daily routine
constraints: Amount of instruction time varies with the length of the preschool day
Small-group time with one teacher requires strategic classroom setup, such as coupling center activities with intentional instruction
target_learners: Children ages 3-5 in preschool programs, including private preschools, district preschools, Head Start, and formal-curriculum daycare
target_learning_goals: Sequential mastery of skills and knowledge leading toward success in kindergarten
examples: Center activities coupled with intentional instruction time so the rest of the class practices while the teacher works with a small group
training children over several days or weeks to participate in center activities
key_sources: Burchinal, M., Krowka, S., Newman-Gonchar, R., Jayanthi, M., Gersten, R., Wavell, S., Lyskawa, J., Haymond, K., Bierman, K., Gonzalez, J. E., McClelland, M. M., Nelson, K., Pentimonti, J., Purpura, D. J., Sachs, J., Sarama, J., Schlesinger-Devlin, E., Washington, J., & Rosen, E. (2022). Preparing Young Children for School (WWC 2022009). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/30

article_title: Identifying Students Who Are Off-Track Academically in 9th Grade: The Role of Social-Emotional Learning Trajectories
citation: Soland, J. & Kuhfeld, M. (2019). Identifying students who are off-track academically in 9th Grade: the role of social-emotional learning trajectories. (NWEA Collaborative for Student Growth Research Brief). https://www.nwea.org
title: SEL status-and-growth framework: middle school SEL constructs as developmental trajectories predicting 9th-grade off-track status
description: This framework treats social-emotional learning constructs (academic growth mindset, self-efficacy, self-management) as developmental processes with their own growth trajectories, asking "whether a student's mean SEL score in 6th grade (status) or growth between 6th through 8th grade is more predictive of being off track academically in 9th grade." The article operationalizes it with latent growth curve models, in which "the random intercept reflects the average 6th grade score and the latent growth factor represents the linear change between 6th and 8th grade." Status and growth factors are then used as predictors of 9th-grade off-track indicators.
requirements: Multiple waves of longitudinal SEL measures scored on a common metric (IRT scoring with tested longitudinal measurement invariance)
At least three data waves, which constrained the article to a linear growth trajectory
constraints: Findings come from a single urban, high-poverty district with many English learners and may not generalize to other settings
Only four years of survey data were available, so three years were used and nonlinear functional forms could not be tested
Measures are student self-report surveys, which may suffer from self-report and social desirability biases
target_learners: Middle school students (grades 6-8) in urban, high-poverty districts
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional competencies (growth mindset, self-efficacy, self-management) as indicators for identifying students off track to graduate
examples: The district administered spring SEL surveys each year; DIF analyses found no problematic differential functioning across grade comparisons before IRT calibration and scoring
key_sources: Soland, J. & Kuhfeld, M. (2019). Identifying students who are off-track academically in 9th Grade: the role of social-emotional learning trajectories. (NWEA Collaborative for Student Growth Research Brief). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/identifying-students-who-are-off-track-academically-in-9th-grade-the-role-of-social-emotional-learning-trajectories/

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: SEERNet initiative
description: SEERNet is a network funded by the Institute of Education Sciences to support research using data from digital learning platforms. According to the paper, it 'has fostered a shared vision for responsible, inclusive, and theory-driven research by convening and supporting the research community.' SEERNet DLPs, researchers, and partners work on shared data infrastructure, standardized data governance, de-identified well-documented datasets, and research-practice partnership models piloted by SEERNet grantees.
requirements: Continued collective effort across researchers, educators, and platform partners; investment in shared data infrastructure and open analytics tools, especially for publicly funded platforms
constraints: The paper notes most commercial platforms offer limited or inconsistent backend data access, which fragments reproducibility and secondary analysis
target_learners: Students using SEERNet digital learning platforms (e.g., ASSISTments, MATHia)
target_learning_goals: Enabling rigorous, ethical, theory-driven research on learning within platforms
examples: SEERNet grantees and collaborators piloted research-practice partnership models shaped by real classroom needs (Digital Promise, n.d.)
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Linking Social-Emotional Learning to Long-Term Success
citation: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org
title: Two-domain structure of school social-emotional value-added: social well-being and work habits
description: The article's value-added analysis organizes school effects on social-emotional development into two distinct domains. It reports that "School effects cluster in two domains, social well-being and work habits, and some schools are better at one than the other." This taxonomy means a school can excel at supporting one dimension while lagging on the other, so a single summary rating would obscure meaningful differences among schools. The domains are measured through students' own survey assessments of their development and school climate.
requirements: Annual detailed student survey data about social-emotional development and school climate administered to students in the school system
constraints: Effects are identified for ninth-grade students in Chicago Public Schools high schools via value-added analysis
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development, including social well-being and work habits
examples: The study identifies individual high schools' impacts on ninth-grade students' social-emotional development and test scores through value-added analysis of annual survey results
key_sources: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org

article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: SEAD integration rests on a three-legged stool: explicit instruction, embedded practice in academics, and a relationship-rich learning environment
description: The guide's central framework holds that integrating social, emotional, and academic development (SEAD) requires three mutually reinforcing components: explicit skill instruction, embedded practice during academic instruction, and a healthy relationship-based environment. The guide states that "Enacting SEAD in practice rests on a three-legged stool" and that schools must address "social, emotional, and academic dimensions of learning together because they are inextricably linked in students' experiences." Integration also means embedding SEAD into overall school improvement rather than treating it as a siloed add-on program.
requirements: School leadership teams treat SEAD as integrated into school improvement strategy rather than a siloed initiative or add-on program
constraints: Each school community must adapt the approach to its own aspirations and values of students, families, faculty, and stakeholders
examples: The guide organizes its five sections (vision, student learning experience, adult learning, climate, asset mapping) around this framework
key_sources: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/

article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: Social-emotional development cannot be color-blind: educators must examine their own identities and biases
description: The guide's equity sections and its Pine View vignette argue that SEL implementation must attend explicitly to race, identity, and bias. The vignette concludes that "SEL cannot be color-blind and it is just as important for adults as it is for children," and the guide recommends educators "do reflective internal work to understand their own identities and how privilege and bias can influence perceptions of and relationships with students." Leaders should create space to discuss equity and power and model leaning into discomfort rather than reaching closure.
requirements: School leaders create space to discuss equity and power; a growth-orientation, non-judgmental process for staff self-reflection
constraints: Staff pushback is anticipated; the vignette reports significant fallout and divisions persisting over time
target_learners: Students of color and other marginalized groups, and all students
target_learning_goals: Healthy integrated identity development and equitable social-emotional support
examples: Pine View's leadership team trained on implicit bias, then rolled out staff PD on identifying and addressing bias; one teacher resisted and rallied dissenters to the district
key_sources: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Melissa Roderick, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller, and Thomas Kelley-Kemple. (2013). From High School to the Future: The Challenge of Senior Year in Chicago Public Schools. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Senior year should be reinterpreted as a bridge into college and work rather than the end of high school
description: The report argues that fixing senior year requires a cultural shift, not just coursework mandates. It states: "For students who hope to attend college, senior year must be reinterpreted as more than the end of high school and should instead function as a bridge into college." Teachers and school leaders should collectively decide what skills and academic behaviors students need for postsecondary success and how these develop across grades nine through twelve. Coursework requirements alone do not address the low challenge of senior year courses.
requirements: School leaders, counselors, and teachers must initiate a culture shift in the purpose of senior year and discuss what skills students need for college
constraints: The report warns that rules-based solutions like mandating fourth-year math may put lower-achieving students at risk of not graduating
target_learners: high school seniors in an urban district, college-bound and non-college-bound
target_learning_goals: successful transition to postsecondary education or work
examples: The report notes that for seniors not in AP classes, English IV often became an anchor presenting clear standards and goals, while most other senior classes lacked this focus
key_sources: Melissa Roderick, Vanessa Coca, Eliza Moeller, and Thomas Kelley-Kemple. (2013). From High School to the Future: The Challenge of Senior Year in Chicago Public Schools. UChicago CCSR Research Report. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-future-challenge-senior-year-chicago-public-schools

article_title: Centering the Experiences and Perspectives of Educational Partners: Five Considerations for Schools and Districts
citation: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Seek input from a diverse range of educational partners before deciding, to avoid solutionitis on complex school climate problems
description: The resource warns that rushed, isolated decision-making leads to "solutionitis," defined by the Carnegie Foundation as "the tendency to jump quickly on a solution before fully understanding the actual problem to be solved." Because school climate problems are multifaceted and intertwined with larger institutional challenges, and because an individual's perspective may be limited by personal experiences or biases, leaders should actively seek input from students, teachers, families, and community members to understand problems broadly before acting.
requirements: Leaders must pause and evaluate the situation in its entirety rather than defaulting to quick fixes made alone under time, resource, and staffing pressure
constraints: Especially important for multifaceted school climate issues such as safety and wellness, sense of belonging, and environment
target_learners: School site and district administrators and staff making budgetary, strategic, or instructional decisions
examples: The resource cites implicit-bias research (Gilliam et al., 2016) showing decisions made without checking biases can cause real harm, and co-design work (Daly-Smith et al., 2020) showing working with partners yields transformative solutions
key_sources: Ojetunde, T., & Chavez, A. (2024). Centering the experiences and perspectives of educational partners: Five considerations for schools and districts. California Center for School Climate at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655789

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Seven features of ambitious teaching for English learners
description: The brief enumerates seven features: integrating concepts, analytic practices, and language; drawing attention to how language makes meaning through authentic tasks; scaffolding beyond current knowledge; developing agency; structured collaborative discussion; asset-based teaching and assessment; and a learning culture where all students support each other's learning. Formative assessment undergirds these features.
requirements: Teachers must design and facilitate instruction positioned between students' current and future abilities
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Incorporating Early Learning Strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) Program: How Three Schools Integrated Early Childhood Strategies into School Turnaround Efforts to Improve Instruction for All Students
citation: Connors-Tadros, L., Dunn, L., Martella, J., & McCauley, C. (2015). Incorporating early learning strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) program: How three schools integrated early childhood strategies into school turnaround efforts to improve instruction for all students. New Brunswick, NJ: National Institute for Early Education Research. https://www.nieer.org
title: Seven key components of effective school turnaround practices prevalent across the three case study schools
description: The brief identifies a set of turnaround components that were prevalent in each of the three studied schools, stating that "Key components of effective school turnaround practices were prevalent in each of the schools we studied." The components are strong leadership, effective teachers, redesigned schedules for additional time, rigorous and aligned instructional programs, use of data for continuous improvement, safe and healthy students, and family and community engagement. The pattern recurs across the three case studies, with early learning strategies woven into each component.
requirements: School turnaround efforts integrating early learning strategies attend to all seven components, from leadership through family engagement
constraints: The brief notes these principles of good practice may look different from grade to grade and across state, district, and school contexts
target_learners: Students in persistently low-performing elementary schools, pre-kindergarten through grade 8
target_learning_goals: Improved academic achievement and school climate in turnaround contexts
examples: Orchard Gardens built teaching teams focused on child data, weekly grade-level meetings, and extended learning time; Horace Mann hired reading, math, and social-emotional specialists with SIG funds
key_sources: Connors-Tadros, L., Dunn, L., Martella, J., & McCauley, C. (2015). Incorporating early learning strategies in the School Improvement Grants (SIG) program: How three schools integrated early childhood strategies into school turnaround efforts to improve instruction for all students. article_title: California Special Education Funding System Study, [Part 1]: A Descriptive Analysis of Special Education Funding in California

title: Statewide SELPA administrator survey and multi-LEA SELPA allocation plan review

"Sixty SELPA administrators (from both single- and multi-LEA SELPAs) responded to the survey, representing nearly half of the state's SELPAs." Researchers triangulated survey data with review of allocation plans from 20 of the 54 multi-LEA SELPAs represented in responses; the intended systematic categorization of allocation methods could not be completed due to nonstandard formats and language.

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Tools to Support Authorizer Data Collection

title: Seven categories of charter school core functions for organizing distress indicators
description: The toolkit organizes indicators of distress around seven categories of charter school core functions. As the report states, "Research has identified seven categories of charter school core functions, and indicators of distress can arise within each one: leadership, governing board, operations, financial management, talent, culture, and instruction." article_title: Effective Teacher Professional Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Hyler, M. E., Gardner, M. (2017). Effective Teacher Professional Development. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-prof-dev
title: Seven shared design elements characterize effective teacher professional development
description: The report's central framework: after coding 35 rigorous studies, the authors identify seven widely shared features of effective PD — content focus, active learning, collaboration, models and modeling, coaching and expert support, feedback and reflection, and sustained duration. They state that "effective professional learning incorporates most or all of these elements." The framework confirms and expands Desimone's earlier five-part consensus, adding specificity about active and collaborative practices.
requirements: PD models must incorporate most or all of the seven elements to be considered effective as defined by the report
constraints: Because studies typically examine comprehensive models incorporating many elements, the paper does not draw conclusions about the efficacy of individual program components
examples: The Reading Recovery program is described as an example possessing all seven elements and generating positive student gains

article_title: Social, Emotional, and Academic Development through an Equity Lens
citation: Duchesneau, N. (2020). Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens (#ReEnvisionSEL). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/social-emotional-and-academic-development-through-an-equity-lens/
title: Social, emotional, and academic development (SEAD) through an equity lens framework
description: The report proposes a framework in which students' social-emotional skills, mindset, and academic learning are shaped by three interacting layers: classroom factors (adult beliefs, mindsets, and behaviors), school/district systems and policies, and societal context. It argues "all learning is social and emotional" and that separating social-emotional learning from academic learning allows for problematic implementation focused too narrowly on behavior modification. The framework shifts from a deficit-based to a strength-based mindset, from one-size-fits-all to recognizing cultural and contextual influences, and from allowing bias to targeted efforts to reduce bias.
requirements: Educators and leaders must shift focus away from fixing kids toward addressing environments and systems
constraints: Approaches that ignore context carry significant risks for students already underserved by the education system
examples: The framework envisions learning environments where students feel they belong, are challenged to reach their potential, and receive academic and holistic supports
key_sources: Duchesneau, N. (2020). Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens (#ReEnvisionSEL). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/social-emotional-and-academic-development-through-an-equity-lens/

title: Professional development should build educators' culturally affirming environments, relationship-building skills, and asset-based mindsets

It recommends high-quality professional learning in asset-based pedagogies, belonging and inclusiveness, adult self-awareness, and environments supporting holistic student development.

article_title: How Does Tennessee Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?
citation: The Education Trust. (2023). How Does Tennessee Support Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)?. https://EdTrust.org
title: SEAD framework: six policy areas for equitable social, emotional, and academic development
description: The brief defines SEAD as "A HOLISTIC APPROACH TO SUPPORTING STUDENTS' DEVELOPMENT AND LEARNING THAT IS INTEGRAL TO ENSURING POSITIVE OUTCOMES IN SCHOOL AND BEYOND." It organizes state policy action into six areas: inclusive discipline and dress code policies, meaningful professional development for all adults, equitable access to rigorous and culturally sustaining curricula, engaging students and families as full partners, integrated wraparound services, and diversifying the educator workforce. The framework treats academic, social, and emotional development as inseparable and equity-centered.
requirements: State and district leaders coordinate policies across all six areas rather than treating SEAD as a single program
constraints: Many of these policy areas are led at the local level, with state leaders playing a supporting role
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color, students from low-income backgrounds, and other underserved students
target_learning_goals: Holistic social, emotional, and academic development and positive school outcomes
examples: The brief audits Tennessee's policies against each of the six areas, listing bright spots and improvement priorities for each

article_title: Survey Development for Assessing Student Computing Career Intentions. Technical Report
citation: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Seven-construct framework of computing career intentions spanning individual, situational, and social factors
description: The article organizes its survey around seven constructs derived from a literature review of career intentions research: coding self-efficacy, barrier-coping self-efficacy, interest in coding, intention to pursue a coding career, practical support, social support, and sense of belonging in computing. Constructs are grouped as "Individual Factors", "Situational Factors", and "Social Factors". Each construct is defined by the degree to which an individual holds a specific belief or perception, such as "The degree to which an individual feels they can be successful in coding-related tasks".
requirements: Items for each construct are administered as 5-point Likert matrix questions with agreement response options
constraints: The framework was operationalized for computing career intentions among participants of computer science education programs, not general career measurement
target_learners: participants of informal and formal computer science education programs, from high school students to adults
target_learning_goals: measuring individual, situational, and social factors shaping students' intentions to pursue computing careers

article_title: Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice
citation: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Integrate social and emotional learning with academic development to address climate-related distress, including through collective action
description: The report's third principle holds that schools should foster students' social and emotional well-being as essential to academic development, since climate change affects well-being through weather disruptions, degraded developmental conditions, and distress over observable and future threats. It argues students need safe, nurturing environments that intentionally incorporate social and emotional learning rather than behavioral interventions aimed at fixing them, and recommends school-based health professionals who can conduct climate-related distress assessments.
requirements: Professional development helping educators recognize students' social and emotional needs in the context of climate change and racial injustices
Investment in school-based health professionals able to conduct climate-related distress assessments and provide interventions
constraints: Educators are not often clinically trained, per the report
target_learners: P-12 students, especially children near industrial pollution, children of color, and children in concentrated poverty
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional coping skills such as self-regulation, social awareness, communication, and collaboration
examples: NEEF and the Climate Mental Health Network found virtually every middle school teacher reported encountering student emotional reactions to climate change but most felt unequipped to help, prompting a toolkit of teacher-tested, standards-aligned resources; the report states students are less likely to exhibit depression symptoms from climate anxiety if engaged in collective action.

article_title: Building a System of College and Career Pathways in New Mexico
citation: Hoachlander, G. (2020). Building a system of college and career pathways in New Mexico. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/new-mexico-education
title: Seven-dimension pathway quality standards spanning outcomes-driven practice, equity culture, industry themes, project-based learning, work-based learning, supports, and distributed leadership
description: The report proposes state quality standards for college and career pathways mirroring the seven dimensions on which certified Linked Learning pathways produced positive impacts. Standards include that "The progress of every student is the driving focus for evaluating pathway quality," a culture of high expectations with nondiscriminatory and inclusive practices, an industry-themed program of study offering dual credit, inquiry- and project-based learning that is "relevant, rigorous, outcome-focused, and collaborative in nature," a personalized continuum of work-based learning for every student, personalized academic and social-emotional supports, and shared responsibility among staff, leaders, and community partners.
requirements: A pathway quality assessment rubric tied to state quality standards, plus metrics and incentives for increasingly higher levels of quality implementation
constraints: The report warns tracking should ensure pathways do not regress into old systems that led to tracking and inequitable outcomes by race, ethnicity, gender, and special needs
target_learners: All high school students in pathway programs, including students with low prior achievement
target_learning_goals: Mastery of college- and career-ready learning outcomes
Academic and professional skills demonstrated through work-based learning
examples: The report recommends metrics such as percentage of students participating in industry-centered, multidisciplinary project-based learning and percentage of students earning dual college credit aligned with their pathway.

article_title: Artificial and Emotional Intelligence: Two Key Forces for Teachers' Professional Development in an Era of Uncertainty
citation: Aponte ML, Vargas Sánchez AD, Chiappe A and Martínez-Pérez S. (2026). Artificial and emotional intelligence: two key forces for teachers' professional development in an era of uncertainty. Front. Psychol. 17:1935683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935683
title: Seven design conditions for AI as relational infrastructure in teacher development, each linked to risks, safeguards, and outcome indicators
description: The article operationalises its thesis through seven design conditions: relational reinvestment of freed time, community as the unit of design, limits on symbolic substitution, affective data governance, critical AI literacy as socio-emotional competence, cultural fragility of algorithmic empathy, and demonstrable relational densification. "Table 1 synthesizes this distinction by linking each design condition with the main risk it addresses, the institutional safeguards required, and possible outcome indicators." Each condition names a failure mode, for example that "AI personalizes support but leaves teachers isolated in individual trajectories."
requirements: Implementation requires institutional safeguards per condition, such as formal policy reinvesting saved time, routing conversational systems toward human support, and separating wellbeing support from performance evaluation
constraints: The table should be read as "a heuristic for design and evaluation rather than as a fixed measurement protocol," since indicators vary by setting, resources, and system type
examples: Illustrative systems include a platform analyzing non-affective workload indicators to recommend protected peer-support time, voluntary mentor matching by declared interests, and a conversational agent limited to orienting teachers toward human support

article_title: AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education
citation: Mahinpei, R., Dean, V., Fong, R., Liu, L. T., & Ribeiro, M. H. (2026). AI Assistance for Discretionary Work: Increasing Feedback Provision in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03095
title: Separate AI-assisted feedback from grading to preserve independent evaluation and reduce over-reliance
description: The article recommends introducing AI assistance only after the primary evaluative task is complete. Instructors "raised concerns about potential over-reliance on AI-mediated feedback," and the design responded by having TAs "first completed grading independently, and only then proceeded to the feedback stage." This sequencing preserves the grader's independent judgment of student work while still lowering barriers to the discretionary feedback step, and it was reinforced by formative-study concerns about graders deferring to drafts without verification.
requirements: A workflow where the primary evaluative task (grading) can be completed before AI assistance is introduced
A platform integration that surfaces drafts only after the primary task is submitted
constraints: Validated in a single 300-level ML course with structured rubric-based grading; generalization to other workflows is not tested
target_learning_goals: preserving independent evaluation of student work
examples: The Chrome extension displayed feedback drafts only after TAs clicked a Done Grading button, ensuring AI assistance was introduced after grading was complete

article_title: 'Why Put in This Much Effort?": How AI Availability Shapes Students’ Motivation in Introductory Programming'
citation: Keith Tran, Colton Harper, and Thomas Price. 2026. "Why Put in This Much Effort?": How AI Availability Shapes Students' Motivation in Introductory Programming. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol. 1 (ICER 2026 Vol. 1). https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811653
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) as a framework for analyzing how AI availability reshapes motivational judgments
description: The study uses Situated Expectancy-Value Theory as its analytical framework, decomposing motivation into expectancy plus four subjective task values. As the article states, "Intrinsic value refers to the enjoyment or satisfaction derived from doing the task itself," alongside attainment value, utility value, and cost, which "works against motivation." SEVT is situated: beliefs are shaped by task context including available alternatives, making it suited to analyzing how AI availability enters students' motivational reasoning. The article also draws on Flake et al.'s cost sub-components: effort cost, opportunity cost, and loss of valued alternatives.
requirements: The framework requires analyzing which specific motivational dimensions students describe as most affected, since AI does not uniformly raise or lower motivation
constraints: The article notes cost has received the least theoretical and empirical attention despite its practical significance for understanding student disengagement
target_learners: end-user programmers who are not CS majors
target_learning_goals: sustained effort and engagement with programming practice
examples: The interview protocol structured questions around all five SEVT dimensions, asking general questions then AI-specific questions for each dimension
key_sources: Keith Tran, Colton Harper, and Thomas Price. 2026. "Why Put in This Much Effort?": How AI Availability Shapes Students' Motivation in Introductory Programming. In Proceedings of the ACM Conference on International Computing Education Research Vol. 1 (ICER 2026 Vol. 1). https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811653

article_title: Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification
citation: Bingjun Li, Christopher Buzaid, Weihao Qu. (2025). Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification. Journal of Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics and Jurisprudence. https://doi.org/10.65879/3070-5789.2025.01.07
title: Sentinel AI-powered security game platform with LLM-driven adversarial persona and badge system
description: Sentinel is an AI-powered mobile game platform offering subgames on phishing detection, password cracking, text scams, and phone call scams. Its core interaction engine uses a Large Language Model (Google Gemini API) fine-tuned with system prompts defining the attacker's persona, with LLM output piped through a low-latency ElevenLabs text-to-speech engine for realistic voice modulation. The platform "provides player analytics and a badge-reward system to enhance motivation and sustained engagement," and adjusts scam sophistication based on the user's initial streak.
requirements: System prompts that restrict the AI to specific social engineering tactics such as urgency and authority and prevent it from breaking character
A bounded adversarial framework that filters user inputs to prevent jailbreaking the scammer bot
constraints: The generative model is limited to the adversarial attacker role only; educational explanations are delivered through standard non-generative interfaces to guarantee pedagogical accuracy
Voice profiles are randomized in gender, tone, and accent to avoid reinforcing stereotypes about attacker demographics
examples: The Phone Scam game simulates a call in which a trained AI bot acts as a scammer attempting to extract sensitive information, and switches to subtler soft-sell tactics if the user easily detects the first clue
key_sources: Bingjun Li, Christopher Buzaid, Weihao Qu. (2025). Security Education in Higher Education through AI-Powered Gamification. Journal of Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics and Jurisprudence. https://doi.org/10.65879/3070-5789.2025.01.07

article_title: Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research
citation: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7
title: Seven-phase framework for reflecting on how AI methodologies may transform science education research
description: The article proposes a framework of seven epistemological phases for AI-based educational research: "(1) problem framing, (2) instrumentation and measurement, (3) experimentation and evidence‑based inference, (4) comparisons and replication, (5) building norms and consensus, (6) implementation and its consequences, and (7) continuous refinement." Each phase is paired with guiding questions and exemplified through both thermometer history and AI analysis of student learning. The framework is intended to help the community interrogate what is analyzed, how analyses acquire meaning, and how practices reshape the field's foundations.
requirements: Researchers use the phases as analytical dimensions paired with guiding questions rather than as a prescribed procedure
constraints: The authors state the phases are "analytical dimensions of epistemic iteration rather than prescribed steps that all research must follow in a fixed order"; phases may repeat, overlap, or be absent
target_learning_goals: reflective evaluation of AI-based research methodologies and their epistemic implications
examples: The article pairs each phase with guiding questions (Fig. 1) and illustrates each with a thermometer-history case and a student-learning-analysis case
key_sources: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7

article_title: WIP: Bridging the Gap Between Instructional Design and Pedagogical Use: A Framework for Mathematics Educators
citation: Estefany Castillo Ventura, Javier Ulises Solis Lastra, Anarosa Alves Franco Brandão. (2026). WIP: Bridging the Gap Between Instructional Design and Pedagogical Use: A Framework for Mathematics Educators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20934
title: Secant–tangent transition applet characterized via the conceptual-structure variables
description: An interactive applet illustrates the metadata characterization: it represents a function graphically with a secant line defined by two points, one varying with a parameter h; as h approaches zero the secant converges to the tangent. It is characterized as derivative at a point (conceptual), with essential prior knowledge of functions, graphical interpretation, and slope, graphical predominant representation with implicit coordination of multiple representations, and process-level conceptual construction.
requirements: The resource must make the secant-to-tangent transition accessible as a process, consistent with the process level in APOS theory
target_learners: high school mathematics students learning the derivative
target_learning_goals: interpreting the derivative as a limiting process
examples: The article states that although the interaction involves actions such as manipulating the parameter, the main contribution is making the secant-to-tangent transition accessible as a process.

citation: Xiaojing Duan, Frederick Nwanganga, and Chaoli Wang. (2026). CODE-GEN: A Human-in-the-Loop RAG-Based Agentic AI System for Multiple-Choice Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03926
title: Seven pedagogical evaluation dimensions for multiple-choice coding questions
description: The Validator assesses each generated question across seven pedagogical dimensions derived from established multiple-choice item-writing guidelines: question stem clarity, code validity, concept alignment, correct answer validity, distractor quality, correct answer feedback quality, and distractor feedback quality. Each dimension receives a Yes/No or Good/Poor classification output plus a rationale output explaining the assessment, producing transparent dimension-level quality signals rather than opaque aggregate scores. The dimensions cover both technical verifiability and pedagogical depth.

constraints: Dimensions requiring deeper instructional judgment (distractor quality, distractor feedback quality) showed lower automated reliability
examples: Table 1 prints each dimension's description, classification output, and rationale output

article_title: Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior
citation: Jordan Gutterman, Ashish Gurung, Lee Branstetter, Kenneth Koedinger, and Vincent Aleven. (2026). Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25308
title: Session-level behavioral measures as content-independent, practitioner-aligned detectors of self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes that session-level measures like delayed start provide "a new opportunity for content-independent detectors, adding a behavioral component to the traditional usage and progress based on student engagement with content." Because the daily class period in K-12 is a bounded work space, its start and end times serve as behavioral anchors for defining self-regulation measures. The framework holds that detectors built from DLP log data already in use require no new diagnostics and frame results in minutes of delay, matching what educators observe. It bridges education research and classroom practice through interpretable measures.
requirements: Digital learning platform log data from which classwork sessions can be inferred via transaction density
K-12 class periods with bounded start and end times to anchor delay measurement
constraints: Results derived from one middle-school context with 45-minute class periods and one math platform; thresholds could differ in other contexts, e.g. 60-minute sessions
The raw minutes metric leaves the predictive power of classroom and contextual factors on the table
The work does not identify precisely which construct delayed start best represents
target_learners: Grade 7 middle school students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning behaviors such as timely task initiation
examples: The classwork-session inference algorithm classified practice instances with more than five concurrent students from the same class during school hours as classwork sessions, identifying 841 sessions across 26 classes
key_sources: Jordan Gutterman, Ashish Gurung, Lee Branstetter, Kenneth Koedinger, and Vincent Aleven. (2026). Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25308

article_title: Using Gemini and LuaLaTeX to transcribe physics videos into PDF/UA-2 and ISO 32005 math-accessible PDFs
citation: Looney, C. W., & Duston, C. L. (2026). Using Gemini and LuaLaTeX to transcribe physics videos into PDF/UA-2 and ISO 32005 math-accessible PDFs.
title: Segment-structure transcript format with boldface labels replacing bracketed nonverbal insertions
description: The v6m system instructions organize transcripts into distinct verbal and descriptive segments marked by boldface labels rather than square brackets, with both segment types able to contain math. Early tests showed that closing display math at the end of a square-bracketed descriptive segment caused numerous compilation failures; the authors report that "Abandoning square brackets and adopting the segment structure delivered an immediate and substantial improvement in stability and overall performance". The labels also provide a less-ambiguous transition signal for screen reader users than bracketed text.
requirements: A prewritten LuaLaTeX preamble compatible with the segment structure
System instructions that define and enforce the segment labels
constraints: Brief bracketed insertions of nonverbal description cannot be injected directly into the verbal flow
target_learners: blind and low-vision students using screen readers
target_learning_goals: accessible comprehension of spoken and board-written mathematical content in lecture videos
examples: Transcripts alternate PRESENTER verbal segments with ACTION descriptive segments, as in the video 14 Gauss's law transcript quoted in Section 5.7

citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T. & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports 15:17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6
title: Design AI tutoring systems around seven research-based pedagogical best practices
description: The article enumerates best practices that foster learning and applies them to AI tutor design: "(i) facilitating active learning, (ii) managing cognitive load, (iii) promoting a growth mindset, (iv) scaffolding content, (v) ensuring accuracy of information and feedback, (vi) delivering such feedback and information in a targeted and timely fashion, and (vii) allowing for self-pacing." Practices i-v were built via system prompts and platform structure; vi-vii are the personalization advantages AI offers over classrooms.

Pedagogical best practices must be explicitly and carefully built into each application

LLM hallucinations pose a significant challenge for educational use

citation: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651
title: Self-reflective LLM annotation agent with iterative criteria refinement and short-term memory
description: An LLM-based agent that labels each discourse sample, then reflects to identify weaknesses in the current coding framework and applies revision actions (modify, add, delete, hold, merge) before labeling the next sample. It "retained short-term memory of the three most recently labeled samples and the three most recent versions of the criteria", enabling progressive self-refinement beyond single-prompt labeling. In experiments the agents consistently chose only to modify existing levels, preserving the seven-level structure. Code is released at https://github.com/HanlingJ/human-icl-llm-agent.
requirements: An initial criteria version, labeled samples, and a foundation LLM (GPT-4o or GPT-5.2); memory buffer of recent samples and criteria versions
constraints: Agent refinement relied solely on each agent's own analysis without discussion; agent-refined frameworks showed greater cross-model variability (QWK 0.655–0.790) than human-refined ones
target_learning_goals: scalable measurement of cognitive engagement in collaborative discourse
examples: The agent's reflection identified gaps such as proposals without justification being implicitly treated as Level 4 and vague turn-taking language for Levels 6–7

title: Seven-enabler framework for trustworthy LA-based educational interventions
description: A framework of seven institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy learning analytics: institutional strategic orientation, pedagogical & other research foundations, available resources, pedagogical support, ethics & data governance, stakeholder engagement, and quality assurance. The article defines enablers as "institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy LA" and positions trustworthiness as the prerequisite without which LA-based interventions are not meaningful. The framework was developed via survey, Delphi, and SNAP prioritization.
requirements: Trustworthy LA as a prerequisite: the article states trustworthiness is the prerequisite without which LA as a tool for informing educational interventions is not meaningful
constraints: The article states the enablers are not to be interpreted as dimensions of trustworthy LA but as conditions enabling LA-based educational interventions
The article states their relative importance may vary depending on institutional context and the maturity of LA systems

target_learning_goals: Learning design and educational change based on trustworthy learning analytics

Single-statement pairs for sentence-level semantic similarity approaches

description: A lesson-video generation workflow with three stages: LLM-based slide generation (Claude 3.5 Sonnet producing Marp Markdown slides), LLM-based TTS-optimized narration generation, and automated speech synthesis and integration via the Gemini TTS API, Marp, Selenium, and MoviePy. The system "was intentionally designed not as a "one-shot" fully automated generation tool but as an interactive and augmentative workflow", positioning educators as retaining final judgment over quality while using AI as an efficient assistant. Educator review occurs after stages 1 and 2; stage 3 is fully automated.

citation: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026
title: Seven-type feedback focus taxonomy adapted from Narciss for written teacher feedback
description: The article adapts and refines Narciss's content-based feedback taxonomy into seven feedback focus types for annotating written feedback: Task Constraints, Concepts, Elaboration, Clarification, Mistakes, Praise, and Other. The authors retain elaborated components that apply to writing, adapt KHP into Elaboration and KCR into Clarification, exclude simple components suited to closed-ended tasks, and add Praise and Other. They argue prior frameworks "either conflate content and function ... or categorize content only broadly," while this taxonomy treats them separately with more precise content focus types.
requirements: Annotator training with a coding manual; labeling priorities when feedback could belong to two types
constraints: Simple feedback components (KP, KR, KCR) excluded as unsuited to open-ended writing tasks; metacognitive feedback excluded as rarely observed
target_learning_goals: characterizing what teacher and LLM feedback focuses on in student writing
examples: A teacher comment 'Nice.' annotated as Praise; a comment asking a student to cut or develop a paragraph annotated as Task Constraints

Purposes ranged from a virtual tutor supporting scientific writing to Socratic chatbots guiding problem-solving and alkene halogenation. By the end of development, "seven distinct yet consistent student-staff-designed cGPT tools had been created, each tailored to its unit's content and learning activities".

description: The system operationalizes a seven-dimensional Behaviorally Anchored Rating Scale (Topic, Content, Clarity, Voice & Talk, Eye Contact, Nonverbal Expressiveness, and Overall Rating), with each dimension anchored at levels 1, 3, and 5 and intermediate ratings permitted. The rubric was adapted from a prior scale through expert workshops to make each dimension observable in single-camera instructor videos. Reconstruction from the frozen bases does not require calling the models.

citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework

description: Self-Directed Growth is defined as "a competency reflects by the increased progression to drive an ongoing, iterative, and sustainable SDL process independently, fueled by an enhanced Capacity to Aspire". It positions the learner as initiator, executor, assessor, and primary agent of their own SDL journey, extending SDL beyond achieving predefined outcomes in pre-assigned tasks toward independently constructing and assessing one's own SDL process guided by an internal compass. The article presents it as an advanced extension of the broader SDL framework and the central construct of the A2PL model.

article_title: Towards Self-Referential Analytic Assessment: A Profile-Based Approach to L2 Writing Evaluation with LLMs
citation: Stefano Bannò, Kate Knill, Mark Gales. (2026). Towards Self-Referential Analytic Assessment: A Profile-Based Approach to L2 Writing Evaluation with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04298
title: Self-referential analytic assessment framework
description: An evaluation paradigm for analytic essay scoring that shifts from normative (inter-learner ranking) to within-learner interpretation of analytic profiles. "Self-referential analytic assessment focuses on intra-learner variability, identifying aspects where a student performs significantly better or worse than their average proficiency." Standardised analytic scores are averaged within a learner, and deviations of each aspect from that average define a dual binary classification task for positive and negative feedback, using a one-standard-deviation threshold. The article positions this as a stricter, more pedagogically relevant test of analytic assessment capability and the first such framework for L2 AES.
requirements: A reference signal that is internally consistent and psychometrically calibrated, obtained here via two-facet Rasch modelling and infit-based rater selection
Standardised scores across all analytic aspects so deviations are comparable
constraints: The one-standard-deviation threshold is described as a heuristic choice, albeit one aligned with psychometric methodology
target_learners: L2 English learners (Asian learners in an English as a Lingua Franca framework in the study data)
target_learning_goals: Diagnostic identification of relative strengths and weaknesses across analytic writing proficiency aspects
examples: The framework was implemented on ICNALE GRA essays with reference fair average scores from 12 Rasch-selected raters, comparing GPT-4.1, Qwen 2.5 72B, Llama 3.1 70B, and operational raters

article_title: From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment
citation: Ivo Bueno, Babette Bühler, Philipp Stark, Tim Fütterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Dorottya Demszky, Heather Hill, Enkelejda Kasneci. (2026). From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05180
title: A general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring combining SHAP attributions with LLM rationales
description: The article proposes "a general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring that combines model-agnostic Shapley value attributions with LLM-generated rationales". It casts rubric-based teaching quality assessment as text scoring with model-agnostic sentence-level explanations, where an explanation method maps an input and model to a ranked list of sentences claimed most influential. Faithfulness is evaluated via a deletion-based protocol that progressively removes top-k units and measures prediction change, extended to cross-model settings where explanations from one architecture perturb another. It was instantiated on the CLASS Quality of Feedback dimension using the NCTE corpus with fine-tuned PLMs and instruction-tuned LLMs.
requirements: Identical sentence segmentation, deletion rules, and deterministic LLM decoding across compared models, as the article states all experiments use
constraints: The deletion-based protocol perturbs natural discourse structure and may alter pragmatic meaning, limiting its ability to reflect true causal influence
The article does not evaluate whether identified sentences align with underlying rubric constructs (construct relevance)
target_learners: teachers receiving automated feedback on classroom transcripts
target_learning_goals: understanding which parts of classroom dialogue drive automated teaching quality assessments
examples: Applied to 6,005 NCTE transcript segments annotated on the CLASS Quality of Feedback 1–7 scale, comparing eight fine-tuned PLMs with nine instruction-tuned LLMs

description: A set of paper-based survey instruments used to measure motivational constructs before and after practice. Favorability items assessed attitudes toward the two instructional methods on a 1–5 Likert scale plus one free-response question. Factor analysis yielded two self-efficacy and two favorability constructs with adequate internal consistency (e.g., graph interpretation αpre = .83).

constraints: A significant proportion of students left at least one question blank; favorability was measured after the posttest
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy and favorability toward tutor-based and paper-based math practice
examples: The full questionnaires are available on OSF at https://osf.io/r5e9z/
