article_title: From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support
citation: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618
title: Validate counterfactual recourse recommendations against explicit semantic feasibility constraints before use in educational decision support
description: The article recommends that educational recourse outputs be treated as machine-checkable intervention plans subject to explicit semantic constraints rather than accepted on model validity alone. The semantic layer's contribution, as the authors put it, is "not to reduce optimization cost, but to distinguish between plans that are merely model-valid and plans that remain feasible" under explicit timing, budget, immutability, and availability constraints. This makes recommendations defensible and interpretable for instructors, advisors, and support services before any practical use.
requirements: An RDF representation of candidate plans and a SHACL validation layer encoding timing, budget, immutability, and availability constraints
A calibrated predictive model defining the recourse target
constraints: The evaluation is offline, model-based, and observational and does not establish that following a generated plan would improve student outcomes
target_learners: students in digital learning environments at risk of poor performance
target_learning_goals: actionable, feasible intervention planning for at-risk students
examples: In the 200-case ablation, activating availability constraints exposed plans that a lighter optimization-only setting accepted, at unchanged optimization cost
key_sources: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618

article_title: Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices
citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Seven dynamic human-GAI paradigms grounded in personal epistemological beliefs
description: The article introduces a framework of seven human-generative AI paradigms: "guarded, possibility-focused, augmented, pioneering, symbiotic, values-based and equity". Each paradigm is outlined and examined against five epistemological dimensions, so that a person's or group's beliefs about knowledge shape how they engage with generative AI. The paradigms are presented as dynamic rather than fixed, offering a lens for interpreting human-GAI interaction in higher education.
requirements: Grounding in personal epistemological beliefs: the framework interprets engagement through beliefs about the source, certainty, organisation, control and speed of knowledge acquisition
constraints: The author notes "the framework remains an exploratory heuristic requiring empirical validation"
target_learning_goals: understanding and shaping human-GAI engagement in learning contexts
examples: The article outlines each of the seven paradigms and examines them against the five epistemological dimensions
key_sources: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11

article_title: Assessing faculty self-perceived knowledge in using generative AI to teach 21st-century skills
citation: Sutedjo A, Chowdhury M and Liu SP (2026) Assessing faculty self-perceived knowledge in using generative AI to teach 21st-century skills. Front. Educ. 11:1913310. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1913310
title: Sequence GenAI faculty development from foundational GenAI literacy toward discipline-specific integration activities
description: The article recommends that professional development first build a shared baseline of GenAI literacy through hands-on experimentation with GenAI tools in teaching and assessment contexts, before introducing complex integration tasks, and that programs be structured around discipline-specific use cases connecting GenAI affordances to faculty subject matter. Investment should be distributed broadly across the full faculty population since low technology-integrated knowledge held across every demographic subgroup.
requirements: Programs must directly engage with disciplinary content rather than remain generic
institutional support including faculty time, recognition, communities of practice, and alignment with promotion and tenure criteria
constraints: The gateway role of TK is an interpretive hypothesis the cross-sectional design cannot test
target_learners: higher education faculty across all career stages and appointment types
target_learning_goals: GenAI integration into teaching to foster 21st-century skills
examples: The survey found low TPK, TCK, and TPACK scores across all subgroups, supporting broad distribution of professional development investment
key_sources: Sutedjo A, Chowdhury M and Liu SP (2026) Assessing faculty self-perceived knowledge in using generative AI to teach 21st-century skills. Front. Educ. 11:1913310. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1913310

article_title: Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning
citation: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613
title: Apply system constraints selectively to inefficient learner task-selection strategies rather than uniformly
description: In shared-control mastery-based ITS, constraints on task and problem selection should target the learner strategies that produce inefficiencies rather than being applied to everyone. The simulations show constraints sharply reduce overpractice for the risk-averse strategy while having little effect on efficient strategies, so "applying the same constraints to all learner types is unnecessary". This preserves learner autonomy and motivational benefits for students whose strategies already align with mastery objectives.
requirements: Estimates of individual learners' task-selection strategies or learner state to decide when constraints apply
Constraints that bound rather than remove learner choice to preserve autonomy
constraints: Overly prominent system constraints may undermine student autonomy perceptions and lower motivation
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students using shared-control ITS
target_learning_goals: efficient mastery of mathematical skills with preserved learner autonomy
examples: The simulation applied closer-to-mastery, further-from-mastery, prefer-easier, and prefer-harder constraints across eight task-selection strategies to identify which learner behaviors warrant targeted constraints
key_sources: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Selection branch of the taxonomy: five categories of conditional-statement difficulties
description: The selection branch classifies difficulties with conditional statements into five categories: the selective nature of selection statements, boundaries of the selection body, the else-branch, timing of condition check, and nesting. Example categories include thinking all branches execute independent of their condition and confusion between "if(C) A; else B;" and "if (C) A; B;". Many categories carry literature references, while others are newly created from the authors' own research.
requirements: Applies to difficulties in reading code containing selection statements, within the paper's conceptual-knowledge scope
constraints: Syntactic and lexical errors are excluded as fundamentally different in nature
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding conditional statements and their execution
examples: The nesting category includes confusion between sequencing versus nesting of if-statements and ignoring an if-condition inside a loop
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

article_title: Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication
citation: Ching-Jung Cheng, Yu-Chan Chung, Bing-Chen Chiu, Yu-Hsuan Lin, and Jia-Wei Liao. 2026. Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication: A Probe-Grounded Co-Design Study. OzCHI '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07503
title: Semantic and pragmatic disciplinary boundaries as the two recurring forms of boundary in interdisciplinary team communication
description: Drawing on boundary-crossing literature, the article frames interdisciplinary collaboration differences as two recurring boundary forms: "semantic boundaries, where the same term carries different meaning across fields, and pragmatic boundaries, where members’ goals and values conflict even when they understand one another". This taxonomy organizes what the Spritz probe was designed to detect and underpins the study's account of why text-based, facilitator-less student teams leave differences implicit until they surface as friction. It also connects to the perspective-making and perspective-taking framing the authors use to describe the probe's support functions.
requirements: Teams whose members hold different disciplinary meanings, goals, and values that must be negotiated through communication
constraints: The article focuses on text-based, unstructured channels such as Slack or Discord in temporary teams lacking a dedicated facilitator
target_learners: university students in interdisciplinary project-based learning teams
target_learning_goals: cross-disciplinary communication and coordination in collaborative problem-solving
examples: The probe's tension detector independently assigned semantic and pragmatic tension confidence scores, selecting the semantic path when both exceeded threshold to clarify interpretations before addressing competing interests
key_sources: Ching-Jung Cheng, Yu-Chan Chung, Bing-Chen Chiu, Yu-Hsuan Lin, and Jia-Wei Liao. 2026. Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication: A Probe-Grounded Co-Design Study. OzCHI '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07503

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Self-reinforcing harm cycle linking cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: An integrative conceptual framework organizing the risks of substitution-style AI in education into four interrelated dimensions — cognition, agency, emotional well-being, and ethics — connected by a reinforcing cycle. As the paper states, "These four dimensions are not independent; they interact through a reinforcing cycle." Cognitive offloading reduces effortful reasoning, diminished effort feeds illusory learning and overtrust, overtrust weakens agency, and reduced agency intensifies emotional harms such as anxiety, lower self-efficacy, and dependency, with ethical and structural factors amplifying individual-level effects. The framework is grounded in learning theory and in students' own reflections, with the clearest student-evidenced link being reliance on AI and diminished thinking.
requirements: Applies to AI systems that substitute for human cognitive effort rather than to every AI system or learner; the authors explicitly disclaim universal claims
constraints: The closing connection of the cycle is described as weakly evidenced in the students' exploratory data (dashed link in Figure 1); the essay cohort is illustrative, not representative
target_learners: school and higher-education learners using AI tools
examples: Figure 1 depicts the cycle: substitution erodes capacities while scaffolding builds critical thinking, agency, resilience, and trust
key_sources: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451

article_title: Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment
citation: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517
title: Deliver repeated communication practice, feedback, and assessment through a fully automated self-service platform to reduce the human-resource barriers of standardized-patient training
description: The article argues that scalability of communication training depends on removing two constraints: the availability of people to conduct simulations and the effort required to assess them. SOPHIE 2.0 lets learners "practice asynchronously with an embodied AI patient, receive personalized feedback, and repeat the experience without a live facilitator or rater", while an LLM assessor replaces expert rating effort. The study's findings on usability, agreement with human raters, and independent completion support the feasibility of this model.
requirements: An automated assessor whose agreement with human raters is adequate (here validated at r=0.759, ICC=0.746)
constraints: The present study demonstrates feasibility, not deployment at scale; performance gains could not be attributed specifically to training without a control condition
target_learners: healthcare professionals and students without prior communication training
target_learning_goals: serious illness and general clinical conversations
examples: SOPHIE 2.0 expanded a single-scenario, human-operated predecessor to 24 scenarios with automated assessment, and 59 participants completed successive encounters independently
key_sources: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517

article_title: Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education
citation: Wei J and Shang Y (2026). Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education. Front. Psychol. 17:1965371. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1965371
title: Seven analytically ordered measurement targets for critical engagement with GenAI outputs
description: The review proposes a construct-validity framework separating seven measurement targets: epistemic evaluation, verification initiation, process quality, success, reliance decisions, immediate task performance, and independent learning. It argues that broad labels such as "critical" or "responsible" AI use "can obscure distinct outcomes" — a learner may check without a strong process, and a correct final answer does not establish retention or unaided performance. The ordering is analytic, not a validated causal sequence.
requirements: Measures must support distinct interpretations within a nomological network rather than being treated as interchangeable indicators
constraints: The map is an analytic ordering rather than a validated causal model
Searches were targeted rather than systematic
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI
examples: Table 1 contrasts how representative studies operationalize verification, reliance calibration, and learning outcomes
key_sources: Wei J and Shang Y (2026). Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education. Front. Psychol. 17:1965371. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1965371

article_title: Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning
citation: Xiaokun Wang, Siyu Song, Wentao Liu, Xiaodong Zou. (2026). Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22996
title: SE and CD: outcome-oriented evaluation metrics for closed-loop Socratic tutoring assessment
description: The article introduces two evaluation metrics for Socratic tutoring beyond surface fluency. Scaffolding Effectiveness (SE) measures the proportion of test questions where the tutor guides a simulated student to self-express the core concept without uttering any keyword in Ki, over up to four dialogue rounds. Conversation Depth (CD) measures the fraction of consecutive guide–student turn pairs whose Sentence-BERT embeddings have cosine similarity below 0.70, indicating semantic progression. The article notes "novelty alone does not guarantee successful scaffolding", so CD is reported with SE and leakage. The student simulator was validated against held-out real follow-ups with mean SBERT similarity 0.449±0.220.
requirements: A fixed gold concept and keyword set Ki per test question
An LLM student simulator and concept judge (Qwen-plus / Qwen-turbo) held fixed across systems
SBERT encoder with threshold θ=0.70 for CD
constraints: SE and CD are simulation-based metrics; simulator validity was checked against 30 questions with recorded follow-ups, yielding on-topic but non-duplicate behavior
target_learners: Simulated and real primary-school science students ages 8-12
target_learning_goals: Assessing whether tutoring dialogues move students to self-express target concepts through progressive inquiry
examples: SE=0.633 and CD=0.722 for the best GRPO variant on the 30-question test set
key_sources: Xiaokun Wang, Siyu Song, Wentao Liu, Xiaodong Zou. (2026). Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22996

article_title: How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis
citation: Sungeun An, Jennifer Hammock, Ashok Goel. (2025). How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00506-5
title: Three-pattern framework of self-directed modeling behavior (Observation, Construction, Exploration)
description: The article proposes a framework for understanding how online learners engage in self-directed modeling outside traditional classrooms, built from learning analytics on VERA logs. It identifies "three distinct behavioral patterns—Observation, Construction, and Exploration—that reflect varying levels of engagement and interaction", links them to learning theories such as constructivism and situated cognition, and maps detailed Markov transition clusters onto the three types. Observation involves parameter experimentation on existing models, Construction short building sessions, and Exploration full construction-parameterization-simulation cycles.
requirements: Behavioral log data capturing modeling actions (construction, parameterization, simulation) so activity sequences can be extracted and clustered
constraints: Developed from log data of unspecified online learners without demographic or contextual information, which the authors state limits generalizability
target_learners: self-directed online learners using ecological modeling tools
examples: Clustering 822 activity sequences from 315 VERA learners into the three types, then mapping nine Markov clusters onto them (Table 1)
key_sources: Sungeun An, Jennifer Hammock, Ashok Goel. (2025). How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00506-5

article_title: Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI
citation: Halani, A. (2026). Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI. Tang Institute at Phillips Academy. https://www.tanginstitute.andover.edu
title: Seven-lever course-design framework for shaping student AI use
description: The framework defines a lever as "a recurring feature of the course environment that students experience, that can be configured differently by someone within the institution, and that may influence what students do with or without direct supervision." The seven levers are Structure (what pays), Material (what they work on and when), Practice (how the room runs), Response (what gets said back), Norms (what is normal), Frame (what they understand about why), and Relationship (what is safe). Every classroom has a setting on all seven, whether chosen or defaulted, and none of the levers is specific to AI.
requirements: Each lever must be a recurring, experienceable feature of the course environment configurable by someone within the institution
constraints: The framework is offered as a heuristic taxonomy, not a validated or necessarily exhaustive model, and does not establish causal effects for particular configurations
Class size, contact hours, and tracking are conditions of the cultural surround, not levers
target_learning_goals: protecting independent thinking when AI use is unobserved
examples: The paper describes three full lever-setting tables for a think-first classroom, a direct-instruction classroom, and a Harkness classroom
key_sources: Halani, A. (2026). Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI. Tang Institute at Phillips Academy. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/t4cd2_v1

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Sensorimotor debilities: the loss of multimodal agency, proprioception, and tactile engagement in digital and GenAI-mediated interaction
description: The article adopts Penny's concept of sensorimotor debilities to name the embodied costs of interaction with digital technologies, particularly GenAI. It states: "These debilities manifest as a loss of multimodal agency, weakening the sense of proprioception, kinesthetic awareness, and tactile engagement that emerge from being alive, moving, and sensorially interacting with the world." The devaluation of craftsmanship and DIY making practices further erodes aesthetic and experiential dimensions tied to acting, feeling, and meaning-making through movement, which the authors link to impoverished educational experiences as AI spreads in education.
requirements: Design must shift AI's reliance on vision and text toward interaction that is lived, embodied, and negotiated in real time
constraints: The article warns that lack of impetus to build an embodied research programme in AI will lead to impoverished educational experiences
target_learners: all learners in AI-mediated educational settings
target_learning_goals: preservation of multimodal agency, proprioceptive awareness, and tacit embodied knowing
examples: The article cites the 'Organs without Bodies' exhibition generating physical objects with AI as provoking reflection on creation without the bodies of artisans.
key_sources: Lb

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Seven design principles for critical and transformative integration of Embodied AI in education
description: The article proposes "a set of pedagogical principles aimed at the critical and transformative integration of Embodied AI in contemporary educational contexts", methodologically grounded in Design-Based Research. The seven principles are: (i) overcoming natural language models as epistemic centers; (ii) situationality to generate meaningful connections; (iii) distributed creativity and co-agency; (iv) embracing uncertainty, failure, and improvisation; (v) critical awareness of bias and algorithmic performativity; (vi) embodied sensorimotor multimodality; and (vii) ecological design for open pedagogical innovation.
requirements: Pedagogical redesign situated in experience, the body, creativity, and emergence, moving away from mere instrumentalization of teaching through technology
constraints: The article notes implementation requires material, institutional, and formative conditions often lacking in educational settings
target_learners: elementary through tertiary learners in AI-integrated curricula
target_learning_goals: creative, critical, collaborative, and situated learning with AI
examples: Principle (vi) calls for educational experiences where vision, gesture, speech, movement, and touch are recognized as legitimate modalities of knowing and expressing.
key_sources: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.1145/3759257

article_title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9434-x
title: Self-explanation as a generative learning process
description: The article defines self-explanation as "a process by which learners generate inferences about causal connections or conceptual relationships". It treats self-explanation as something that can be induced in learners through prompts delivered while they are studying material or solving problems, and the meta-analysis evaluates learning outcomes for participants who received such prompts. This framing positions self-explanation as a constructive, inference-generating activity rather than mere restatement.
requirements: Learners must receive self-explanation prompts while studying or solving problems for the induced process to occur as studied in the meta-analysis.
target_learners: learners across education levels studied in the included self-explanation research
target_learning_goals: generating inferences about causal connections and conceptual relationships
examples: The meta-analysis located studies in which participants received self-explanation prompts while studying text, studying worked problems, or solving problems.
key_sources: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9434-x

article_title: A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect
citation: Rey, G.D., Beege, M., Nebel, S., Wirzberger, M., Schmitt, T.H., & Schneider, S. (2019). A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 389–419. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9456-4
title: Explanatory accounts of the segmenting effect: designer-imposed chunking and structuring, more processing time, and individual pace adaptation
description: The meta-analysis frames the segmenting effect within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning and tests three candidate explanations: that segmenting by the instructional designer facilitates chunking and structuring of the material, that it provides more time for processing the instruction, and that it allows learners to adapt the presentation pace to their individual needs. The article states: "The meta-analysis tests different explanations for the segmenting effect that concern facilitating chunking and structuring due to segmenting the multimedia instruction by the instructional designer, providing more time for processing the instruction and allowing the learners to adapt the presentation pace to their individual needs."
requirements: Explanations are tested against the meta-analytic evidence from 56 investigations of segmented versus continuous multimedia instruction.
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of multimedia instruction content
examples: The meta-analysis evaluates these explanations using moderation analyses, including the prior-knowledge moderation of retention performance.
key_sources: Rey, G.D., Beege, M., Nebel, S., Wirzberger, M., Schmitt, T.H., & Schneider, S. (2019). A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 389–419. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9456-4

article_title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
citation: Yeager, D. S., Hanselman, P., Walton, G. M., Murray, J. S., Crosnoe, R., Muller, C., Tipton, E., Schneider, B., Hulleman, C. S., Hinojosa, C. P., Paunesku, D., Romero, C., Flint, K., Roberts, A., Trott, J., Iachan, R., Buontempo, J., Yang, S. M., Carvalho, C. M., Hahn, P. R., Gopalan, M., Mhatre, P., Ferguson, R., Duckworth, A. L. & Dweck, C. S. (2019). A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement. Nature 573. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1466-y
title: Seed-and-soil account: sustained intervention effects require both an adaptive belief change and a congruent school context
description: The article's explanatory framework for its moderation findings: a psychological intervention supplies a high-quality seed (an adaptive belief system), but the effect is sustained only in conductive soil, a school context congruent with the proffered belief system. The authors write that "Sustained change may therefore require both a high-quality seed (an adaptive belief system conveyed by a compelling intervention) and conductive soil in which that seed can grow (a context congruent with the proffered belief system)". It explains why GPA effects were larger where peer norms supported challenge-seeking.
requirements: An intervention that conveys a compelling adaptive belief system
A school context, such as supportive peer norms, congruent with the proffered belief system
constraints: The article notes it cannot draw causal conclusions about school norms because norms were measured, not manipulated
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in secondary school, especially lower-achieving students
target_learning_goals: Sustained academic improvement in grades and rigorous course-taking
examples: In the National Study of Learning Mindsets, GPA effects among lower-achieving students were larger in low- and medium-achieving schools with supportive behavioural challenge-seeking norms

article_title: Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools
citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Mary M. Mitchell, & Philip J. Leaf. (2010). Examining the Effects of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Student Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial in Elementary Schools. Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions, 12(3), 133-148. https://doi.org/10.1177/1098300709334798
title: Seven-step schoolwide implementation of universal SWPBIS
description: The article describes the universal SWPBIS model as "implemented by following these seven steps, which map onto the model's critical features": forming a SWPBIS team of 6 to 10 staff with an administrator; an external behavioral support coach providing on-site consultation; defining three to five positively stated schoolwide expectations; teaching those expectations to all students; a schoolwide reinforcement system; an agreed-upon system for responding to behavioral violations; and a formal system to collect, analyze, and use disciplinary data for data-based decision making. These steps were measured by the 29-item School-Wide Evaluation Tool.
requirements: Administrator participation, staff training in referral procedures, and an Internet-based data entry and reporting system (SWIS) for disciplinary data
constraints: Pattern is at the whole-school, universal tier; the article notes it did not examine targeted or indicated tiers
target_learners: all students in an elementary school
target_learning_goals: positive behavioral expectations, consistent discipline, reduced problem behavior
examples: Schools established expectations such as "Be respectful, responsible, and ready to learn" posted in all classrooms and nonclassroom settings, with tangible reinforcers like "gotcha" tickets

citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Sentence-level interpretation and production tasks as pretest-posttest measures of grammar instruction effects
description: This element is the assessment battery used in the experiment: pretest and posttest measures "involving both a sentence-level interpretation (comprehension) task and a sentence-level production task," with scores "submitted to an analysis of variance." target_learners: second language learners in instructed settings

examples: The experiment administered these tasks as pretests and posttests across the processing instruction and traditional instruction conditions.

article_title: Self-Monitoring Interventions for Students with ASD: a Meta-analysis of School-Based Research
citation: Davis, J.L., Mason, B.A., Davis, H.S., Mason, R.A., & Crutchfield, S.A. (2016). Self-Monitoring Interventions for Students with ASD: a Meta-analysis of School-Based Research. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 3, 196–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-016-0076-y
title: Self-monitoring intervention framework for students with ASD organized around student, intervention, and setting variables
description: The article organizes its synthesis of self-monitoring (SM) interventions around three levels: "student-, intervention-, and setting-level variables". It examines "characteristics of students with ASD that react favorably to the intervention, what procedures are necessary for implementation, and how settings within schools affect outcomes". The framework structures the meta-analysis of 16 single-subject studies and identifies four key implementation components.
requirements: Requires identification of a target behavior and its definition, plus self-assessment and self-recording procedures for implementation
target_learners: students with autism spectrum disorders in school settings
key_sources: Davis, J.L., Mason, B.A., Davis, H.S., Mason, R.A., & Crutchfield, S.A. (2016). Self-Monitoring Interventions for Students with ASD: a Meta-analysis of School-Based Research. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 3, 196–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-016-0076-y

article_title: A Review of Self-Management Interventions Targeting Academic Outcomes for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders
citation: Mooney, P., Ryan, J. B., Uhing, B. M., Reid, R., & Epstein, M. H. (2005). A Review of Self-Management Interventions Targeting Academic Outcomes for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Journal of Behavioral Education, 14, 203–221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-005-6298-1
title: Self-management intervention taxonomy for academic outcomes: self-evaluation, self-monitoring, strategy instruction, self-instruction, and multiple-component interventions
description: The review organizes academic self-management interventions for students with emotional and behavioral disorders into five technique types, reporting that "Self-monitoring interventions were the predominant type of self-management technique used by researchers." The taxonomy distinguishes self-evaluation, self-monitoring, strategy instruction techniques, self-instruction techniques, and multiple-component interventions, each with its own mean effect size in the synthesis. It serves as the organizing axis for the review's analysis of intervention effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable into one of the five intervention types for the taxonomy's effect-size comparisons
constraints: Derived from 22 single-subject studies of children and adolescents with emotional and behavioral disorders published in 20 articles
target_learners: children and adolescents with emotional and behavioral disorders
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes including math calculation, writing, reading, and social studies skills
examples: The review classified each of the 22 included studies by intervention type and computed mean ES per type, from self-evaluation (1.13) to self-instruction techniques (2.71)
key_sources: Mooney, P., Ryan, J. B., Uhing, B. M., Reid, R., & Epstein, M. H. (2005). A Review of Self-Management Interventions Targeting Academic Outcomes for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Journal of Behavioral Education, 14, 203–221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-005-6298-1

article_title: The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Nückles, M., Roelle, J., Glogger-Frey, I., Waldeyer, J., & Renkl, A. (2020). The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09541-1
title: The self-regulation view in writing-to-learn: combining genre-free expressive journal writing with systematic prompting of self-regulatory processes
description: The self-regulation view holds that journal writing scaffolds self-regulated learning through cognitive offloading: written text serves as an external representation and memory aid that frees working-memory capacity for metacognitive reflection, and the genre-free principle further offloads writers from rhetorical demands. The authors term this idea of combining free and expressive writing with systematic prompting of self-regulatory processes the self-regulation view of writing-to-learn, positioning it between the romantic view (spontaneous expressive writing suffices) and the classic view (rhetorical genre instantiation produces learning). It draws on models of self-regulated learning theory and cognitive load theory.
requirements: Instructional support via prompts eliciting cognitive (elaboration, organization) and metacognitive (monitoring, regulation) learning strategies, because learners spontaneously keep invested mental effort at a minimum
constraints: Learners need sufficient mastery of transcription skills (spelling, handwriting/typing); the approach was developed for university students and extended to secondary school students
examples: Learning journal entries after lectures or seminar sessions in which students identify main points, elaborate with examples, monitor comprehension gaps, and plan remedial strategies
key_sources: Nückles, M., Roelle, J., Glogger-Frey, I., Waldeyer, J., & Renkl, A. (2020). The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09541-1

article_title: Promoting Self-Determination in Early Elementary School
citation: Palmer, S.B., & Wehmeyer, M.L. (2003). Promoting self-determination in early elementary school: Teaching self-regulated problem-solving and goal-setting skills. Remedial and Special Education, 24, 115-126. http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/07419325030240020601
title: Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction
description: The Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction is a model of teaching that enables students to set goals for learning and work toward achieving them, framed as a component of self-determination. The article describes and validates it for use in early elementary grades, where it structures "the investigation of student interests, the facilitation of choices, and the goal setting and attainment of young children." It functions as a self-regulated problem-solving and goal-setting instructional model teachers can apply across subjects.
requirements: Teachers implement the model within existing curricula and programs across a variety of subjects and settings.
target_learners: Early elementary students, including students with diverse learning needs
key_sources: Palmer, S.B., & Wehmeyer, M.L. (2003). Promoting self-determination in early elementary school: Teaching self-regulated problem-solving and goal-setting skills. Remedial and Special Education, 24, 115-126. http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/07419325030240020601

article_title: Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning
citation: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4
title: Choose support procedures for visual displays based on knowledge of the difficulties learners have with them
description: The review recommends that support for learning from visual displays be selected on a diagnostic basis: because displays "pose substantial demands on learners," knowledge of "the main difficulties that learners have when learning from visual displays" is "an important basis for selecting appropriate support procedures." The review then maps such procedures onto the material-oriented versus learner-oriented taxonomy, so that the chosen intervention addresses the diagnosed difficulty rather than being applied indiscriminately.
requirements: A prior analysis of which difficulties learners actually have with the displays in question
target_learners: Learners using visual displays in learning materials
target_learning_goals: Learning from pictures and multimedia materials
examples: The review structures its overview of empirically tested support procedures by first identifying learner difficulties and then presenting material-oriented and learner-oriented interventions matched to them.
key_sources: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4

article_title: Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning
citation: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5
title: Dual-process account: self-explanation promotes learning via knowledge integration and knowledge generalization
description: The article's explanatory account holds that self-explanation aids comprehension "by promoting knowledge integration" — linking new information together or with prior knowledge — and aids comprehension and transfer "by guiding attention to structural features over surface features," increasing generalization. These two cognitive processes jointly explain why self-explanation helps transfer in principle-governed domains yet can impair detail recall and the learning of exceptions.
requirements: Learners must generate inferences that go beyond the given information, whether about expert-presented content or their own problem solving
constraints: The account presupposes domains where generalization of principles or heuristics is appropriate; generalizing can overlook exceptions and reduce attention to details
target_learners: learners across a range of prior knowledge levels, particularly those with limited prior knowledge
examples: Learners' explanations of worked examples often linked solution steps to prior knowledge or information in the text
key_sources: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Self-assessment should focus on eliciting and using criteria and standards rather than generating grades
description: The paper argues that self-assessment research has over-emphasised comparing student-generated marks with teacher marks, a strategy that can be added with little disruption. For developing evaluative judgement, the emphasis should instead be on "eliciting and using criteria and standards as an embedded aspect of learning and teaching strategies", helping students develop multiple criteria and qualitatively review their own work against them.
requirements: Self-assessment tasks must involve students in identifying and considering criteria, and provide feedback on the quality of the judgements made
constraints: Self-assessments that solely generate grades or contribute to final grades, without criteria engagement or feedback on judgement quality, are identified as sub-optimal
target_learning_goals: judging quality of one's own work
examples: The paper's Table 1 contrasts grade-generating self-assessments with improvements such as feedback on how the self-assessment might be improved and self-assessments spanning units
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction
description: The self-determined learning model of instruction is "designed to enable teachers to teach students a self -regulated problem -solving process in which students set their own goals and select and use one or more student -directed learning strate gies (e.g., self -monitoring, self -instruction) to achieve them." It comprises three instructional phases — set a goal, take action, and adjust goal or plan — each presenting a problem the student solves through a means-ends sequence connecting the student's actual state to a goal state. In this study, students used the model to select target behaviors and self-evaluate progress in general education classes.
requirements: Students must be able to identify a desired goal and the actions or learning needed to achieve it, with teacher facilitation; one student in the study required a higher level of teacher assistance
target_learners: middle school students with intellectual or developmental disabilities in general education classes
examples: Each student completed two worksheets leading through the first two phases, responding to questions such as "What do you have to do or change to reach your goal?"
key_sources: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1177/07419325020230050301

article_title: Promoting Learning and Achievement Through Self-Assessment
citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html
title: Self-regulated learning as the rationale for journal-based self-assessment
description: The article grounds journal use in self-regulated learning, citing O'Malley and Valdez Pierce: 'Student self-assessment is a key element in authentic assessment and in self-regulated learning.' Self-regulated learners collaborate, see the connection between effort and success, monitor their own performance, and evaluate their progress and accomplishments. Journals operationalize these behaviors by prompting regular reflection and self-assessment.
requirements: Learners must be given regular opportunities to reflect on and assess their own progress for self-regulation to develop.
constraints: The framework is attributed to O'Malley and Valdez Pierce's book on authentic assessment for English language learners; the article applies it rather than testing it.
target_learning_goals: monitoring and evaluating one's own progress
examples: The article quotes the source's claim that self-regulated learners 'monitor their own performance and evaluate their progress and accomplishments' as the goal journals serve.
key_sources: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html

article_title: The impact of patient, intervention, comparison, outcome (PICO) as a search strategy tool on literature search quality: a systematic review
citation: Mette Brandt Eriksen, PhD; Tove Faber Frandsen, PhD. (2018). The impact of patient, intervention, comparison, outcome (PICO) as a search strategy tool on literature search quality: a systematic review. Journal of the Medical Library Association 106 (4). https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2018.345
title: Three-criterion risk-of-bias framework for studies evaluating search strategy tools
description: Because no validated risk-of-bias tool existed for studies evaluating search strategy tools, the review authors developed, by consensus, a self-developed set of three criteria: "searcher skills", "match between model and question", and "quality of searches". Each criterion comprises individual considerations (e.g., searcher training and prior familiarity with tools, fit of model to topic, number of search blocks, relevance assessment against a gold standard, and consistent adaptation of searches across databases) judged as low, high, or unclear risk of bias. The framework is used to assess the three included studies and proposed as guidance for future research on this topic.
requirements: Studies must report searcher skills, the fit between the conceptualizing model and the research question, and how searches were performed and adapted per database for the criteria to be assessable.
constraints: The review states the tool "was not validated", and applying a model not fit for the research area, unequal search blocks, or relevance assessment without a gold standard or expert group is treated as high risk of bias.
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating literature search strategies for evidence synthesis
examples: Applied to the three included studies, the criteria yielded high or unclear risk of bias for all three: searcher skills high for Hoogendam et al., model-question fit high for Agoritsas et al. and Methley et al., and quality of searches low only for Methley et al.
key_sources: Mette Brandt Eriksen, PhD; Tove Faber Frandsen, PhD. (2018). The impact of patient, intervention, comparison, outcome (PICO) as a search strategy tool on literature search quality: a systematic review. Journal of the Medical Library Association 106 (4). https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2018.345

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Set acceptable agreement levels according to the costs of drawing invalid conclusions, with suggested alpha thresholds of .800 and .667 for scholarly work
description: The article argues that the minimum acceptable agreement must depend on the stakes of the analysis: "An acceptable level of agreement below which data are to be rejected as too unreliable must be chosen depending on the costs of drawing invalid conclusions from these data." For scholarship, the author suggests requiring alpha >= .800, or alpha >= .667 where tentative conclusions suffice, while insisting there are no magical numbers except perfect agreement and that standards should be verified by experiments. Confidence intervals should be consulted; null-hypothesis tests against chance have no bearing on reliability.
requirements: Thresholds must be chosen by weighing the consequences of invalid conclusions, with higher stakes such as legal or policy decisions requiring far higher criteria
constraints: The suggested .800 and .667 standards were proposed for alpha only; other coefficients may require different standards
examples: The article contrasts content analyses informing legal decisions or war-and-peace questions with those merely supporting scholarly arguments
key_sources: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm

article_title: Promoting Access to the General Curriculum by Teaching Self-Determination Skills
citation: Palmer, Susan B.; Wehmeyer, Michael L.; Gipson, Krista; Agran, Martin. (2004). Promoting access to the general curriculum by teaching self-determination skills. Exceptional Children, 70(4), 427-439. https://hdl.handle.net/1808/10978
title: Promote self-determination linked to standards as an entry point for access to the general curriculum for all students, including those with severe disabilities
description: The article argues that access models often overlook students with more severe disabilities, and that promoting self-determination tied to academic standards is a practical entry point for including them in the general curriculum. It states that "Promoting self-determination linked to standards is an entry point to ensuring access to the general curriculum for all students, including students with severe disabilities." The principle works by giving students strategies, such as problem-solving and study planning, that they apply to standards-aligned academic content. The article's intervention demonstrated this approach with middle school students with intellectual disabilities.
requirements: Self-determination instruction must be linked to academic standards (language arts, science, social studies) rather than taught in isolation
constraints: The article notes that existing models to achieve access often neglect students with more severe disabilities
target_learners: middle school students with intellectual disabilities, including students with severe disabilities
target_learning_goals: access to and participation in the general curriculum
self-determination skills such as problem-solving and study planning
examples: Middle school students with intellectual disabilities alternately learned problem-solving and study planning skills linked to language arts, science, and social studies standards.
key_sources: Palmer, Susan B.; Wehmeyer, Michael L.; Gipson, Krista; Agran, Martin. (2004). Promoting access to the general curriculum by teaching self-determination skills. Exceptional Children, 70(4), 427-439. https://hdl.handle.net/1808/10978

article_title: Promoting Access to the General Curriculum by Teaching Self-Determination Skills
citation: Palmer, Susan B.; Wehmeyer, Michael L.; Gipson, Krista; Agran, Martin. (2004). Promoting access to the general curriculum by teaching self-determination skills. Exceptional Children, 70(4), 427-439. https://hdl.handle.net/1808/10978
title: Self-determination skills function as access strategies that supplement students' means of reaching the general curriculum
description: The article frames self-determination not merely as a personal competency but as a functional mechanism of curricular access: teaching these skills supplies students with additional means of engaging the general curriculum. As the authors put it, "Promoting self-determination provides students with disabilities with additional strategies to access the general curriculum." In this account, problem-solving and study planning operate as strategies students deploy to participate in standards-based academic work. The framework was substantiated in an intervention with middle school students with intellectual disabilities in which both skill groups outperformed an alternating control condition.
requirements: Skills must be taught in connection with the general curriculum content they are meant to give access to
constraints: The account addresses students with disabilities, including severe disabilities, for whom standard access models are described as often neglectful
target_learners: students with disabilities, including students with severe intellectual disabilities
examples: The intervention operationalized the account by teaching problem-solving and study planning linked to language arts, science, and social studies standards.
key_sources: Palmer, Susan B.; Wehmeyer, Michael L.; Gipson, Krista; Agran, Martin. (2004). Promoting access to the general curriculum by teaching self-determination skills. Exceptional Children, 70(4), 427-439. https://hdl.handle.net/1808/10978

article_title: Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities
citation: Michael Wehmeyer, Michelle Schwartz. (1997). Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-Up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities. Exceptional Children, 63(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Self-Determination+and+Positive+Adult+Outcomes+Wehmeyer+Schwartz
title: Wehmeyer's definitional framework of self-determination as acting as the primary causal agent in one's life, with four essential characteristics
description: The article defines self-determination as "acting as the primary causal agent in one's life and making choices and decisions regarding one's quality of life free from undue external influence or interference". An act is self-determined if it reflects four essential characteristics: the individual acts autonomously, the behaviors are self-regulated, the person acts in a psychologically empowered manner, and the person acts in a self-realizing manner. The framework was empirically validated with more than 400 adults with mental retardation and operationalized in The Arc's Self-Determination Scale.
requirements: Measurement requires a validated instrument capturing each essential characteristic, as operationalized in The Arc's Self-Determination Scale
constraints: The framework was developed and validated with people with cognitive disabilities; the article measures it via self-report for adolescents with cognitive disabilities
target_learners: students with mental retardation or learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: self-determination as an educational and transition outcome
autonomy, self-regulation, psychological empowerment, and self-realization
examples: The Arc's Self-Determination Scale was used to measure students with mental retardation and learning disabilities during their final year of high school
key_sources: Michael Wehmeyer, Michelle Schwartz. (1997). Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-Up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities. Exceptional Children, 63(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Self-Determination+and+Positive+Adult+Outcomes+Wehmeyer+Schwartz

article_title: Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole‐word visual processing
citation: Marie-Line Bosse, Nathalie Chaves, Pierre Largy, Sylviane Valdois. (2015). Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole-word visual processing. Journal of Research in Reading, 38, pp.141-158. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01551.x
title: Self-teaching hypothesis: orthographic knowledge is acquired incidentally during reading through phonological recoding
description: The self-teaching hypothesis holds that knowledge of words' orthographic structure is acquired incidentally as children read, driven by phonological recoding of the printed string. In this article it frames the research question: the study tested whether visual processing of the whole letter string additionally contributes to orthographic learning beyond recoding. The authors conclude that "the ability to process the entire orthographic letter string at once during reading contributes to efficient orthographic learning", extending the account.
requirements: Reading experience with decodable letter strings, since acquisition occurs incidentally during reading through phonological recoding.
target_learners: French children in third to fifth grade learning to read
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of word-specific orthographic knowledge (spelling) during reading
examples: The study asked French children to read pseudowords and then assessed memorisation of the targets' orthographic form.
key_sources: Marie-Line Bosse, Nathalie Chaves, Pierre Largy, Sylviane Valdois. (2015). Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole-word visual processing. Journal of Research in Reading, 38, pp.141-158. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01551.x

article_title: Cognitive and emotional math problems largely dissociate: Prevalence of developmental dyscalculia and mathematics anxiety.
citation: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety.
title: Treat cognitive and emotional mathematics problems with different interventions: anxiety-focused support for high MA, skills and working-memory-focused support for DD
description: Because cognitive and emotional mathematics problems largely dissociate, the article recommends that interventions be matched to the problem type. It states that "Different intervention methods need to be developed to prevent and treat emotional and cognitive blocks of mathematical development." Children with MA are likely to benefit from anxiety-focused interventions such as systematic desensitisation, cognitive restructuring, or expressive writing, whereas children with DD without high MA are likely to benefit from interventions targeting mathematical skills, working memory and visuo-spatial processing.
requirements: Identifying MA in the classroom is essential so that children can be equipped with appropriate coping strategies for dealing with anxious reactions towards mathematics, particularly around assessment.
constraints: The article's cross-sectional design could not determine the direction of the MA–performance association; the recommendation rests on the observed dissociation of prevalence rather than a tested intervention in this study.
target_learners: primary and secondary school children with mathematics anxiety or developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: numerical skills and working memory development
examples: The article cites Hembree (1990): interventions focusing on systematic desensitisation or cognitive restructuring resulted in improvements in mathematics performance.
The article cites Ramirez and Beilock (2011): writing about one's anxieties before an examination produced performance benefits, theorised to free up working memory resources.
key_sources: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000222

article_title: Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review
citation: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89
title: Taxonomy of sensory processing problem types: over-responsivity, under-responsivity, sensory-seeking, and sensory discrimination problems
description: The review organizes sensory processing problems as impairments in detection, modulation, or interpretation of stimuli, and distinguishes named types: sensory over-responsivity, where individuals "respond to sensory stimuli in the way that is faster, longer, or more intense than what is expected"; under-responsivity, where individuals are unaware or slow to respond; sensory-seeking, where individuals crave sensory experiences; and sensory discrimination problems, characterized by difficulty interpreting specific characteristics of stimuli. Modalities are not separate and interact with each other.
requirements: Assessment of sensory profiles of children with behavioral problems in clinical practice, as the review recommends
constraints: The etiology of sensory processing is unknown according to the review
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing sensory processing problems that affect daily responses and classroom behavior
examples: The review gives examples such as defensiveness to hair-brushing for tactile sensitivity, and being puzzled about a sound's origin for auditory hyposensitivity
key_sources: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89

article_title: Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review
citation: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89
title: Sensory Profile parent-reported questionnaire and related checklists for assessing sensory processing in children with ADHD
description: The review describes the Sensory Profile as "a widely used parent reported standardized questionnaire" in which children's responses to sensory events in daily life are rated by their parents. It assesses auditory, visual, taste/smell, body position, movement, and touch processing, plus activity level and social/emotional responses. Related instruments include a parent-reported auditory processing problem checklist (hypersensitivity and hyposensitivity to sounds) and a tactile sensory dysfunction checklist covering hypersensitivity, hyposensitivity, and poor tactile perception and discrimination.
requirements: More developed, valid, and reliable measurements are required, per the review's conclusion
constraints: Most published studies rely on parent reports, and parents of these children often suffer from psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety, which may impact their reports
target_learning_goals: identifying sensory processing problems to guide management and educational support
examples: The 11 reviewed studies all used questionnaire or parent-reported measures, including the Short Sensory Profile and the Sensory Over-Responsivity Inventory
key_sources: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89

article_title: Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students
citation: Donald E Grant Jr. & Jerell B. Hill. (2020). Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students. Journal of Education and Learning, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v9n5p45
title: Self-determination theory: goal-driven behavior resting on competence, autonomy, and relatedness
description: The article describes self-determination theory as aimed at explaining an individual's goal-driven behaviors, incorporating four motivational valences (intrinsic, introjected, extrinsic, and identified). The theory rests on a foundation of three psychological needs thought to be universal and instinctive: competence, the belief that one has the skills and tools to perform well; autonomy, the belief that one acts out of one's own volition; and relatedness, the belief that shared experience can support meaningful relationships. The article also cites its model in which school engagement mediates the influence of autonomy and belongingness on academic and psychological outcomes.
requirements: School-based autonomy and belongingness are emphasized as important to academic achievement and psychological adjustment.
constraints: The article notes the mediation model had only been evaluated on academic outcomes to date (Van Ryzin, Gravely, & Roseth, 2009).
examples: The article uses the four motivational types (intrinsic, introjected, extrinsic, identified) in Table 1 to frame its discussion.
key_sources: Donald E Grant Jr. & Jerell B. Hill. (2020). Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students. Journal of Education and Learning, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v9n5p45

article_title: The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective
citation: Stevens, Courtney; Bavelier, Daphné. (2012). The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective. Developmental cognitive neuroscience, vol. 2S, p. S30–S48. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2011.11.001
title: Target selective attention skills in education because they are relevant to academic foundations and amenable to training
description: The article proposes that selective attention deserves an important place in education because it both matters for early academic skills and can plausibly be improved. The abstract states: "To the extent that selective attention skills are relevant for academic foundations and amenable to training, they represent an important focus for the field of education." The review develops this principle through its sections on neural bases, development, academic domains, and training.
requirements: Evidence that selective attention is relevant to academic foundations and that it is amenable to training
constraints: The principle is conditional: it holds to the extent that both relevance and trainability are established
target_learning_goals: selective attention skills supporting language, literacy, and mathematics foundations
examples: The review's final section examines applying these principles to educationally-focused attention-training programs for children
key_sources: Stevens, Courtney; Bavelier, Daphné. (2012). The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective. Developmental cognitive neuroscience, vol. 2S, p. S30–S48. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2011.11.001

article_title: A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions.
citation: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://www.create.usu.edu
title: Seven design constituents for pedagogical agents as learning companions
description: The article proposes seven design constituents for instructional PALs drawn from the social-cognitive framework: "(a) competency, (b) interaction type, (c) gender, (d) affect, (e) ethnicity, (f) multiplicity, and (g) feedback." Each constituent is traced to supporting theoretical concepts—for example, distributed cognition suggests competency, interaction type, multiplicity, and feedback, while Bandura's theory suggests gender, ethnicity, and multiplicity. The pattern serves as a design checklist for specifying PAL characteristics in computer-based learning environments.
requirements: Designers should consider learner characteristics such as "competency, age, learning styles" when determining optimal PAL-learner interaction.
Effective PAL feedback should consider feedback type, scope, timing, learner characteristics, and learning goals and contexts simultaneously.
constraints: The constituents are explicitly "not comprehensive" and the literature review is described as modest.
Research on some constituents (ethnicity, feedback) is lacking, and suggestions for optimal design are sometimes contradictory.
target_learners: Learners using computer-based learning environments with simulated peer agents
target_learning_goals: Designing PAL characteristics to support learning, motivation, and social interaction
examples: Table 4 of the article maps each constituent to research variables and outcomes, e.g., low-competent PALs enhancing self-efficacy and proactive PALs enhancing recall.
key_sources: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-0637-3

article_title: A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment
citation: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844
title: Design peer assessment marking criteria to separate objective grading criteria from students' subjective opinions
description: The review reports that making an explicit split between objective grading criteria and personal opinion improves review quality. Kali and Ronen (2005) introduced a fourth, non-graded criterion for students' own opinions, and the review states that "an explicit distinction between objective and subjective criteria improves the quality of the review." Students like expressing a subjective view that does not affect grading, and the distinction improves correlation between student and instructor marks.
requirements: The tool must support a rubric with both graded criteria and a separate non-graded opinion field
constraints: Evidence comes from one undergraduate educational philosophy course using the CeLS system
target_learning_goals: distinguishing objective evaluation from personal opinion
examples: In CeLS, a fourth criterion was introduced to allow students to write their own opinion, which was not considered to be a grading criterion
key_sources: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844

article_title: Synthesizing frameworks of higher education student learning outcomes
citation: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher
title: Seven critical domains synthesize higher education student learning outcome frameworks
description: The report reviews seven higher education outcome frameworks and synthesizes them into seven common domains: creativity, critical thinking, teamwork, communication, digital and information literacy, citizenship, and life skills. Domains were retained only when included in a majority of frameworks: "determining those factors that were included in a majority (at least four of seven) of the frameworks reviewed". Each domain is defined by operational outcomes drawn from the source frameworks.
requirements: Frameworks must target bachelor's-level higher education, span disciplines and institutions, and provide operational definitions of the knowledge, skills, and abilities they name
constraints: The synthesis reflects only the seven frameworks reviewed; domains absent from a majority, such as quantitative skills, were excluded even if considered important
examples: Table 2 summarizes the seven domains and maps each to ETS products such as the ETS Proficiency Profile, Criterion, TOEFL/TOEIC, iSkills, and the Personal Potential Index
key_sources: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher

article_title: Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety
citation: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230
title: Self-regulated learning theory as a framework for textbook reading at the university level
description: The article frames textbook reading as a highly autonomous, cognitive and effortful activity governed by self-regulated learning theory. Self-regulated learning is defined as "an active, constructive process whereby learners set goals for their learning and then attempt to monitor, regulate, and control their cognition, motivation, and behavior". The framework comprises two strategies (self-regulation and cognitive strategy use) and two motivational factors (self-efficacy and intrinsic value), which the study measured with the MSLQ and used to test whether textbook format influences strategy use.
requirements: Motivation to read and employment of cognitive strategies while reading are treated as highly autonomous aspects of university-level learning, so learners must self-direct their textbook reading
constraints: The article notes research on e-textbook influence on the academic process is in its infancy and needed prior to widespread adoption
target_learners: university students reading course textbooks in face-to-face or online courses
examples: The study operationalized the framework with five MSLQ subscales (text anxiety, cognitive strategy use, self-regulation, self-efficacy, intrinsic value), each with Cronbach's alpha above .70
key_sources: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230

article_title: Self-efficacy, motivation, and performance
citation: Schunk, D. H. (1995). Self-efficacy, motivation, and performance. Journal of Applied Sport Psychology, 7(2), 112-137. http://www.taylorandfrancis.com/
title: Self-efficacy theory: beliefs about capability shape choice, effort, persistence, and achievement
description: The article presents Bandura's self-efficacy framework, defining self-efficacy as "People's judgments of their capabilities to organize and execute courses of action required to attain designated types of performances."
