People appraise efficacy from performances, vicarious experiences, persuasion, and physiological reactions. A model (Figure 1) depicts initial efficacy deriving from prior experience, personal qualities, and social support, with task-derived cues feeding back to sustain efficacy and motivation.
requirements: Efficacy information acquired vicariously or persuasively requires validation by actual performance to remain credible
constraints: High self-efficacy will not produce a competent performance when requisite knowledge and skill are lacking
Self-efficacy and outcome expectancies are related but distinct constructs with no automatic relation
examples: The article reviews interventions using models, goal setting, and feedback as levers for raising self-efficacy across cognitive and sport tasks
key_sources: Schunk, D. H. (1995). Self-efficacy, motivation, and performance. Journal of Applied Sport Psychology, 7(2), 112-137. http://www.taylorandfrancis.com/

article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: Consider learners' sensory preference together with presentation modality when designing APA lessons
description: The paper proposes that sensory preference be considered an important student characteristic taken into account together with other instructional factors when designing an APA-based lesson. Because most people are brought up using sight more than hearing, and training produces proficiency in one modality, effective APA learning cannot rely on good presentation principles alone; the presentational modality must match coherently with the learner's characteristics. The review cites reports that about 60% of people are visual learners and that about 70% of learners learn well in any given modality.
requirements: The presentational modality must match coherently with the learner's characteristics, like a classroom teacher adopting a style that appeals to students' background
constraints: The review notes research did not discern whether sensory channels are trainable to handle one modality better than the other
target_learners: learners with differing visual and auditory proficiencies
target_learning_goals: balanced visual-auditory interaction in multimedia learning
examples: The review cites the typist shadowing experiment (via Low & Sweller 2005) showing attention for a task depends on familiarization and experience with that task
key_sources: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x

article_title: First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction
citation: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003
title: Working model of self-regulation supporting academic growth through teacher practices
description: The article proposes a working model in which self-regulation, defined as "the deliberate modulation of one's responses to stimuli", enables students to focus cognitive resources on learning tasks, ignore distractions, and maximize learning time, thereby producing more efficient literacy learning. Key to the model is the assumption that teacher practices — planning, classroom management, use of routines, and opportunities to work independently and with peers — support the development of stronger self-regulation and hence stronger academic skills. The ISI intervention was designed to test this model (Fig. 1).
requirements: Teachers must be trained in planning, organizing, and classroom management strategies, and provide opportunities for students to practice managing their own behavior
constraints: The evidence for teacher practices contributing to self-regulation was largely correlational prior to this study; the self-regulation effect was evident only for students with initially weak self-regulation
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills including reading comprehension and vocabulary
examples: The ISI intervention operationalized the model through professional development on organizing, minimizing non-instructional time, and planning, delivered via the A2i software
key_sources: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Self-efficacy theory: three dimensions (magnitude, strength, generality) grounded in social learning and outcome expectation
description: Drawing on Bandura, the article describes self-efficacy as a person's belief in their capability to perform specific tasks, consisting of three dimensions: Magnitude (level of task difficulty believed attainable), Strength (confidence in attaining that level), and Generality (degree of generalization across situations). Self-efficacy is context-specific and researchers should capture both magnitude and strength when measuring it. The article applies this to computer self-efficacy in LMS use.
requirements: Measurement should capture both the magnitude and strength dimensions of self-efficacy
constraints: Self-efficacy is context specific, so measures must be tied to the specific technology or task domain
target_learning_goals: understanding how self-efficacy beliefs shape technology-based learning behavior
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

article_title: Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes
citation: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884
title: Second-order bi-factor model with LMS latent interactions for parsing unique value-component effects
description: A latent variable modeling approach integrating a second-order model with a bi-factor model, applied via Mplus with the LMS approach (Klein & Moosbrugger, 2000). The model partitions value-item covariance into "a global (general) value factor representing the common variation shared by all 37 value items", ten orthogonal facet factors, and four second-order value components, allowing each component's unique contribution to be tested over and above global value. The LMS approach "corrects for measurement error of latent constructs and provides unbiased estimates of latent interaction effects".
requirements: Multi-item facet measures per value component and latent variable software (Mplus) supporting the LMS approach
constraints: Fit statistics such as CFI and RMSEA are not available for SEM models including latent interactions, so AIC and BIC were used for model comparison
target_learners: secondary school students (German ninth-grade academic-track students)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement, effort, and behavioral engagement as outcomes of motivation
examples: Model SO-B-4V fit the data better (CFI = .955; TLI = .949; RMSEA = .039) than the second-order CFA model (Model SO-4V)
key_sources: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884

article_title: Peer victimization (bullying) on mental health, behavioral problems, cognition, and academic performance in preadolescent children in the ABCD Study
citation: Menken, M. S., Isaiah, A., Liang, H., Rivera, P. R., Cloak, C. C., Reeves, G., Lever, N. A., & Chang, L. (2022). Peer victimization (bullying) on mental health, behavioral problems, cognition, and academic performance in preadolescent children in the ABCD Study. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 925727. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.925727
title: Bullying intervention strategies should account for sex-specific effects in preadolescent children
description: The article's findings indicate that bullying affects preadolescent boys and girls differently: boys show greater behavioral problems while girls show greater cognitive impacts. The authors state that "Approaches to prevent bullying and mitigate its negative impact must keep in mind the sex of the youth." This principle calls for differentiated intervention design that addresses the distinct profiles of impact by sex.
requirements: Interventions must be designed for preadolescent children in school settings with awareness of sex-specific vulnerability profiles
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional and cannot establish directionality
Bullying was measured solely by caregiver report
examples: The authors recommend that sex-specific effects of bullying on episodic memory, reading, and vocabulary "should also be noted when designing intervention strategies for preadolescent children in a school setting"
key_sources: Menken, M. S., Isaiah, A., Liang, H., Rivera, P. R., Cloak, C. C., Reeves, G., Lever, N. A., & Chang, L. (2022). Peer victimization (bullying) on mental health, behavioral problems, cognition, and academic performance in preadolescent children in the ABCD Study. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 925727. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.925727

article_title: Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults
citation: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1
title: Self Memory System: autobiographical knowledge stored hierarchically with spreading activation across levels
description: The Self Memory System (Conway, 2005; Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000) proposes that "autobiographical knowledge is stored in a hierarchy," with information accessible as lifetime periods, general events, and specific event memories. Retrieving information at any level results in "spreading activation to related elements," such that accessing one specific memory activates other related specific memories or details within that memory.
requirements: Episodic memory processes are needed to access specific event information at any level of the hierarchy
constraints: The article notes debate about whether fluency deficits reflect purely episodic decline or also executive decline
key_sources: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1

article_title: Effects of Socioeconomic Status (SES) Information on Cognitive Ability Inferences: When Low-SES Students Make Use of a Self-Threatening Stereotype
citation: Isabelle Regner, Pascal Huguet, Jean-Marc Monteil. (2002). Effects of socioEconomic status (SES) information on cognitive ability inferences: When low-SES students make use of a self-threatening stereotype. Social Psychology of Education, 5(3), 253-269. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016313908667
title: The SES stereotype: the belief that low-SES individuals are intellectually inferior to their high-SES counterparts
description: The article defines the SES stereotype as "the belief that the low-SES individuals are intellectually inferior to their high-SES counterparts." It treats this stereotype as a shared social belief that can be activated by social class information or by memory performance information, shaping inferences in either direction between SES and cognitive ability. The two studies use this construct to interpret why low-SES students generate stereotype-consistent inferences about targets.
requirements: Social class or memory performance information about targets must be available to trigger stereotype-based inferences
constraints: The reported evidence concerns students' inferences about targets, not their own intellectual performance
target_learners: students of low and high socioeconomic status
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic stereotypes shape inferences about intellectual ability
examples: Study 1 gave participants social class information about targets and asked for memory-ability inferences; Study 2 gave memory performance information and asked for inferences about possessions and cultural activities as SES indicators.
key_sources: Isabelle Regner, Pascal Huguet, Jean-Marc Monteil. (2002). Effects of socioEconomic status (SES) information on cognitive ability inferences: When low-SES students make use of a self-threatening stereotype. Social Psychology of Education, 5(3), 253-269. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016313908667

article_title: Working Memory for Serial Order Is Dysfunctional in Adults With a History of Developmental Dyscalculia: Evidence From Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data
citation: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993
title: Serial order working memory as a distinct component underlying numerical cognition and vulnerable in dyscalculia
description: The article advances the view that short-term memory for serial order is a distinct working memory component, separable from item-based verbal short-term memory, that supports numerical and alphabetical ordered processing. The authors argue that "a specific dysfunction of short-term memory for serial order in developmental dyscalculia" links the behavioral deficit to reduced left intraparietal activation, positioning this component as functionally related to number processing networks.
requirements: Assessment of serial order recall must be separated from item recall measures to observe the specific deficit
constraints: Evidence concerns adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia; generalization to other populations is not established in this article
target_learners: adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: ordered information processing in working memory
examples: Adults with dyscalculia and controls completed short-term memory tasks distinguishing serial order from item recall, with fMRI recorded during serial order processing
key_sources: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993

article_title: Working Memory for Serial Order Is Dysfunctional in Adults With a History of Developmental Dyscalculia: Evidence From Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data
citation: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993
title: Serial order versus item recall short-term memory task battery with fMRI
description: A task battery contrasting short-term memory for serial order with short-term memory for item information, administered behaviorally and inside the fMRI scanner to adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia and matched controls. The design allows the article to report that participants "were impaired for serial order recall but not for item recall", and to localize serial order processing to left intraparietal cortex.
requirements: Tasks must separately probe serial order and item information to yield the dissociation
constraints: Administered to adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia and controls; not validated here for other groups
target_learners: adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia
examples: Behavioral serial order and item recall tasks paired with fMRI sessions in the same adult participants
key_sources: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993

article_title: Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience
citation: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x
title: Sensitive period for auditory access supporting early spoken word learning begins to close during the first 2 years of life
description: The article proposes that a sensitive period for having access to sound in order to develop the ability to associate spoken words to their referents begins to close during the first 2 years of life. The authors state the findings 'are consistent with the possibility that a sensitive period for access to sound in order to develop the ability to associate spoken words to their referents begins to close during the first 2 years of life but that this sensitive period does not finish closing until at least after 5 years of age'. This account explains why very early implantation facilitates word-learning skills while later implantation does not.
requirements: Requires investigation of age at implantation effects on specific language processes rather than general outcome measures alone
constraints: The sensitive period does not finish closing until at least after 5 years of age, so effects are not absolute after age 2
target_learners: Prelingually deaf children receiving cochlear implants before 2 years of age
target_learning_goals: Early spoken word learning (associating word sound patterns to referents)
examples: The study tested whether congenitally deaf children implanted between 6 and 24 months showed an effect of age at implantation on novel word learning
key_sources: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x

article_title: The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students
citation: Clemente Rodríguez-Sabiote, Eva María Olmedo-Moreno and Jorge Expósito-López. (2022). The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101063
title: Serial multiple mediation model (Hayes model 6) linking teamwork, work skills, educational motivation and critical thinking
description: The article specifies an explanatory theoretical model in which teamwork (X) influences critical thinking (Y) through two sequential mediators, work skills (M1) and educational motivation (M2), estimated with Hayes' model 6 in PROCESS. The authors describe it as "a multiple mediational model with two sequential variables" and estimate five regression equations with bootstrapped confidence intervals. It organises the study's hypotheses Ind1, Ind2 and Ind3 and was tested on 1159 Spanish secondary and vocational students.
requirements: A predictor (teamwork), two sequential mediators (work skills, educational motivation) and a criterion (critical thinking) measured on the same students
Bootstrapping in PROCESS to obtain confidence intervals for indirect effects
constraints: Ex post facto and cross-sectional design with a single measurement, so no causal manipulation was performed
Intentional sample of Spanish secondary and vocational students, limiting generalisation beyond that population
target_learners: Secondary school students in Spain, including baccalaureate and vocational training students
examples: The study estimated five regression equations and three indirect effects with 10000 bootstrap samples in PROCESS v3.5.3
key_sources: Clemente Rodríguez-Sabiote, Eva María Olmedo-Moreno and Jorge Expósito-López. (2022). The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101063

article_title: Development of control of attention from different perspectives
citation: Wetzel N (2014) Development of control of attention from different perspectives. Front. Psychol. 5:1000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01000
title: Selective attention as a key function of human information processing that facilitates goal-relevant and inhibits goal-irrelevant processing
description: The editorial frames attention control within an information-processing account: because "The information processing capacity of our brain is limited and we cannot process all incoming stimuli concurrently—we need to select." Selective attention mechanisms "facilitate processing of goal-relevant events and inhibit the processing of goal-irrelevant events." It is described as essential for other cognitive functions like learning, thinking, or memory, and its development is tied to prefrontal maturation and increasing working memory resources.
requirements: A limited processing capacity requiring selection among concurrent stimuli, as the article states
constraints: The framework is presented as an organizing overview of the Research Topic, not as a newly tested model
target_learning_goals: attention control and resistance to distraction
examples: The Research Topic organizes studies of involuntary attention and distraction, emotion effects on attention control and response inhibition, and ADHD-related distractibility
key_sources: Wetzel N (2014) Development of control of attention from different perspectives. Front. Psychol. 5:1000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01000

article_title: The Effect of Self-Efficacy on Visual Discrimination Sensitivity
citation: Zacharopoulos G, Binetti N, Walsh V, Kanai R (2014) The Effect of Self-Efficacy on Visual Discrimination Sensitivity. PLoS ONE 9(10): e109392. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0109392
title: Self-efficacy theory as a social-cognitive account of behavioural change
description: The article adopts Bandura's self-efficacy theory, described as "perhaps the most widely used model of behavioural change", providing "a novel social-cognitive account of how change in behavioral performance change occurs". The theory predicts that behavioural change is a direct function of the individual's beliefs in one's ability to exercise control over that particular behaviour. The study tests whether this account generalises to low-level perceptual skills, which are otherwise considered a relatively stable trait requiring prolonged training to change.
requirements: The theory presupposes sources of efficacy information such as success or failure experiences in the actual performance, which the article calls "the pivotal source of information influencing one's SE".
constraints: The article notes perceptual sensitivity is known to be a relatively stable trait within individuals that cannot easily be changed without prolonged training, making perceptual tasks a demanding test case for the theory.
target_learning_goals: improving task performance through beliefs about one's own competence
examples: The study operationalised the theory by inducing high and low self-efficacy with fake percentile feedback and fictional research findings about ability malleability, then measuring objective perceptual thresholds.
key_sources: Zacharopoulos G, Binetti N, Walsh V, Kanai R (2014) The Effect of Self-Efficacy on Visual Discrimination Sensitivity. PLoS ONE 9(10): e109392. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0109392

article_title: Moderating effects of executive functions and the teacher–child relationship on the development of mathematics ability in kindergarten
citation: Blair, Clancy; McKinnon, Rachel D.; the Family Life Project Investigators. (2016). Moderating effects of executive functions and the teacher–child relationship on the development of mathematics ability in kindergarten. Learning and Instruction, 41, 85–93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.001
title: Promote early school progress for children in poverty through approaches that focus on self-regulation and social competence, since these can compensate for weak academic preparedness
description: The article proposes that strength in one school-readiness domain can offset weakness in another: children entering kindergarten with low measured academic ability made greater-than-expected math gains when they had higher executive function or a more positive teacher relationship. It concludes that "innovative approaches to promoting early school progress that focus on self-regulation and social competence" are warranted, citing experimental programs such as the Chicago School Readiness Project and Tools of the Mind as consistent with this view.
requirements: Assessment of children's early academic ability to identify those with low preschool math preparedness who are most likely to benefit
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and cannot be interpreted as causal
Moderation was observed in a predominantly low-income rural sample and at the lower end of the preschool math distribution; generalization across SES remains untested
The moderation appeared on the ECLS-K Math battery but not the Applied Problems subtest
target_learners: Kindergarten children from low-income families with low preschool academic preparedness
examples: The study followed 1005 children from predominantly low-income rural communities and found that for children with low preschool ECLS-K Math scores, higher executive function or a more positive kindergarten teacher relationship was associated with higher-than-expected kindergarten math ability
key_sources: Blair, Clancy; McKinnon, Rachel D.; the Family Life Project Investigators. (2016). Moderating effects of executive functions and the teacher–child relationship on the development of mathematics ability in kindergarten. Learning and Instruction, 41, 85–93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.001

article_title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Regulation and Achievement in Third-Grade Students
citation: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367
title: Self-regulation as coordinated executive functioning: working memory, attentional flexibility, and inhibitory control
description: The article defines self-regulation as an active process of controlling behavior, cognition, motivation, and emotions, supported by three executive functions. The authors state: "We define self-regulation as being supported by executive functioning, specifically working memory, inhibitory control, and attentional flexibility." The RRRP was designed to rely on the coordinated regulation of all three functions, rather than measuring them independently, on the conjecture that coordination matters most for school success.
requirements: Measures must capture the coordination of the three functions rather than each in isolation
constraints: The article notes prior measures typically assessed the three skills independently of one another
target_learners: elementary school children, particularly middle elementary grades
target_learning_goals: understanding how self-regulation supports academic achievement in reading and mathematics
examples: The RRRP requires children to remember block colors, objects, and order (working memory), wait for 'go' (inhibitory control), and switch colors in Part 2, coordinating all three
key_sources: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367

article_title: Sensori‐motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain
citation: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x
title: Sensori-motor (embodied) account of functional specialization for letters
description: The article proposes that functional specialization for letters in the developing visual system emerges from sensori-motor experience: perceptual processes "are not encapsulated modules, but instead receive feedback from sensori-motor networks, the strength of which is based on previous experience with the class of stimulus." Writing letters stores sensori-motor associations that are re-activated during visual perception and strengthen visual association cortex responses. The fMRI results — increased letter activation after printing but not visual-only training — are presented as the first evidence that functional specialization emerges from this perceptual-motor coupling in the developing brain.
requirements: Learning must involve integrated sensory and motor activity with the stimulus class, not mere exposure
constraints: The study did not exhaustively test all possible associations; visual-only practice also involved an oral motor response, so results may reflect manual versus oral motor association differences
An attentional-difference alternative explanation is acknowledged and under investigation
target_learning_goals: letter recognition and the neural specialization supporting early literacy
examples: Adults who learned pseudo-letters by writing developed fusiform specialization for them, while visually trained adults did not (James & Atwood, 2009, as cited in the article)
key_sources: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x

article_title: The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders’ Multiplication Fact Ability
citation: Schleepen TMJ, Van Mier HI, De Smedt B (2016) The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders' Multiplication Fact Ability. PLoS ONE 11(6): e0158335. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0158335
title: Semantic-coding account: multiplication facts are stored as phonological/verbal codes in an interrelated semantic network, and symbolic magnitude comparison shares semantic mapping processes with fact retrieval
description: The article proposes that multiplication facts are stored in long-term memory as phonological (verbal) codes within a meaningfully organized, interrelated network of arithmetic facts. It argues that "magnitude" is a candidate dimension along which meaning is assigned to stored facts, so faster magnitude comparators can more easily access number-semantic fact representations. It further hypothesizes that symbolic magnitude comparison and multiplication fact retrieval "share the same semantic mapping processes", supported by cited neuroimaging work showing overlapping left temporo-parietal activation.
requirements: Multiplication facts must have been practiced enough that problem-answer pair associations are stored in long-term memory
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation, supported by cited prior work rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: elementary school children learning single-digit multiplication tables
examples: The study tested this account by correlating symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitude comparison speed with multiplication fact speed in 63 fourth graders
key_sources: Schleepen TMJ, Van Mier HI, De Smedt B (2016) The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders' Multiplication Fact Ability. PLoS ONE 11(6): e0158335. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0158335

article_title: Sight word acquisition in first grade students at risk for reading disabilities: an item-level exploration of the number of exposures required for mastery
citation: Steacy LM, Fuchs D, Gilbert JK, Kearns DM, Elleman AM, Edwards AA. (2020). Sight Word Acquisition in First Grade Students At-Risk for Reading Disabilities: An Item-Level Exploration of the Number of Exposures Required for Mastery. Annals of Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11881-020-00198-7
title: Lexical-feedback account: poor readers rely on the semantic processor when mapping orthography to phonology
description: The article interprets its findings within connectionist models of word reading (e.g., the triangle model), in which lexical feedback from semantics assists mapping between orthographic and phonological forms. It proposes that when sub-lexical mapping is difficult, "meaning is particularly important," and that "students with RD are relying heavily on the semantic processor in word learning efficiency." This explains why imageability and vocabulary grade mattered most for the poorest readers.
requirements: Applicable to word learning contexts where orthographic-phonological mapping is difficult, such as irregular or less decodable words
constraints: The authors state they do not have the correct data to make causal inferences about this relationship
target_learners: First grade students at risk for reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: Efficient acquisition of word-specific orthographic representations for high-frequency words
examples: The authors interpret the significant imageability and vocabulary-grade interactions as evidence that poor readers use semantic feedback to clean up mismatches between phonology and orthography

Sight Word Acquisition in First Grade Students At-Risk for Reading Disabilities: An Item-Level Exploration of the Number of Exposures Required for Mastery. Annals of Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11881-020-00198-7

article_title: Math Anxiety in Second and Third Graders and Its Relation to Mathematics Achievement
citation: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162
title: Scale for Early Mathematics Anxiety (SEMA), a 20-item math anxiety measure for second and third graders
description: The SEMA is a 20-item questionnaire the authors developed to assess math anxiety in second and third graders, modeled on the MARS and MARS-E. Its first 10 items assess anxiety about grade-appropriate math problems (number sense, basic functions, measurement, geometry, mathematical reasoning) and the last 10 assess anxiety in social and testing situations. Children rate each item on a five-point scale using graded anxious and non-anxious faces, administered one-on-one with items read aloud. The authors are making SEMA freely available to researchers.
requirements: Items must remain equally representative of second and third grade curriculum to avoid confounding by differential exposure
constraints: The authors note continued development and evaluation with larger samples is needed to further validate and standardize SEMA
target_learners: second and third graders (7- to 9-year-old children)
target_learning_goals: assessment of mathematics anxiety in early elementary school
examples: In the study, 162 children completed the SEMA individually; the mean SEMA score was 34.35 (SD = 11.60) with Cronbach's alpha of 0.870
key_sources: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162

article_title: Math Anxiety in Second and Third Graders and Its Relation to Mathematics Achievement
citation: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162
title: Two-factor structure of early math anxiety: Numerical Processing Anxiety and Situational and Performance Anxiety
description: Exploratory factor analysis of the SEMA confirmed a two-factor structure replicating the MARS and MARS-E. One factor, Numerical Processing Anxiety, captures anxiety about numerical concepts and loaded seven items (e.g., checking whether 9 + 7 = 18 is right); the other, Situational and Performance Anxiety, captures anxiety about situations involving the execution of math and loaded eight items (e.g., doing a math problem on the board in class). The two factors correlated 0.529 (p < 0.001) and had Cronbach's alphas of 0.802 and 0.770 respectively.
requirements: Items loading at least 0.50 on one factor and no greater than 0.40 on the other, per the authors' extraction criteria
constraints: The authors note future studies should explore including additional items related to test, as opposed to performance, anxiety in third and possibly second graders
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of math anxiety in early elementary learners
examples: Principal components analysis with varimax rotation accounted for 29.73% and 8.56% of variance in the first and second factors respectively
key_sources: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162

article_title: Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn
citation: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4
title: Seven trialogue designs for two-agent conversations with a human learner, adaptively administered by learner knowledge
description: Trialogues involve a human interacting with two agents, typically a tutor agent and a student peer agent. Graesser et al. (2015b) identified seven designs: (1) vicarious learning with human observer; (2) vicarious learning with limited human participation via yes/no or single-word prompts; (3) tutor agent interacting with human and student agent; (4) expert agent staging a competition between human and peer agent; (5) human teaches a student agent with tutor facilitation; (6) human interacts with two peer agents varying in proficiency; and (7) human interacts with two agents expressing contradictions or different views. The two agents can model good questions and answers or stage arguments that create cognitive disequilibrium, productive confusion, and deeper learning. The student agent can also fill in missing words when the human's answer is incomplete, circumventing negative short feedback.
requirements: Two agents that can take on different roles, typically one tutor and one student peer, with conversation mechanisms adaptive and flexible like AutoTutor
constraints: The article states research needs to be conducted to assess empirically the conditions under which different trialogue designs facilitate learning and motivation
target_learners: more capable students attempting deeper knowledge (designs 5 and 7)
target_learning_goals: modeling good answers and reasoning, deeper learning through cognitive disequilibrium and productive confusion, motivation through game competition
examples: Trialogues are routinely incorporated in recent AutoTutor applications such as Operation ARIES/ARA for scientific reasoning, iSTART for reading comprehension, CSAL reading interventions for adults, and ETS assessment using ASAT and ACE.
key_sources: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4

article_title: Collaboration scripts and scaffolding
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1
title: Three-cluster taxonomy of seven discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussion
description: Fu, van Aalst, and Chan classify discourse in asynchronous online discussions using a coding scheme with dimensions such as agency, community, idea, information, linking, meta-discourse, and questions. The editors state "The authors identify seven discourse patterns within three modes of discourse. These discourse patterns can be divided into three clusters": knowledge sharing (disputational talk), knowledge construction (explanatory and problem-centered inquiry, complex argumentation), and knowledge building (progressive inquiry, sustained discourse and community advancement). The taxonomy shows not all patterns are equally productive for learning.
requirements: Coding via thematic analysis, qualitative coding, and narrative analysis using the multi-dimensional scheme
constraints: Not all discourse patterns are equally productive for learning
target_learners: students in asynchronous online discussion settings
target_learning_goals: advancing understanding and participation toward an epistemic orientation
examples: Teachers aware of different discourse patterns can scaffold students toward an epistemic orientation when planning work across subjects
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rosé, & Gerry Stahl. (2016). Collaboration scripts and scaffolding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9247-1

article_title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
citation: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7
title: Network-driven and person-driven selection patterns in the initiation of scientific collaborations
description: The article organizes the onset of collaboration around three types of selection of new collaboration partners: face-to-face contact opportunity, network-driven patterns, and person-driven patterns. Network-driven patterns rest on the assumption that "the way in which persons choose relations is strongly influenced by the (local) structure of their social network", making easily accessible network partners more likely, via reciprocity and transitivity. Person-driven patterns are preferences for specific others, studied as homophily (seeking similar others) versus heterophilous selection, with heterophily linked by social capital theory to gaining new resources such as complementary expertise.
requirements: Selecting suitable partners requires cognitive and social group awareness of other community members' personal and social resources.
constraints: Network-driven selection patterns benefit participants with many existing contacts most; newcomers with few previous contacts can benefit much less, and the article notes these mechanisms had only been shown previously in friendship and small-group contexts, not for collaboration onset.
target_learners: Researchers in interdisciplinary scientific communities, especially newcomers
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting how researchers select collaboration partners at scientific events
examples: The framework structured the analysis: effects implemented in RSiena as reciprocity, transitivity, ego/alter/homophily effects for career level and discipline, and contact duration.
key_sources: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7

article_title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9
title: Self-regulation as a meta-level mechanism reconfiguring internal collaboration scripts and grounded in group awareness
description: The article proposes an integrative account: metacognitive knowledge about learning processes "is used to reconfigure the currently activated internal script" by activating components from other scripts or integrating newly acquired ones. Group awareness is inherently linked to regulation because self-regulation requires monitoring internal and external conditions, which in collaboration includes social conditions. External scripts can scaffold self-, co-, and shared regulation.
requirements: Learners need self-regulation skills to monitor internal and external conditions, set goals, apply strategies, evaluate success, and adapt strategies against internal standards
constraints: Learners often lack the level of self-regulation skills demanded by social learning scenarios; explicit empirical and theoretical connections among all three concepts remain scarce
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, evaluation and adaptation of individual and social learning
examples: Group awareness tools build on self-regulated learning mechanisms by providing information without prescribing activities, relying on learners' skills to use the information
key_sources: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9

article_title: Linguistic demands of instructions: Effects on students’ expectancy-value beliefs
citation: Lina Wirth, Timo Ehmke, Jan Retelsdorf, Poldi Kuhl. (2026). Linguistic demands of instructions: Effects on students’ expectancy-value beliefs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09799-y
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) as a framework for treating linguistic demands as task difficulty shaping motivational beliefs
description: The article uses SEVT to argue that linguistic demands in educational contexts can be conceptualized as a form of task difficulty: "students who encounter task difficulties due to linguistic demands … may have lower expectancy and value beliefs, resulting in a lack of motivation to actively engage in these tasks". SEVT holds that expectancies of success and task value are shaped in the moment by contextual features such as task difficulty, and that the interaction between contextual and individual features is crucial, with difficulty needing to match individual abilities to promote adaptive motivation. The study operationalized this by experimentally varying linguistic difficulty and testing its main and moderated effects plus mediation into achievement.
requirements: Applied to contexts where linguistic features of instructions vary in difficulty and can be experimentally manipulated
constraints: In this study the framework's fit prediction was only partly supported; expectancies were not fostered by a good fit between demands and abilities
target_learning_goals: achievement motivation and engagement in academic tasks
examples: The study drew on SEVT to derive four hypotheses about linguistic conditions, language abilities, and expectancy-value beliefs measured mid-video.
key_sources: Lina Wirth, Timo Ehmke, Jan Retelsdorf, Poldi Kuhl. (2026). Linguistic demands of instructions: Effects on students’ expectancy-value beliefs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09799-y

article_title: Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students
citation: Jaeseo Lim and Jooyong Park (2026). Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students. Instructional Science (2026) 54:56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09801-7
title: Self-study and discussion model: preparatory self-study enhances learning by transforming the quality of subsequent peer discussion
description: The model, proposed by Lim and Park (2023) and extended here to high school students, holds that self-study supports individual cognitive construction while peer discussion facilitates the social construction of knowledge. The article argues its effectiveness "lies in how preparation transforms the quality of peer interaction rather than in activity level alone": self-study functions as a constructive activity that activates and reorganizes prior knowledge, enabling more substantive and co-constructive dialogue. Interpreted through the ICAP framework, discussion primarily activates and elaborates knowledge, whereas preparatory self-study establishes stable knowledge representations that persist over time.
requirements: Self-study must precede peer discussion; the article reports prior work found no difference between self-study and lecture when not followed by discussion
constraints: Prior studies were conducted with high-achieving college students; the mediating role of substantive comments did not extend to long-term outcomes in this study
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of conceptual knowledge
examples: Seventy-three grade-12 students studied a seven-page criminal procedure text or watched an 18-minute video lecture, then discussed in triads for 15 minutes with no prompts, scripts, or guiding questions
key_sources: Jaeseo Lim and Jooyong Park (2026). Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students. Instructional Science (2026) 54:56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09801-7

article_title: Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students
citation: Jaeseo Lim and Jooyong Park (2026). Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students. Instructional Science (2026) 54:56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09801-7
title: When incorporating peer discussion into instruction, precede it with structured individual self-study rather than lecture-based preparation
description: The article recommends that, when peer discussion is used, students first engage in individual preparation: "allowing students to engage in self-study enables them to activate prior knowledge and set clear learning goals, thereby fostering deeper and more meaningful discussions." It further suggests encouraging individual preparation prior to class while allocating more time for discussion during instruction. The recommendation rests on the randomized experiment showing outcome and dialogue-quality advantages for self-study-prepared discussion, including at one-week delay.
requirements: A preparatory individual learning phase before discussion
Discussion time allocated after preparation
Instructional materials equivalent across preparation formats
constraints: The mediating role of substantive comments did not extend to delayed learning; discussion should not be regarded as universally superior to other active learning formats such as retrieval practice
examples: Students studied written materials independently for 18 minutes (or watched an 18-minute video lecture), then engaged in a 15-minute unscripted triad discussion, with tests immediately and one week later
key_sources: Jaeseo Lim and Jooyong Park (2026). Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students. Instructional Science (2026) 54:56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09801-7

article_title: The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation
citation: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7
title: For novices facing complex, high-intrinsic-load material, prefer sequential text-plus-equation formats over tree diagrams
description: The article argues that format decisions are most critical for learners with little or no prior knowledge dealing with complex material. For combinatorics, where problem solving requires reasoning steps in a specific order, the Text + Arithmetic format "preserves the strictly sequential nature of problem solving in this domain": learners are led step-by-step through an explicit, sequential line of reasoning in everyday language, followed by an equation repeating these steps arithmetically. Tree diagrams, whose reasoning steps are implicit and require advanced diagram knowledge, are better suited to learners who already possess the relevant schemata.
requirements: Material in which problem solving requires a set of reasoning steps taken in a specific order; the text and equation components should be informationally equivalent to alternatives
constraints: The finding comes from one study with secondary pupils in one domain; the authors note the advantage of a particular format is not universal but depends on task nature, student ability, prior knowledge, and practice time
target_learners: secondary school students with little or no prior knowledge of the domain
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge: executing action sequences to solve combinatorial problems
examples: In the experiment, pupils in the Text + Arithmetic condition read textual reasoning followed by an equation in each of five simulation sections, and outperformed the Diagram condition on procedural post-test items
key_sources: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Selective horizons model of technological mediation in laboratory inquiry
description: The article proposes a simplified model (Fig. 1) of the reductions of horizons in human inquiry using experimental technologies, in which "Amplifications & reductions, revelations & concealments, and enablements & constraints are involved in each step of the subject matter—object of study—tools for measuring and collecting data—tools for processing and (re-)presenting data chain". Mediating technologies are not neutral transmitters of information; they strongly influence figure–background relationships in experience. Human foci can be shifted through educational interventions, and what a student actually perceives depends on instructional features such as scaffolding.
requirements: Consideration of the limitations of human perception alongside the affordances of the technology
Scaffolding from the teacher and instructions to shift what students actually perceive
constraints: The categorizations in the model are solely for analytical purposes; in a real case there are no sharp boundaries between the steps
target_learners: students in science and engineering laboratories
target_learning_goals: experiencing physical phenomena through mediating technologies
examples: The model is illustrated with Galileo's telescope, which amplified perception of faint stars while reducing the visual field (magnification–reduction and revealing–concealing structures)
key_sources: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: Use semiempty (moderately-directed) concept maps rather than fully student-generated maps to scaffold collaborative reasoning
description: The article argues that semiempty concept maps, which provide predetermined concepts with a limited number of blank squares to complete, scaffold collaboration by reducing cognitive cost. The authors chose them because "the research showed positive outcomes of semiempty concept maps", and the discussion states that "completing a semiempty concept map might have provided scaffolding that freed up sufficient cognitive resources to enable reasoning about the relationships between ideas". In their tasks, the incomplete map focused students on key components of historical reasoning such as causes, intentions and contexts.
requirements: Predetermined nodes must target key relations of the content; students need a training session and an individual preparation phase before collaboration
constraints: The article cautions that concept maps have no practiced reading order and impose low-level decision-making load when students are not used to working with them
target_learners: secondary education students unfamiliar with concept mapping
examples: Tasks used 3 semiempty concept maps with 19, 8 and 7 predetermined concepts and 12, 9 and 9 empty squares, completed by dyads after reading textbook texts on 19th-century Western imperialism
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams
citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Seven design principles underpinning the design of a hybrid learning configuration
description: Generated in an educational design research project over six one-semester iterations of the 'Value in the Valley' HLC, the set comprises seven principles: fostering authenticity, inter-linking of working and learning, utilizing diversity, facilitating reflexivity, creating a learning community, enabling organization, and enabling ecology. For example, fostering authenticity means the "Working/learning environment (context, tasks, activities, roles, and communication) reflects working practice, a professional working culture and organization". The principles are abstract meta-principles that designers adapt to their context.
requirements: Designers must creatively develop context-specific features for each principle, since the principles do not prescribe how an intervention should be designed
constraints: Derived from a single case study; the authors note transposing them to another context might be considered problematic, though participants almost unanimously affirmed relevance and completeness
target_learners: students and staff in senior secondary vocational and higher education working on authentic assignments for external clients
target_learning_goals: integrating working and learning around ill-defined authentic tasks requiring transboundary, multidisciplinary learning
examples: In Value in the Valley, students collaborated in multidisciplinary teams on assignments such as a sustainability strategy for villages and rainwater storage ideas for Groningen
key_sources: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5

article_title: Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals
citation: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4
title: Seven facilitation strategies for responding to teacher emotional displays in PD discourse
description: The article identifies and defines seven facilitation strategies with their key moves: ignoring the emotion, quick transition from emotion to practice, acknowledging the emotion to prevent further discussing it, mitigating and normalizing the emotion, exploring the emotion's role in a problem of practice, normalizing and problematizing the emotion, and exploring alternative responses to the emotion. Each strategy is defined by "the discursive objectives the facilitator promotes vis-à-vis the emotion" and operationalized through specific moves such as redirecting, relabeling, revoicing, and reframing. The classification is intended to help facilitators develop awareness of their discourse patterns and open up new response possibilities.
requirements: Facilitators who lead PD groups and moderate discussions where emotions arise
constraints: Strategies were identified in one problem-based PD science program; the authors note the classification offers a repertoire rather than a manual of best practices
target_learners: PD facilitators working with in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Managing emotional and relational dynamics in collaborative teacher learning discourse
examples: Ignoring the emotion: redirecting the discussion without referring to the emotion; Exploring the emotion's role: pressing to examine the emotional dimension by contrasting what teachers know with what they do
key_sources: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4
grain_size: lesson-level discursive moves within PD sessions

article_title: Reciprocal interactions between teachers’ instructional moves and students’ social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions
citation: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7
title: Seven-category teacher instructional move coding scheme for collaborative small-group discussions
description: The study adapted a coding scheme from Lin et al. (2015) classifying teacher talk into "seven research-informed teachers' instructional moves: high level prompting, low level prompting, modeling, specific praise, nonspecific praise, management, information provision," each with subcategories. High-level prompting asks for logical reasoning and perspective taking (e.g., reasons/evidence); low-level prompting asks for clarification, definitions, or repetition; modeling demonstrates good reasoning; specific praise reinforces particular cognitive or social strategy use; management regulates cognitive, participatory, and behavioral issues; information provision supplies facts or clarifications. Inter-coder reliability was Cohen's K = 0.72–0.74.
requirements: Two trained coders with reliability checks on 20% of transcripts and discussion to 100% agreement on ambiguous moves
constraints: The authors note the list of moves "is far from comprehensive"; moves were coded in a peer-led small-group context rather than teacher-centered whole-class instruction
target_learning_goals: teacher scaffolding of student reasoning and participation
examples: In Week-4 discussions, low-level prompting (221 turns) and high-level prompting (212 turns) were the most frequent moves; specific praise was rare (25 turns)
key_sources: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Select a self-report instrument by matching the strategies and learning task it measures to the measurement aims, not by popularity
description: The article argues that when administering a self-report instrument, practitioners and researchers should first define which learning strategies are to be measured and for which learning tasks, and then check that the chosen instrument actually measures those strategies for a representative task. It warns against simply choosing a popular questionnaire such as the MSLQ or MAI. Standard validity and reliability requirements and generalisability of the measures must also be considered.
requirements: Define the aims of measurement (which strategies, which tasks) before choosing an instrument
Check that the target task is representative of the tasks to which results will be generalised
constraints: Generalisability is an issue for all measuring methods, not only self-report questionnaires
target_learners: school learners whose strategies teachers or researchers assess
target_learning_goals: cognitive, metacognitive and affective learning strategies
examples: The article names MSLQ (Pintrich and De Groot 1990) and MAI (Schraw and Dennison 1994) as popular instruments that should not be selected merely for their popularity
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion
citation: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z
title: Three-level regulation framework distinguishing self-regulation, co-regulation and shared regulation
description: A recently-advanced framework for regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning distinguishes three levels of regulation. The review reports that it "distinguishes between “self-regulation”, “co-regulation”, and “shared regulation” based on how they pertain to different processes such as monitoring, standards, control; self, task and strategy knowledge". Shared regulation emphasizes shared goals and joint understanding of the team as a whole, with regulation occurring at self, member(s) and group levels. The review treats it as a fruitful model for future co-regulation research.
requirements: Analytic schemes and instructional experiments to examine the complex nature of co-regulated learning
constraints: The review states these models of shared and collective regulation need further examination
target_learners: students working in groups in computer-supported collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: regulation of collaborative inquiry and learning
key_sources: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z

article_title: The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion
citation: Veenman, M. V. J. (2007). The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9017-6
title: Self-regulation in computer-based environments requires both valid assessment and targeted instruction, as framed in Veenman's discussion article
description: The article is framed as a discussion of how self-regulation should be assessed and instructed when learning occurs in computer-based environments. Its title states this dual focus: "The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments". The keyword list signals the constructs the discussion organizes around, including "Convergent Validity", "Metacognitive Skill", "Intelligent Tutor System", and "Metacognitive Activity", indicating that measurement quality and intelligent tutoring systems are central concerns of the framework.
requirements: Assessment of metacognitive skill must address convergent validity, as indicated by the article's own keyword "Convergent Validity"
constraints: The piece is a discussion article (its subtitle is "a discussion"), not a report of new empirical data
examples: The article situates its discussion within a literature on self-regulated learning with hypermedia and scientific discovery learning with computer simulations, as shown in its reference list
key_sources: Veenman, M. V. J. (2007). The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9017-6

article_title: Linking teachers’ and students’ motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted?
citation: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory as a framework linking teachers' and students' SRL motivation
description: The article applies Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) to conceptualise both teachers' motivation to promote SRL and students' motivation to use strategies. According to the article, "one's choices, effort, or persistence are influenced by a person's values and expectancies for success", with values specified as intrinsic, attainment and utility value plus perceived costs. SEVT's situated, dynamic character motivates the study's expectation that transmission from teachers to students runs indirectly through instructional behaviour (SRL promotion) rather than directly.
requirements: Motivational constructs (self-efficacy/expectancies, attainment value, utility value, cost) must be measured for both teachers and students to model transmission paths
constraints: The article notes values and expectancies are situated and change over time, so links are not static across classes and situations
target_learning_goals: Students' motivation to apply self-regulated learning strategies
Teachers' motivation to promote self-regulated learning
examples: The study modelled teachers' self-efficacy and attainment value as predictors of SRL promotion, which in turn was modelled as predictor of students' self-efficacy, utility value, attainment value and cost
key_sources: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y

article_title: Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings
citation: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y
title: Self-validation theory: perceived validity of primary cognitions determines whether they guide judgment and action
description: Self-validation theory holds that after a primary cognition forms, people generate second-order thoughts about its validity, and the perceived validity of the primary thought determines the extent to which it is used in judgment and behavior. The article defines metacognitive confidence as "a subjective belief regarding the validity of any primary cognition," independent of accuracy. Unlike accuracy-focused metacognitive research, it identifies sources of validity (e.g., head nodding, ease, recalled confidence episodes) unrelated to correctness. The theory predicts that confidence magnifies whatever valenced thought is accessible, producing opposite performance effects for positive versus negative thoughts.
requirements: Primary cognitions must be accessible and performance-relevant
Perceived validity must be measured or induced following the primary cognition
constraints: Validation processes are more likely when thinking is relatively high and the topic is of high personal relevance
The approach concerns opinion-based thoughts where there is no objectively correct answer, not accuracy judgments
target_learning_goals: academic performance on knowledge tests and standardized assessments
self-relevant beliefs about one's abilities as a student
examples: Study 2 induced validation by framing questionnaire anchors so any answer implied high certainty, and invalidation by framing answers to imply distance from one's thoughts
Study 3 induced validation by asking participants to recall and describe a past episode of feeling confidence in their thoughts
key_sources: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y

article_title: Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts
citation: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7
title: Seven-text climate change reading task with conflicting source documents
description: The reading task comprised seven separate one-page texts about different aspects of climate change: a neutral textbook excerpt plus six texts with partly conflicting information on causes, consequences, and solutions to global warming, drawn from sources including newspapers, a research magazine, a pollution control authority, and an oil company. Readability scores ranged from 41 to 61 with a mean of 47.6, which the authors say "suggesting that the reading material represented a sufficient challenge for the participants and was well suited for eliciting effortful, strategic processing." Source, author, credentials, and date were printed on each text.
requirements: Texts presented in random order; participants instructed to imagine writing a report based on the texts
constraints: Used with Norwegian education undergraduates reading to construct arguments in the subsample condition
examples: Texts included a liberal daily's article on negative consequences of warming and a conservative daily's article on positive consequences
key_sources: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7

article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory account of effort-by-allocation: self-initiated effort as outcome of expectancy and value appraisals
description: Effort-by-allocation refers to the initiation, intensity, and persistence of learning behavior as a direct outcome of momentary motivation. From SEVT, "effort-by-allocation is the out- come of future-directed expectancy and value appraisals concerning a specific task or activity": the more likely a person deems solving a task and the higher its judged incentives, the more willing they are to start and persist. SEVT also considers three motivational costs — effort cost, opportunity cost, and emotional cost — as negative valences weighed before task execution. The article links opportunity cost to motivational interference, where students miss valued leisure when deciding to learn.
requirements: Expectancy and value beliefs need to be high to support learning and effort allocation
constraints: Effort-by-allocation does not refer to task characteristics but to students' self-initiated allocation; metacognitive information alone may not raise it when task values are low
target_learners: students in formal learning settings including homework contexts
target_learning_goals: initiation, intensity, and persistence of effective learning behavior
