examples: The article cites interventions offering compensation to top-50% performers or performance feedback after strategy use as attempts to change expectancy and value beliefs
key_sources: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7

article_title: A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes
citation: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y
title: Multidimensional, activity-specific conceptualization of student engagement (affective, behavioral, cognitive)
description: The review organizes SE as a multifaceted construct comprising affective, behavioral, and cognitive components, always tied to a specific learning activity. It defines affective engagement as "positive (interest, alertness) or negative feelings of activation (tiredness, boredom)", behavioral engagement as "the effort students intentionally exert", and cognitive engagement as the degree to which students concentrate and think strategically. It also notes extensions: social-affective/behavioral/cognitive engagement, agentic engagement, and productive disciplinary engagement, and a dynamic perspective treating SE as changing over time.
requirements: A clear and explicit definition of the term engagement in each study to support conceptual coherence and cumulative understanding
constraints: The review adopts the learning-engagement perspective (active involvement in learning) rather than school engagement, given its undergraduate mathematics focus
target_learning_goals: engagement in mathematics learning activities such as problem-solving, self-study, and lectures
examples: The review used Wong and Liem's (2022) comprehensive definitions to infer the appropriate SE dimension when papers did not align indicators to dimensions
key_sources: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y

article_title: A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes
citation: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y
title: Corpus of 48 peer-selected empirical studies of SE in undergraduate mathematics (2009–2024)
description: The review's evidence base: 48 papers identified via PRISMA-guided searching of SCOPUS, Science Direct, Web of Science, and ERIC in September 2024, screened with PICo-based inclusion criteria and a 7-item quality appraisal checklist adapted from Liu and Khalil (2023). Publication years "ranged from 2009 to 2024", with most (n = 30, 63%) published after 2019; 85% were journal articles. Studies were mainly quantitative (n = 35, 73%) and set in 23 different countries, with first-year students well represented (n = 20).
requirements: Papers must explicitly use the term engagement and state the specific mathematics learning activity in which SE was observed
constraints: Studies referring only to related terms such as participation, involvement, or interest without referencing engagement were excluded
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students across STEM, social sciences/humanities, and business/finance programmes
target_learning_goals: engagement in mathematics subjects including statistics (16 papers), algebra (10), and calculus (10)
examples: Four papers from additional sources supplemented the 1,579 database records; 52 papers passed full-text screening and 48 met quality criteria
key_sources: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y

article_title: Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7
title: Do not treat statistically significant cross-lagged effects with good model fit in observational SEM data as strong evidence of causality
description: The article argues that structural equation models reproduce covariances and correlations, and well-fitting models minimize the difference between reproduced and empirical correlations, but correlations do not prove causality. Statistically significant parameter values in SEMs fitted to observational data do not prove causality, not even if the model has good fit; the question of causality is more about how data were generated than about the structure of overlapping variance.
requirements: Causal questions should be addressed by how data were generated, e.g. observational versus randomized controlled trial designs
constraints: This inability to prove true causal effects from correlations in observational data is stated to be general to all structural equation models
target_learners: researchers analyzing longitudinal observational educational data
target_learning_goals: drawing valid causal inferences about self-concept and achievement relationships
examples: The authors note Núñez-Regueiro et al. partly agree, writing that causal directionality cannot easily be assessed
key_sources: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7

article_title: Socioeconomic Status and Student Learning: Insights from an Umbrella Review
citation: Tan, C. Y. (2024). Socioeconomic Status and Student Learning: Insights from an Umbrella Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09929-3
title: Expanded conceptualization of SES: objective and subjective, individual and collective, capital mobilization, asset-based
description: The umbrella review argues that researchers need to expand the conceptualization of SES from an objective, individual attribute measuring hierarchical differences in access to resources to a construct incorporating "objective and subjective evaluations of individual and collective SES attributes", emphasizing students' mobilization of capital, and adopting a diverse, asset-based perspective. It traces four shifts: adding subjective to objective indicators; recognizing collective attributes (school, neighborhood SES); shifting from access to resources to mobilization of capital (economic, cultural, social); and moving from a hierarchical, deficit perspective to an asset-based one (community cultural wealth).
requirements: Researchers should consider both objective and subjective SES indicators and both individual and collective attributes
constraints: The review notes subjective measures may be invalid due to mood, reference groups, or tendency to identify as middle class
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic status relates to student achievement and learning outcomes
key_sources: Tan, C. Y. (2024). Socioeconomic Status and Student Learning: Insights from an Umbrella Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09929-3

article_title: How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach
citation: Catrysse, L., van Daal, T., Jarodzka, H., Kaakinen, J. K., Donche, V., & Gijbels, D. (2025). How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10000-y
title: Sentence-level social network analysis pipeline for eye-tracking reading data (OSF dataset and scripts)
description: A reusable analytic pipeline in which fixations are filtered (Tobii I-VT), sentence AOIs are classified as topic-introducing, topic-medial or topic-ending, AOI strings are converted to transition matrices, and weighted networks are built in R with igraph to compute strength, betweenness, harmonic centrality and local clustering coefficient. The authors state "The dataset and scripts are available at osf.io (https:// osf. io/ qbctd/)", supporting reuse and replication of the approach.
requirements: Eye-tracking fixation data exportable per AOI; R packages igraph and DirectedClustering for metric computation
constraints: Applied here to three short Dutch expository texts read by 31 participants; generalization to other texts and populations is not demonstrated
target_learning_goals: measuring moment-to-moment integration processes during reading
examples: 31 networks per text were constructed from the eye-tracking data of the reused Catrysse et al. (2018) dataset
key_sources: Catrysse, L., van Daal, T., Jarodzka, H., Kaakinen, J. K., Donche, V., & Gijbels, D. (2025). How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10000-y

article_title: Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools
citation: Castro, C., Barata, M. C., Alexandre, J., & Santos, R. (2026). Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10192-x
title: Integrative model of the social and emotional domain permeating all school climate dimensions
description: The review proposes that the social-emotional domain should not be treated as an additional school climate dimension but as a domain that permeates all dimensions. Relationships, safety, teaching practices and leadership all have inherent social and emotional aspects, operationalized as behavioral, relational, or policy-oriented forms of SEL support that affect students' social and emotional development. The article states the domain "is not to be framed as an additional dimension of school climate, but rather as a domain that permeates all school climate dimensions", illustrated by Figure 4 revisiting the study's conceptual framework.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners measuring school climate should critically assess the extent to which available instruments embed SEL support across dimensions
constraints: The model was developed from a scoping review of measures for upper middle and secondary school settings
target_learners: Upper middle and secondary school students (grades 7-12)
target_learning_goals: Support for students' social and emotional learning within school climate measurement and practice
examples: The review illustrates the model with students collaborating to solve a disagreement, a teacher motivating a struggling student, and a SEL-focused instruction hour led by the principal as part of the curriculum.
key_sources: Castro, C., Barata, M. C., Alexandre, J., & Santos, R. (2026). Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10192-x

article_title: Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review
citation: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736
title: Seven primary team learning behaviours framework used to categorise change
description: The review adopts the framework of seven primary team learning behaviours: knowledge sharing, constructive conflict, co-construction, boundary crossing, team activity, team reflexivity, and storage and retrieval. These are forms of social interaction between team members while accomplishing work tasks, such as "giving feedback, sharing, storing and retrieving knowledge, jointly reflecting on work strategies, and communicating with individuals outside the team". The seven behaviours served as the categories in the narrative synthesis of the included studies.
requirements: Team members who are interdependent regarding task accomplishment, share common goals and interact socially
constraints: The review focuses on single team learning behaviours separately rather than combinations or sequences
target_learners: members of natural work teams in organisations
target_learning_goals: understanding which team learning behaviours change over time and relate to outcomes
examples: The synthesis categorised study variables such as sharing, reflection, boundary spanning, and asking for feedback under these seven behaviours
key_sources: Andreas Widmann, Regina H. Mulder. (2025). Change in team learning behaviours in work teams – A systematic review. Educational Research Review 49. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100736

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Situated expectancy-value theory: expectancies and subjective task value as proximal predictors of achievement choices
description: SEVT is the conceptual framework that initially grounded utility-value interventions. The article states that "SEVT identifies individuals' expectancies of success and subjective task value as the most proximal predictors of students' achievement-related choices." Task value has components including intrinsic value, attainment value, and utility value, with perceived cost also discussed, and value components are combined and weighed relative to perceived cost to predict engagement and persistence.
requirements: The theory presupposes intervening processes between external factors (e.g., culture, parents' beliefs) and students' expectancies and values, including students' perceptions of those factors
constraints: The article notes the model's depiction may suggest external factors matter only as precursors, but Eccles and Wigfield view expectancies and values as enmeshed in and influenced by different levels of environments and cultures
target_learning_goals: achievement-related choices and persistence in coursework
examples: UVIs target the utility value component of SEVT because it has been systematically evaluated through experimental research and randomized control trials in high school and college classes
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Homo Curious: Curious or Interested?
citation: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x
title: Appendix table of self-report measures of situational interest and curiosity
description: The article's appendix compiles sample items from self-report scales used to measure situational interest and curiosity, organized by citation year. It illustrates measurement problems: the review states that "measures of curiosity and situational interest suffer from both jingle ... and jangle ... fallacies," with some interest items actually measuring curiosity and vice versa, and items relying on transparent self-report susceptible to social desirability.
requirements: Triangulating assessment approaches and developing valid measures to capture the two constructs distinctly
constraints: The validity of alternative measures (related constructs, observation, resource spending, fMRI) remains in question per the review
target_learners: Researchers measuring curiosity and interest in learners
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of curiosity versus situational interest
key_sources: Shin, D. D., & Kim, S. (2019). Homo Curious: Curious or Interested? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09497-x

article_title: Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4
title: Seufert's discussion paper models self-regulation as an inverted U-shaped function of task difficulty
description: In the first discussion paper of the special issue, Seufert describes "how self-regulation can be seen as an inverted U-shaped function of task difficulty, with an optimal balance between resources and load, and thus optimal self-regulation, at medium task difficulty". She emphasizes understanding how learners' effort is used as a cue and how it can bias students' judgments of their learning. She concludes that more elaborate analyses of effort appraisals, including research into the different origins of load, are needed, and that research should broaden the scope to include appraisals of learning resources, including motivational and affective states.
requirements: More elaborate analyses of effort appraisals, including research into the different origins of load, are needed
constraints: The scope should broaden to include appraisals of learning resources, including motivational and affective states
target_learning_goals: accurate effort appraisals and self-regulation of learning
examples: The model posits optimal self-regulation at medium task difficulty, where resources and load are balanced
key_sources: de Bruin, A. B. H., Roelle, J., Carpenter, S. K., & Baars, M. (2020). Synthesizing Cognitive Load and Self-regulation Theory: a Theoretical Framework and Research Agenda. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09576-4

article_title: The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach’s Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025)
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5
title: Semantic similarity heuristic: alpha indicates reliability to the degree that test items are semantically similar
description: The article proposes a heuristic for judging when Cronbach's alpha can be read as a reliability index: researchers should examine how semantically similar a test's items are. When items vary only in wording but not content, as in the Satisfaction with Life Scale, wording variation cancels measurement error across items and alpha is meaningful. The article states: "a good heuristic is to examine semantic similarity among items: the higher the similarity, the more accurately alpha indicates reliability." For knowledge tests, whose items tap different facets, the heuristic signals that alpha should not be read as reliability.
requirements: Applicable when judging whether a test's items assess the same homogeneous construct or different facets of a heterogeneous construct
constraints: The article presents this as a heuristic, not a formal test
target_learners: Researchers and test developers in educational measurement
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the reliability of knowledge tests
examples: The Satisfaction with Life Scale illustrates high semantic similarity; Hofer et al.'s bMCU mechanics test illustrates low semantic similarity because its items tap inertia, force and acceleration, balance of forces, and reciprocal action
key_sources: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Reliability, But Not the Cronbach's Alpha, of Knowledge Tests Matters: Response to Zitzmann and Orona (2025). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10023-5

article_title: Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture’s Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0
title: Semantic relatedness account: typical gestures benefit narrative comprehension because they are more semantically related to accompanying speech
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which gesture type matters for narrative comprehension because of the semantic relationship between gesture and speech. As the authors put it, "It may be that typical gestures benefit narrative comprehension more than atypical gestures due to the typical gestures being more semantically related to accompanying speech." The account is supported by the second study's finding that typical gestures were rated as more semantically related to speech than atypical gestures. It explains why gesture observation benefits learning by providing an external support to speech.
requirements: Gestures used must be semantically related to the accompanying speech for the benefit to arise
constraints: The article frames this as a proposed explanation ("It may be that..."), supported by a rating study rather than a direct test of the mechanism
target_learners: Children and adults learning from narrated stories
examples: The second study had participants rate how semantically related typical and atypical gestures were to the accompanying speech.
key_sources: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0

article_title: The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners’ Resources and Self-regulation
citation: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1
title: Seufert's model of self-regulation as a function of resources and perceived cognitive load
description: The model describes how task difficulty drives two counteracting forces that determine the intensity of self-regulatory activities: cognitive load, which increases with difficulty, and learner resources, which decrease with difficulty. It predicts an inverted U-shaped curve, since "Optimal self-regulation occurs with tasks of moderate difficulty, where resources and load are balanced". The present study operationalized the model's parameters across four exams and tested its mediation assumptions empirically.
requirements: Empirical support for its assumptions about task difficulty, load, and resources as parameters of self-regulatory activity
constraints: The article notes resource-based strategies are not specifically focused in the model and were excluded from analysis
target_learners: secondary school students preparing for exams
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use during exam preparation
examples: The study surveyed 67 grade-11 students after each of four exams (English, Mathematics, German, profile subject) on difficulty, load, resources, and strategy use
key_sources: Seufert, T., Hamm, V., Vogt, A., & Riemer, V. (2024). The Interplay of Cognitive Load, Learners' Resources and Self-Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09890-1

article_title: Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead
citation: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2
title: Anchoring Big Five personality traits and states within Situated Expectancy–Value Theory
description: The article proposes concrete placements for personality within Situated Expectancy–Value Theory: Big Five traits are added to the component relabeled "Goals, general self-schemata, and personality traits", and personality states are added to the box containing affective reactions and memories. The authors argue "Personality traits likely influence both expectancies and task value beliefs", illustrating that trait curiosity may raise task value, while state neuroticism in a learning situation is likely to interfere with assigning high value to the task. Because SEVT is situationally specific and culturally bound, the authors deem it a compelling framework for embedding motivation–personality integrations and for deriving testable hypotheses.
requirements: SEVT components represent general categories whose example listings are not exhaustive, which is what allows the proposed additions
constraints: The authors note their proposal for where traits and states belong in the model differs from that of Eccles et al. (in press), and researchers should examine which approach better aligns with their theoretical assumptions
target_learning_goals: formation of expectancies and task value beliefs, learning behaviors, performance, and educational choices
examples: A student low in trait curiosity whose curiosity is sparked in the moment (state curiosity) may come to see the value of the task at hand
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Luise von Keyserlingk, Jacque S. Eccles. (2026). Motivation and Personality: Current Integrative Perspectives and the Way Ahead. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10147-2

article_title: Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5
title: When availability does not arise naturally, learners should recruit antecedent strategies and behavioral scripts to self-activate SRL and flip the contributor-detractor ratio
description: The article recommends that learners who find themselves unavailable to learn can "recognize the assets at their disposal, recruit these into their perception of their capacity as a learner who can succeed in a task and overcome challenges sufficient to activate their capacity for SRL." Antecedent strategies include clearing the environment, meeting bodily needs, establishing intent, and enacting familiar behavioral scripts such as reviewing notes to initiate productive learning behavior.
requirements: Learners need metacognitive knowledge of themselves, their learning process, and their learning environment to recruit sufficient resources
constraints: The article states this applies to experienced adolescent and adult learners with sufficient metacognitive knowledge; disruptions can still overwhelm antecedent preparation, as in Sarah's scenario
target_learning_goals: Establishing availability to learn under suboptimal internal and external conditions
examples: Sarah investigated the noise source, made a pact to return within a few minutes, and initiated a familiar note-review strategy, thereby regulating emotion, attention, and behavior to establish availability
key_sources: Adar Ben-Eliyahu · Matthew L. Bernacki. (2026). Availability to Learn: An Essential, Achievable Condition for Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10144-5

article_title: Semantic congruence in arithmetic: A new conceptual model for word problem solving
citation: Hippolyte Gros, Jean-Pierre Thibaut, Emmanuel Sander. (2020). Semantic Congruence in Arithmetic: A New Conceptual Model for Word Problem Solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1691004
title: The SECO model: semantic congruence between world semantics and mathematical semantics governs arithmetic word problem encoding, recoding, and solving
description: The SECO model is a theoretical account of arithmetic word problem solving in which solvers abstract an interpreted structure from a problem statement under the joint constraints of world semantics (daily-life knowledge about the entities) and mathematical semantics (applicable mathematical knowledge). The article introduces it as "a theoretical model depicting how world and mathematical semantics interact in the encoding, recoding and solving of arithmetic word problems". When the interpreted structure cannot be specified into a tractable algorithm, a costly recoding process drawing on mathematical semantics builds a representation closer to the problem's deep structure; experts may encode the deep structure directly.
requirements: Solvers possess world semantics about the problem entities and mathematical semantics applicable to the problem's relations
constraints: The article states SECO does not intend to resort solely to world semantics to account for every variation in solving, since other sources of differences exist, such as algorithm computation abilities or reading comprehension
target_learners: kindergarten to adult learners solving arithmetic word problems
target_learning_goals: selecting and flexibly switching solving algorithms for arithmetic word problems
overcoming semantically incongruent initial problem representations
examples: The article reinterprets six case studies, including Bassok et al.'s transfer asymmetry and Coquin-Viennot and Moreau's bouquet factorization effect, through the SECO architecture with figures S1-S7 in supplemental materials
key_sources: Hippolyte Gros, Jean-Pierre Thibaut, Emmanuel Sander. (2020). Semantic Congruence in Arithmetic: A New Conceptual Model for Word Problem Solving. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1691004

article_title: Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors
citation: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656
title: SEC School Model
description: The Social and Emotional Competence (SEC) School Model (Collie, 2020) frames social-emotional competence as a process involving mechanisms and manifestations. It posits two intrapsychic mechanisms—social-emotional perceptions and motivation—that drive socially and emotionally competent behaviors. As the article states, "the SEC School Model posits that social-emotional perceptions promote social-emotional motivation and that both factors boost adaptive behaviors." The present study tested this central process using perceived-SEC as the perception mechanism.
requirements: Grounding in motivation theories (self-determination theory, social-cognitive theory) linking perceptions to motivation and adaptive behaviors
constraints: Examined here cross-sectionally among 13-16-year-old Australian adolescents; causal ordering could not be assessed
target_learning_goals: social-emotional competence, social-emotional motivation, prosocial behavior, reduced conduct problems
examples: The study operationalized the model's central process with perceived-SEC, autonomous/controlled motivation, and parent-reported prosocial behavior and conduct problems
key_sources: Collie, R.J. (2022). Perceived social-emotional competence: A multidimensional examination and links with social-emotional motivation and behaviors. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101656

article_title: Student perceptions of teacher messages about the value of science in the classroom
citation: David W. Putwain, Andrea Mallaburn, Hanna Gaspard. (2026). Student perceptions of teacher messages about the value of science in the classroom. Learning and Instruction 104 (2026) 102365. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102365
title: Situated Expectancy Value Theory (SEVT)
description: Situated Expectancy Value Theory is described as "an influential theory of educational achievement and choice that combines dynamic relations between contextually sensitive developmental and socio-cultural influences with socio-cognitive task appraisals." Task appraisals comprise expectancy of success, subjective task values (intrinsic, attainment, utility), and cost. The study uses SEVT to model perceived teacher value messages as proximal socio-cultural classroom cues shaping motivational beliefs, which in turn predict achievement and aspirations, with relations hypothesized as recursive rather than unidirectional.
requirements: Relations between motivational beliefs, achievement, and choices are modeled as recursive, requiring longitudinal data with autoregressive controls
constraints: The study focused on utility value and effort cost as the appraisals most responsive to teacher value messages, since intrinsic and attainment value are more task-intrinsic
target_learners: adolescent students aged 11-14 in early secondary science
key_sources: David W. Putwain, Andrea Mallaburn, Hanna Gaspard. (2026). Student perceptions of teacher messages about the value of science in the classroom. Learning and Instruction 104 (2026) 102365. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102365

article_title: The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings: Feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement
citation: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715
title: Two-motive account of feedback preference: self-enhancement versus self-verification
description: The article frames feedback preference as motivated by two main drivers in the educational context: "the desire for positive evaluation (self-enhancement motive) and the desire for subjectively accurate information (self-verification motive)". The self-enhancement motive "produces positivity bias", while self-verification "is seen in the preference for feedback consistent with one's established self-perception". The two laboratory studies test how these motives interact when self-enhancement motivation is increased.
requirements: Measuring or manipulating self-enhancement motivation and assessing established self-perception to distinguish the two motives' effects on feedback preference.
constraints: Studied in the educational context with feedback about social abilities; the positivity effect under increased self-enhancement was mainly observed for participants with positive self-perception.
target_learners: learners receiving evaluative feedback on their abilities
target_learning_goals: feedback processing and self-perception in educational evaluation
examples: Participants were presented with two evaluations of their social abilities, one positive and one negative, and their preferences were tested under increased self-enhancement motivation.
key_sources: Szumowska, Ewa; Szwed, Paulina; Wójcik, Natalia; Kruglanski, Arie W. (2023). The interplay of positivity and self-verification strivings : feedback preference under increased desire for self-enhancement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101715

article_title: Self-derivation through memory integration: A model for accumulation of semantic knowledge
citation: Bauer, P. J., Esposito, A. G., & Daly, J. J. (2020). Self-derivation through memory integration: A model for accumulation of semantic knowledge. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101271
title: Self-derivation through memory integration as a model for accumulation of semantic knowledge
description: Self-derivation through memory integration is the authors' proposed model of how semantic knowledge accumulates: information explicitly taught in separate learning episodes is integrated into a single memory representation, and inferential processes over that representation generate new factual knowledge that was never directly taught. The article argues it is a particularly viable candidate model because it uses true, factual knowledge, its products are rapidly incorporated into the knowledge base, and they are retained over time. The classroom experiments reported here test its retention, generalizability to science curricula, and episodic consequences.
requirements: Both members of a pair of related facts must be explicitly learned in separate episodes; if only one member is taught, children do not self-derive new knowledge.
A prompt or demand to integrate (e.g., a question such as How does a pod talk?) is needed for children to engage the integration process at test.
constraints: In children, the processes supporting self-derivation seemingly occur on demand at the time of test rather than at encoding; performance falls substantially when delay is imposed before the self-derivation test.
Classroom performance is nominally lower than laboratory performance, and cue-distinctiveness is lacking in classroom contexts.
target_learners: Elementary school children, particularly second-grade students ages 7-9 years
target_learning_goals: Accumulation of factual semantic knowledge, including science curriculum content
examples: Second-graders heard pairs of illustrated story passages in class (e.g., tigers are the largest cats; the largest cats swim to cool off) and answered questions requiring integration, such as What do tigers do to cool off?
key_sources: Bauer, P. J., Esposito, A. G., & Daly, J. J. (2020). Self-derivation through memory integration: A model for accumulation of semantic knowledge. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101271

article_title: Primary school students’ awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy
citation: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907
title: Second-order judgments (SOJs) as a measure of accuracy awareness in self-regulated learning
description: This framework distinguishes first-order monitoring and regulation judgments (evaluating performance and deciding on subsequent learning actions) from second-order judgments — students' ratings of their confidence in the accuracy of those first-order judgments. Students show accuracy awareness when they "feel relatively more confident about the accuracy of a more accurate judgment than of a less accurate judgment." The article applies this framework to primary school mathematics, measuring SOJ-m and SOJ-r on a 6-point Likert scale with smiley faces, and analyzing within-student relationships across two measurement days. It argues awareness matters because confidence affects whether students act upon their judgments.
requirements: Multiple measurement points per student to analyze within-student relationships between judgment accuracy and confidence
Students must understand the second-order judgment questions, which the authors verified through pilot interviews
constraints: The article notes awareness findings depend on analysis level: between-student analyses (as in Nederhand et al., 2021) can yield different conclusions than within-student analyses
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring and regulation of mathematics problem solving
examples: Students completed parallel multiplication and division tasks on two days, making monitoring/regulation judgments, SOJs, and self-scoring on both occasions
key_sources: Oudman, S., van de Pol, J., Janssen, E., & van Gog, T. (2024). Primary school students' awareness of their monitoring and regulation judgment accuracy. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101907

article_title: Supplemental Material for Boosting Students’ Academic Self-Concepts: A Self-Concept Intervention About Comparison Processes
citation: Boosting Students' Academic Self-Concepts. (2024). https://osf.io/xbv4q/?view_only=62ce423079de44dba59a9e7b132417e6
title: Scales measuring academic self-concepts and social, dimensional, and temporal comparison-related beliefs
description: The article documents parallel German-language Likert scales for students' self-concepts in math and German (five reverse-coded items each) and for comparison-related beliefs: social comparison-related belief in math and German, dimensional comparison-related belief, and temporal comparison-related belief in math and German. Students responded "on a Likert scale ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree" and all items were reverse-coded. The questionnaires were identical in both subjects and administered at pretest (T1) and posttest (T2).
requirements: Items are presented randomly, and the comparison-module questionnaires differ only in the knowledge quiz about the respective module
constraints: Items 3 and 4 of the social comparison-related belief scale were not used because of unsatisfactory reliability
target_learners: secondary school students in the academic track in Germany
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in math and German
beliefs about social, dimensional, and temporal comparison
examples: Table S2 lists five self-concept items per subject, e.g., 'Even though I try my best, math is hard for me.'

article_title: Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning - Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1911). Mental adaptation during the school day as measured by arithmetical reasoning.—Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Mental+adaptation+during+the+school+day%22+Winch+1911
title: Place severe mental work of a rational kind later in the school session, except in very poor schools whose boys work before school
description: The article derives a timetabling principle from its adaptation experiments: hard reasoning work such as problematic arithmetic should not occupy the earliest school period. It states that "Severe mental work of a rational kind, except in the very poor schools where the boys rise early and \"go to work\" before school, should be placed later in the school session than it is at present", arguing that if well grounded "a considerable change in school time-tables seems desirable".
requirements: The class must be one whose children's mental adaptation is not already at its height early in the morning, as the article claims for boys who work before school.
constraints: The article excepts very poor schools where boys rise early and go to work before school, for which early placement may suit better.
target_learners: elementary school children in England, of various social classes, ages, and grades of mental ability as measured by school standards
target_learning_goals: problematic arithmetic and other severe rational mental work
examples: In the experiments, one equal group worked the same problematic arithmetic tests early in the morning session and the other worked them later, under the same teacher.

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: SEEQ-S and TEEQ-S: parallel 15-factor student and teacher instruments for secondary-school teaching effectiveness
description: The article introduces two parallel multidimensional instruments: the Student Evaluation of Educational Quality–Secondary, gathering student feedback, and the parallel Teacher Evaluation of Educational Quality–Secondary, a self-evaluation tool for teachers. Both "assess the same 15 factors of teaching effectiveness", with TEEQ-S items rephrasing SEEQ-S items for teacher self-evaluation. They are designed for formative use within an ongoing school feedback program.
requirements: Administered to intact classes with the teacher completing a parallel self-rating for the same class, linked by class identifiers
constraints: Designed for formative feedback and professional learning rather than summative evaluation
The study sample is a convenience sample and is not nationally representative
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional evaluation of teaching effectiveness for teacher reflection and professional growth
examples: Students completed the SEEQ-S on school devices via Qualtrics and later a TXcel platform; each student evaluated a single identified class while the corresponding teacher completed a parallel self-rating

article_title: Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Knoester, C. E., Pfeiffer, M., Hattie, J., Dicke, T., Guo, J., Reeve, J., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., Vasconcellos, D., & Huang, D. (2026). Measuring teaching effectiveness in secondary schools: Multitrait–multimethod analyses of student–teacher agreement across 15 teaching effectiveness factors and student growth. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001035
title: A 15-dimension taxonomy of secondary teaching effectiveness organized by self-determination theory need-supportive facets
description: The article articulates 15 theoretically and empirically grounded dimensions of teaching effectiveness for secondary schools, nine adapted from the university SEEQ tradition and six added as secondary-appropriate scales: classroom management, cognitive activation, organization/explaining, choice, relevance, and technology. Self-determination theory organizes the profile: "Autonomy-supportive practices (e.g., choice, relevance, elements of group interaction/climate) foster students' sense of volition", while competence-supportive and relatedness-supportive practices scaffold challenge and belonging. Table 2 provides concise conceptual definitions for all 15 scales.
requirements: Items must be lesson-proximal practices directly experienced by students during lessons
Facets retained require strong theoretical grounding and consistent empirical links to student learning or well-being
constraints: Additional possible facets (e.g., management of time) were not retained because they lacked strong theoretical grounding and/or consistent empirical links
Using fewer facets would underrepresent theoretically and empirically established components of instructional quality
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive multidimensional definition and feedback on teaching effectiveness
examples: Table 2 defines each dimension with what high student ratings indicate, e.g., cognitive activation: the teacher encourages students to think deeply and figure out and complete classroom activities for themselves

article_title: Students’ motivational trajectories and academic success in math-intensive study programs: Why short-term motivational assessments matter.
citation: Daria Katharina Benden and Fani Lauermann. (2021). Students' Motivational Trajectories and Academic Success in Math-Intensive Study Programs: Why Short-Term Motivational Assessments Matter. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000708
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as a framework for understanding situationally sensitive motivational fluctuations
description: The article draws on Eccles and Wigfield's (2020) situated expectancy-value theory, which posits that students' expectancy and subjective task values are not only developmental but also "situationally sensitive (i.e., influenced by situational characteristics)." The framework distinguishes expectancy from self-concept of ability and differentiates intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, and cost components (effort, opportunity, psychological). The authors apply SEVT to argue that short-term, situation-specific motivational fluctuations in gateway math courses can serve as early warning signs of academic struggles and dropout.
requirements: Situation-specific assessments that reference lesson-, class-, or content-specific expectancies and values rather than global motivations
constraints: Educational research on situation-specific motivational fluctuations is still relatively scarce; it is not yet clear whether, when, and for whom these fluctuations serve as early warning signs
target_learners: First-semester university students in math-intensive study programs
target_learning_goals: Persistence in math-intensive STEM study programs
Academic achievement in gateway math courses
examples: The study measured expectancy, intrinsic value, utility value, psychological cost, and effort cost at multiple time points during the semester using situation-specific items referencing the specific math course.
key_sources: Daria Katharina Benden and Fani Lauermann. (2021). Students' Motivational Trajectories and Academic Success in Math-Intensive Study Programs: Why Short-Term Motivational Assessments Matter. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000708

article_title: The cost of multiple representations: Learning number symbols with abstract and concrete representations.
citation: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations.
title: Seductive details account of the multiple-representation cost
description: The authors propose that the so-called 'seductive details' effect explains why single representations outperformed multiple ones. Concrete pictures activate irrelevant prior knowledge — for example, "showing a child an array of five frogs may bring to mind knowledge about frogs that is irrelevant to the fiveness of the representation" — which the child must inhibit to succeed. Inhibition is easier when the same knowledge is activated on every trial than when new knowledge is activated from trial to trial, accounting for the single-concrete advantage in Experiment 3.
requirements: Learners must inhibit irrelevant prior knowledge activated by concrete items for the account to apply
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive account of the findings, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: young children learning number words and symbols
target_learning_goals: attaching magnitude meanings to number symbols
examples: In Experiment 3, children learning with one repeated picture (e.g. fish only) outperformed children learning with twenty different pictures
key_sources: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000318

article_title: Supplemental Material for Test Boredom While Working on Difficult Versus Easy Tasks: The Same Emotion but Different Effects on Performance
citation: Test Boredom While Working on Difficult Versus Easy Tasks: Online Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Test+Boredom+While+Working+on+Difficult+Versus+Easy+Tasks%22
title: Assessment-timing rationale separating over-/underchallenge and boredom measures within experimental blocks
description: Supplemental Material S6 documents the authors' rationale for when and where state assessments were placed during Study 2's experimental blocks. They separated the assessment of over-/underchallenge and boredom "to keep the individual assessments as brief as possible," assessed both constructs "as late as possible within the manipulation blocks" so the manipulation had time to take effect, and assessed over-/underchallenge first because these perceptions were assumed to be antecedents of boredom. The authors acknowledge this ordering does not permit causal conclusions.
requirements: Over-/underchallenge perceptions must be assessed before boredom, as the authors assumed these perceptions to be antecedents of boredom.
constraints: The authors acknowledge that this assessment order does not allow for causal conclusions.
target_learners: Adult participants completing working-memory tasks in a laboratory experiment
target_learning_goals: Understanding how task difficulty (overchallenge vs. underchallenge) relates to state boredom and performance during cognitive tasks
examples: In Study 2, over-/underchallenge and boredom were assessed at separate, late points within each manipulation block of difficult or easy digit-span tasks.

article_title: The problem of sense training.
citation: G. M. W. (1915). The Problem of Sense Training. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 9. https://worldcat.org/search?q=Journal+of+Educational+Psychology+Volume+VI+1915
title: The doctrine of sense training as commonly interpreted
description: The editorial names and critiques the doctrine of sense training: the assumption, taken for granted in modern kindergarten practice, methods of educating the feeble-minded, and the Montessori fad, that devices for training the senses of young children are both necessary and valuable. The author argues that apparent sensory improvements reflect central factors like attention rather than training of the sense organs themselves, and calls for a careful critique of the doctrine.
requirements: The doctrine, to be meaningful as commonly interpreted, would require that presenting sense impressions improves sensory capacity in ways not attributable to central factors
constraints: The author's argument applies to sense training as commonly interpreted, while conceding that systematic instruction with concrete objects may in some instances produce noticeable, measurable improvement in young children's capacity to identify objects
target_learning_goals: sensory discrimination of pitch, color, form, weight, length, and duration
examples: The editorial cites kindergarten practice, education of the feeble-minded, and the Montessori movement as practices that take the doctrine for granted

article_title: School and teacher measurement.
citation: Ernest C. Witham. (1913). School and Teacher Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Witham+school+and+teacher+measurement
title: Self-rating before supervisory criticism prepares a teacher to receive feedback
description: The article recommends that a superintendent have a teacher rate herself on the scale before filling in the sheet and discussing it. The author argues the process is "an excellent preparation for any verbal constructive criticism that the superintendent might wish to make", whether the teacher is weak or fairly strong with defects.
requirements: A completed rating scale and a superintendent willing to review the teacher's self-rating with her graphically.
constraints: The author acknowledges the self-rating may be inflated, though he expects that usually it will not be.
target_learning_goals: accepting and acting on constructive criticism
examples: A superintendent calls a weak teacher to his office, has her rate herself, then fills in the sheet graphically to show her standing as rated by herself.

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Three-part theoretical distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy (prospective, descriptive-evaluative, frame-of-reference)
description: The article proposes three characteristics distinguishing self-efficacy from self-concept. First, self-efficacy is prospective and task-specific ('what I can do') whereas self-concept rests on past accomplishments. Second, 'appropriately constructed self-efficacy responses are designed to be purely descriptive, whereas self-concept responses are both descriptive and evaluative', with self-concept incorporating worthiness and social comparison. Third, negative frame-of-reference effects (BFLPE and I/E) should be largely eliminated in pure self-efficacy items that contain their own referent. The authors argue against globality and content specificity as useful distinguishing features.
requirements: Distinguishing features hold only for appropriately constructed pure self-efficacy items with an explicit criterion of successful performance
constraints: The distinction depends more on item wording than on construct labels; some generalized self-efficacy measures are indistinguishable from self-concept
target_learning_goals: measurement and interpretation of math self-beliefs
examples: The article cites experimental work showing that more purely worded can-do self-efficacy items reduced predictive validity compared with items conflating capability and motivation
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: A priori classification of five math self-belief constructs into self-concept-like and self-efficacy-like categories
description: This classification pattern sorts self-belief measures by item construction rather than by label: whether items provide 'a specific description of a referent against which to judge competence'. The article states it 'classify a priori the five math self-belief constructs ... into two categories: three self-concept-like constructs (math self-concept, outcome expectancy, and generalized math self-efficacy) and two self-efficacy-like constructs', namely test-related and functional math self-efficacy. The classification is then validated against factor structure, frame-of-reference effects, and outcome prediction.
requirements: Item wording must be inspected for an explicit referent criterion before assigning a measure to either category
constraints: The classification is a priori and validated empirically; the article treats test-related and functional self-efficacy as not fully clear-cut in practice
target_learning_goals: measuring and distinguishing academic self-belief constructs
examples: Test-related self-efficacy items asked 'How confident are you that you can solve this math problem?' about items administered prior to the test; functional items asked about everyday tasks such as working out a discounted price
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). article_title: The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study.
citation: Helmke, A., & van Aken, M. A. G. (1995). The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 624-637. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.87.4.624
title: Model marks and test performance as separate achievement constructs in longitudinal studies of self-concept and achievement
description: The article recommends that future investigations on causal ordering include both marks and test performance as distinct latent variables rather than a single achievement indicator, because single-indicator models yield artificially reciprocal patterns. The authors state this complex model was "recommended for future investigations on this issue," and that single-indicator use "may lead to artificially high regression coefficients." This applies to longitudinal panel research on motivation–achievement relations.
requirements: Longitudinal data with both teacher-given marks and standardized achievement tests collected at each measurement wave, as in the SCHOLASTIC project
constraints: Requires school systems where both marks and tests are available; the article notes that in German schools only one official mark per year and domain exists, and that using a single indicator for marks requires assumptions about reliability
examples: Models 2a/2b (single indicator) versus Model 3c (separate latents with cross-lagged paths between marks and tests) were fit to 3 waves of data from 697 students
key_sources: Helmke, A., & van Aken, M. A. G. (1995). The causal ordering of academic achievement and self-concept of ability during elementary school: A longitudinal study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 87(4), 624-637. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.87.4.624

article_title: Short- and long-term effects of over-reporting of grades on academic self-concept and achievement.
citation: Sticca, F., Götz, T., Nett, U. E., Hubbard, K., & Haag, L. (2017). Short- and Long-Term Effects of Over-Reporting of Grades on Academic Self-Concept and Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 842-854. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000174
title: Self-enhancement as a short-term self-concept booster that risks a vicious cycle of declining self-concept and achievement
description: The article proposes that over-reporting grades raises self-concept in the short term but, because the boost rests on unrealistic self-evaluation, it sets up expectations students cannot meet, threatening the self-concept and re-triggering self-enhancement. As the authors put it, "a vicious cycle could arise from these dynamics." Protective causal attributions (success to ability, failure to luck) and underestimated learning effort are proposed as reinforcing and moderating factors, though these roles remain hypothetical and untested in this study.
requirements: Short-term self-concept benefits depend on unrealistic self-evaluation that later fails to match attained achievement
constraints: The potential moderating role of learning effort and the mediating role of attributions remain hypothetical and would need to be examined in future studies
No causal interpretations are possible from the latent growth models
target_learning_goals: Sustaining academic achievement over multiple school years
examples: The three-wave TPPLGM showed self-enhancement raised self-concept in Grade 9 (β = .28) while predicting more negative self-concept slopes and, via self-concept, more negative achievement slopes
key_sources: Sticca, F., Götz, T., Nett, U. E., Hubbard, K., & Haag, L. (2017). Short- and Long-Term Effects of Over-Reporting of Grades on Academic Self-Concept and Achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 842-854. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000174

article_title: Graded mental tests. Part I. Attention, perception, comprehension and memory.
citation: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Seven critical points of mental efficiency as the organizing axis for graded mental age-norms
description: The article proposes that mental efficiency in school children be estimated by "sinking shafts" at seven critical points: attention, perception, comprehension, memory, association, invention/construction, and judgment. The author argues these are "some of the most significant factors in the determination of mental efficiency" and that age-norms at these points would furnish more accurate evidence of a child's development than examination of school-subject knowledge. The tests reported in this paper operationalize the first four points, with the remainder to follow in later installments.
requirements: Tests must be applicable to all stages of development and comparable from age to age
Each test must present a problem the child can grasp and arouse effort
Tests must be completable without undue fatigue, with a minimum of apparatus, within two or three school periods of at most thirty minutes
constraints: The series is offered as a tentative answer; norms are established only for unretarded pupils whose chronological, physiological, pedagogical and psychological ages correspond
This installment covers only attention, perception, comprehension and memory; association, invention and judgment are deferred to later parts
target_learners: elementary school children aged six to thirteen
target_learning_goals: establishment of age-norms of mental capacity
examples: Eight groups of ten children from the School of Education, University of Chicago, were tested individually with a series requiring no apparatus except a stopwatch
key_sources: Squire, C. R. (1912). Graded Mental Tests. Part I. Attention, Perception, Comprehension and Memory. The Journal of Educational Psychology, III(7). https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych

article_title: Tests of Trade Proficiency and Their Adaptation to Educational Use.
citation: L. Z. (1921). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Self-administrative performance tests in trades as incentive and economy device
description: A testing arrangement recommended in Toops' book in which learners administer performance tests themselves and see immediately how their performance compares with a norm or scale point. The review states "the person tested can see how his performance compares with the norm or with any point on a scale without the loss of interest due to delayed scoring," citing use in two engineering schools. The one-word-answer form is also self-scorable and appeals to student interest.
requirements: Tests must be self-administrative and self-scorable so scoring can occur without delay
examples: The investigator cites the use of self-administrative performance tests in two engineering schools.

article_title: Nonlinear relations between achievement and academic self-concepts in elementary and secondary school: An integrative data analysis across 13 countries.
citation: Keller, L., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2020). Nonlinear Relations Between Achievement and Academic Self-Concepts in Elementary and Secondary School: An Integrative Data Analysis Across 13 Countries. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000533
title: Self-protection as a mechanism underlying nonlinear achievement–self-concept relations
description: The article proposes self-protection as the mechanism that weakens the achievement–self-concept relation for low achievers: negative self-evaluations threaten the self, so "low-achieving students are likely to engage in self-protective strategies that lead to more positive self-evaluations". Strategies include changing the comparison group, poorer recall of self-threatening feedback, and downplaying negative events. The authors argue this mechanism plausibly drives the observed nonlinearity.
requirements: Students must be asked to evaluate their own abilities (e.g., via self-concept questionnaires), which may trigger self-protective strategies
constraints: The article presents self-protection as one plausible explanation; it also notes self-enhancing motives may contribute to some extent, and the mechanism is not directly tested in this study
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of domain-specific academic abilities
examples: The article cites prior studies in which students with poorer grades overestimated their grades more than students with better grades did, and poorly performing students showed no increase in performance predictions despite feedback
key_sources: Keller, L., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2020). Nonlinear Relations Between Achievement and Academic Self-Concepts in Elementary and Secondary School: An Integrative Data Analysis Across 13 Countries. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000533

article_title: Reading for university or for myself? Effects of context and beliefs about science on college students’ document selection.
citation: Cornelia Schoor, Jean-François Rouet, and M. Anne Britt (2024). Reading for University or for Myself? Effects of Context and Beliefs about Science on College Students' Document Selection. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116 (3), pp.317-345. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000849
title: SERP-based document-selection task with scientific-expertise and personal-experiences sources
description: The core experimental material was a simulated Google search result list for each of four target topics (health, sports, or education domains), from which participants ticked checkboxes for documents to read further. Per the article, "Four of the relevant documents had a source with scientific expertise (e.g., a professor of a relevant field), while another four had a source with personal experiences (e.g., the head of a support group)", plus two irrelevant titles to conceal the study's intent; SERP order, title-source pairings, and topic order were counterbalanced. The task question (write an overview vs. write an opinion) was manipulated independently from the external context.
requirements: Topics must be addressable by both scientific studies and personal experiences
Participants must encode the external context scenario before selecting
constraints: Sources and titles were fictitious, created only for the experiment
target_learners: university students from a German university, mainly teacher education and social science enrollees
target_learning_goals: document selection and source evaluation for further reading about science
examples: For each topic participants received the topic question and selected as many documents as they wanted from the ten-title SERP for later essay writing.
key_sources: Cornelia Schoor, Jean-François Rouet, and M. Anne Britt (2024). Reading for University or for Myself? Effects of Context and Beliefs about Science on College Students' Document Selection. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116 (3), pp.317-345. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000849

article_title: The interplay of personal and situational factors in situated expectancy-value theory: Cross-classified analyses of students’ situation-specific motivations in the Math domain.
citation: Benden, D. K., & Lauermann, F. (2026). The Interplay of Personal and Situational Factors in Situated Expectancy-Value Theory: Cross-Classified Analyses of Students' Situation-Specific Motivations in the Math Domain. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001032
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as a framework for person- and situation-specific motivational beliefs
description: SEVT holds that students' "expectancies for success and the subjective value they assign to a task—are proximal predictors of their achievement-related choices," including engagement, persistence, and disengagement from math tasks. Within a situation, beliefs are shaped by person factors (stable attributes and cumulative experience histories), situational factors (task demands, domains, social contexts), and their interactions. The study applies SEVT by measuring situation-specific ability self-concept, intrinsic and utility value, and cost four times during one math test, and by modeling Person × Situation interactions theorized by SEVT but not previously tested for situation-specific beliefs.
requirements: Measurement of motivational beliefs referring to specific time points and contexts (situated beliefs) rather than only domain-general beliefs
constraints: The article notes direct evidence on how personal and situational factors jointly shape motivational beliefs remains scarce, particularly in demanding STEM contexts
target_learners: beginning postsecondary students in math-intensive STEM programs
target_learning_goals: math-related expectancy and value beliefs in authentic achievement situations
examples: Students rated test-specific motivation after each of four test parts while working on different math content areas such as basic arithmetic, geometry, and calculus
key_sources: Benden, D. K., & Lauermann, F. (2026). The Interplay of Personal and Situational Factors in Situated Expectancy-Value Theory: Cross-Classified Analyses of Students' Situation-Specific Motivations in the Math Domain. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0001032

article_title: Fostering cultural change in research through innovative knowledge sharing, evaluation, and community engagement strategies
citation: Junsuk Rho, Jinn-Kong Sheu, Andrew Forbes, Din Ping Tsai, Andrea Alú, Wei Li, Mark L. Brongersma, Joonhee Choi, F. Javier Garcia de Abajo, Laura Na Liu, Alexander Szameit, Tracy Schloemer, Andreas Tittl, Mario Chemnitz, Cheng Wang, Jiejun Zhang, Yuri Kivshar, Tie Jun Cui, Ren-Min Ma, Cheng-Wei Qiu, Cuicui Lu, Yao-Wei Huang, Miguel Angel Solis Prosser, Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus, Rachel Grange, Sungjin Kim, Anderson S. Fostering cultural change in research through innovative knowledge sharing, evaluation, and community engagement strategies. npj Science of Learning 11:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00449-z
title: Segmented peer review landscape balancing community-driven, publication-driven, and funding-driven evaluation
description: The article proposes that 'The current review process must be seg- mented and branched out, seeking a balance between community-driven, publication-driven and funding-driven research evaluation', with an open-knowledge system mediating assessment of reproducibility, accessibility, and broader impact. Community peer review would let researchers submit research modules with DOIs for transparent expert feedback before journal submission, while publisher peer review and professional editorial oversight retain a validation role to counterbalance community risks.
requirements: A federated knowledge-sharing infrastructure offering data, indicators, tools, services, and guidance; each community specifies its own evaluation parameters
constraints: The article warns that relying solely on community peer review risks echo chambers, uneven resource allocation, and misinformation
target_learners: Researchers, editors, reviewers, and evaluators of research
target_learning_goals: Assessing research quality through reproducibility, accessibility, and community engagement rather than citations and journal prestige alone
examples: OPUS project stakeholder-driven feedback loop developing a comprehensive evaluation matrix; CoARA strategies for evaluation without heavy reliance on publication metrics

article_title: Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively
citation: Utkarsh Upadhyay, Graham Lancashire, Christoph Moser and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez. (2021). Large-scale randomized experiments reveals that machine learning-based instruction helps people memorize more effectively. npj Science of Learning 6:26. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8
title: SELECT algorithm and open-source trial dataset released for research at the intersection of cognitive science and machine learning
description: The authors released an open-source implementation of their algorithm and all data gathered during the randomized controlled trial, "to facilitate research at the intersection of cognitive science and machine learning". The data and code are available at the GitHub repository Networks-Learning/spaced-selection. The trial data comprise more than ~16.75 million answers to ~1900 questions by ~50,700 learners in ~628,000 study sessions.
requirements: Consent-based participation data from app users; preprocessing removed reinstallers and learners who used the app less than 2 days
target_learners: Researchers in cognitive science and machine learning
target_learning_goals: Studying machine learning-based instruction sequencing and memorization
examples: The trial recorded ~16.75 million answers to ~1900 questions by ~50,700 learners in ~628,000 study sessions.
