article_title: Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall
citation: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9
title: SBL benefits arise from immersive, embodied, and interactive engagement that supports sensorimotor internal simulation and internal feedback
description: The article proposes that SBL's benefits stem from its "immersive, interactive, and embodied design" which enhances sensorimotor engagement and internal simulation, fostering "a robust internal feedback mechanism that reinforces both prediction and its verification." Drawing on the Integrated Model of Text–Picture Comprehension, the authors treat SBL as a depictive, embodied route and text as a descriptive route converging on a single mental model. This account is used to interpret both the memory advantages and the confidence–accuracy calibration observed in the SBL condition.
requirements: Learning material must be representable through bodily movements and realistic encounters, as with clinical cases
constraints: The study operationalized SBL narrowly as standardized-patient encounters, excluding feedback, decision-making, and iterative practice components
Findings pertain to the embodied-interactive bundle relative to text, not to SBL writ large
target_learners: naïve adult learners without medical or psychological background
target_learning_goals: acquisition and long-term retention of novel structured clinical information
examples: Participants interviewed a professional actor portraying a fictitious clinical case, touching the actor to feel symptom manifestations, over two spaced 10–12 minute sessions
key_sources: Angélique Lebert & Óscar Vilarroya. (2025). Prior text-based learning enhances the benefits of simulation-based learning on confidence and long-term recall. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00380-9

article_title: Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution
citation: Li, Z., Wang, J., Chen, Y., Li, Q., Yin, S. & Chen, A. (2024). Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution. npj Science of Learning 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00256-4
title: Control account of self-referential facilitation of conflict processing via early identification and active inhibition of task-irrelevant dimensions
description: The article substantively describes a control-hypothesis mechanism account in which self-referential information is "readily retrieved with reduced top-down cognitive resource consumption". Early identification of self-relevance frees resources for active inhibition of the task-irrelevant (word-meaning) dimension, which the authors say binds more easily to self-referential information via semantic processing. Early processing weakens competition between task-relevant and task-irrelevant dimensions, yielding earlier conflict monitoring (earlier decoding) and lower conflict intensity at resolution (smaller SP). The article presents this as the first neurophysiological evidence for the account, combining ERP and MVPA time courses.
requirements: Self-referential information must be identifiable early in processing; the account presupposes self-referential content has a processing advantage over other-referential information
constraints: The CE reduction appears in block designs but not in event-based designs, which the authors attribute to insufficient time to mobilize attentional resources per trial

The study used a single Chinese possessive pronoun ('wo de') to represent self; the authors recommend incorporating varied stimuli (names, faces, handwriting) and third-person terms to avoid stimulus-property confounds
EEG has inherent limitations in precisely localizing brain activity; the leftward bias should be checked with fMRI
target_learners: adult participants in cognitive-control tasks (mean age 20.84 years)
target_learning_goals: efficient cognitive control and interference resolution in conflict tasks
examples: In the modified Stroop task, participants named ink colors of carrier words carrying 'my' (self-reference) or 'the' (non-self-reference) across 6 blocked sessions of 97 trials, with an ABBA block-order procedure
key_sources: Li, Z., Wang, J., Chen, Y., Li, Q., Yin, S. & Chen, A. (2024). Attenuated conflict self-referential information facilitating conflict resolution. npj Science of Learning 9, 47. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00256-4

article_title: Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching
citation: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3
title: Segment-and-refresh habituation account of short-video effects on event segmentation
description: The article proposes an explanatory account, extending Event Segmentation Theory, in which frequent rapid context shifts during short-video watching habituate the cognitive system to a high-frequency "segment-and-refresh" processing mode. This habituation is said to lower the threshold for perceiving event boundaries, causing over-segmentation of continuous streams, and to impair sustained attention as a downstream consequence. When viewers later watch a continuous narrative, the habituated state persists, so minor fluctuations are over-interpreted as event boundaries, disrupting the formation of coherent event models needed for durable memory encoding.
requirements: Exposure to a rapid, fragmented stream of context shifts in the manipulation phase
A subsequent continuous encoding task that depends on event segmentation
constraints: The authors note the observed effects are limited to the acute effects of short-video exposure, since the memory encoding task was administered immediately after the manipulation phase, and the persistence of these cognitive alterations remains an open question
target_learners: University students who are typical daily short-video users
Adolescents and other heavily engaged age groups (suggested extension)
target_learning_goals: Memory encoding of continuous, temporally unfolding information
examples: Study 1 exposed four groups (Short-R, Short-P, Long, Schema) to 25 minutes of video manipulation before encoding a ~20-min BBC Sherlock episode with eye-tracking and a free recall test
key_sources: Li, H., Li, J., Hao, X., & Liu, W. (2025). Behavioral and eye-tracking investigation of event segmentation following short video watching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00378-3

article_title: Does tapping in sync reflect cognitive control? Links between sensorimotor synchronization, social context, and executive function in early childhood
citation: Yunhee Kim, Doyeon Chae, Jaehwan Jang, Kyeong Taek Oh, Byeong-Sun Park & Min-gu Kim. (2026). Does tapping in sync reflect cognitive control? Links between sensorimotor synchronization, social context, and executive function in early childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00443-5
title: Sensor-embedded bongo drum platform with DTW-based synchronization measurement
description: A custom bongo drum platform embedded with thin-film pressure sensors was used to measure preschoolers' tapping. The article states this "intuitive and child-friendly interface facilitated consistent participation among young children and ensured reliable measurement across conditions". Synchronization was quantified with the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm, which "flexibly compar[es] the overall flow and shape of the sequences", making it robust to occasional missed strikes unlike strict onset-to-onset asynchrony measures.
requirements: Requires pressure-sensor bongo drums recording strike data in real time and DTW analysis of tapping sequences against reference rhythms.
constraints: Hand dominance was not directly assessed; data and code are available only upon request from the corresponding author because public repository consent was not obtained.
The study's design and analysis were not preregistered.
target_learners: Children aged 4-5 years in preschool settings
examples: Four drums (two for the child and two for the experimenter) equipped with thin-film pressure sensors; reference signals generated from the exact temporal structure of the auditory stimuli.

article_title: Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future
citation: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7
title: Seven-challenge framework for the future of AIED
description: The paper's central organizing framework is a set of seven challenges derived by comparing the utopian and dystopian visions: intercultural and global dimensions, practical impact, privacy, interaction methods, collaboration at scale, effectiveness in multiple domains, and the role of AIED in educational technology. The author writes that a comparison of the two visions "leads to seven challenges that AIED might have to face in the future" and discusses each as both a risk and an opportunity depending on how the field positions itself.
requirements: Interpretation of the external trends and the two contrasting scenarios together
constraints: The challenges are speculative; the author states they cannot be proven or falsified now
target_learning_goals: strategic orientation of artificial intelligence in education research
examples: Each challenge is elaborated in the Discussion section, e.g., privacy best practices for stakeholders and moving beyond Constraint Based Modeling comfort zones

article_title: Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9
title: Sequence alignment and clustering as an analytic method ('microscope') for characterizing collaboration quality in asynchronous group work
description: The article adapts sequence alignment from bioinformatics: group action logs are human-coded into contribution types — "coordination, monitoring, minor contribution, and major contribution" — plus a "gap" code for more than 24 hours of inactivity. Pairwise edit distances (a Levenshtein variant, with gap operations costed 2) form a similarity matrix that is clustered with partitioning around medoids (PAM), with k chosen by silhouette analysis. The authors claim this method "can serve as a kind of microscope to capture differences in the underlying collaboration processes", and distinguish it from sequential pattern mining, which finds recurring subsequences rather than whole-string similarity.
requirements: Human coding of action types (coordination and monitoring depend on human judgement; inter-rater Cohen's Kappa of 0.79 was considered sufficient)
constraints: Encoded collaboration actions are attributed to the group as a whole, not to individual group members
The method is data-driven but based on sequence alignments, not sequential patterns; hypothesis-driven pattern approaches require predefined patterns and miss unexpected behavior
target_learners: higher education students in large online courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building and coordination in small-group online tasks
examples: Study 1 aligned and clustered action sequences of 65 groups into three clusters (19, 17, 29 sequences); Study 2 replicated this with two clusters (19 and 10 sequences)
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe, et al. (2021). Using Sequence Analysis to Determine the Well-Functioning of Small Groups in Large Online Courses. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00229-9

article_title: Speech Enabled Reading Fluency Assessment: a Validation Study
citation: van der Velde, M., Harmsen, W., Veldkamp, B. P., Feskens, R., Keuning, J., & Swart, N. (2025). Speech Enabled Reading Fluency Assessment: a Validation Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00480-y
title: SERDA: Speech Enabled Reading Diagnostics App for Dutch oral reading fluency
description: SERDA is a Dutch oral reading fluency assessment instrument for primary school, administering word decoding (150 words in three 50-word subtasks with progressive demasking) and passage reading tasks on a tablet while recording children's speech. The article states that "Through the incorporation of speech recognition, speech-based diagnostics, and their conversion into didactic suggestions for practitioners, SERDA allows for the provision of individualized feedback on children's oral word and passage reading performance". It extracts item-, subtask- and person-level accuracy, speed and WCPM measures and derives LNIRT ability and speed estimates, with short administration duration and automatic scoring intended to reduce testing burden.
requirements: Administered individually on a tablet with microphone recording; the ASR requires optimization for children's speech before high-stakes use
constraints: Excludes prosody metrics; the ASR only produces speed scores for correctly read words; recommended for formative rather than high-stakes settings
target_learners: Children in Grades 2 and 3 of Dutch primary education
target_learning_goals: Oral reading fluency: word decoding accuracy, speed and automaticity (WCPM)
examples: In this validation, 176 hours of speech data from 653 Grade 2–3 children across 19 schools were collected and scored
key_sources: van der Velde, M., Harmsen, W., Veldkamp, B. P., Feskens, R., Keuning, J., & Swart, N. (2025). Speech Enabled Reading Fluency Assessment: a Validation Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00480-y

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: SemEval '13 Task 7 shared-task corpus and grading scheme for ASAG
description: SemEval '13 Task 7, the Joint Student Response Analysis and Eighth Recognizing Textual Entailment Challenge, was the first large-scale and non-commercial ASAG competition. Its corpora draw from a tutorial dialog system for high school physics (Beetle) and primary school science questions from grades 3-6 (SciEntsBank); "Approximately 8,000 student answers are included across all questions." A 5-way categorical grading scheme uses labels "correct", "partially correct incomplete", "contradictory", "irrelevant", and "non domain", with collapsed 3-way and 2-way variants.
requirements: Solutions must handle a degree of domain adaptation, with test data spanning unseen answers, unseen questions in the same domain, and questions in unseen domains
constraints: The review concentrates on the 5-way task, unseen domains, and macro-averaged F1 because accuracy and micro-averaged F1 lack a mechanism for accommodating class imbalance
There is no notion of an overall winner in the competition
target_learners: high school physics students and primary school students in grades 3-6
target_learning_goals: 5-way categorical grading of student responses to objective questions
examples: The review identifies SoftCardinality, UKP-BIU, and ETS as the best performing systems by its stated definition, with Dzikovska '12 as the strongest baseline
key_sources: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8

article_title: Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash
citation: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3
title: A seven-position matrix of interests and agendas structures AIED debates in the 2020s
description: The article proposes that AIED controversies cannot be reduced to informed proponents versus uninformed critics. Instead it offers "a loose matrix of interests and agendas" (Fig. 1) distinguishing at least seven positions: technical, educational, corporate and social proponents, and social, educational and technical critics, each framing AI in education through its own values, from an engineering mindset to critical pedagogy.
requirements: Understanding any given AIED debate requires identifying which of the distinct stakeholder positions are speaking, since each frames AI issues differently
constraints: The article presents this as a broad guide rather than an exhaustive classification
target_learners: AIED researchers, developers, and education stakeholders engaging with AI debates
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure of controversies around AI in education
key_sources: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3

article_title: Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures
citation: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8
title: Seventeen log-derived help-seeking features for assessing help seeking in intelligent tutors
description: A set of 17 behavioral features distilled from tutor log files and normalized as a percentage of total student actions, designed to "encompass a wide array of possible help-seeking behaviors". Features include help avoidance (NHP), help abuse (HPQ), self-explanation pauses after help use (HPL), help non-use on well-known skills (NHW), pauses before and after hints and bug messages, and first-encounter hint requests, each labeled with a predicted positive, negative, or ambiguous relationship to help seeking.
requirements: Threshold parameters for each feature (time or Bayesian Knowledge Tracing knowledge probability) are optimized by brute-force grid search with leave-one-out cross-validation per dataset
constraints: The article notes the feature set was generated based on U.S.-focused research, so indicators of successful help seeking in other contexts may not be captured
target_learners: Middle-school mathematics students (ages 12-14) using the Cognitive Tutor
target_learning_goals: Assessing effective versus ineffective help seeking within intelligent tutoring systems
examples: Features were operationalized with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and used in forward-selection regression models in all three countries
key_sources: Amy Ogan, Erin Walker, Ryan Baker, Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo, Jose Carlo Soriano, Maynor Jimenez Castro. (2015). Towards Understanding How to Assess Help-Seeking Behavior Across Cultures. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0034-8

article_title: Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice
citation: Benedict du Boulay. (2024). Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:116–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00355-0
title: Seven-dimension framework of AIED progress from Scholar to the present
description: The article organises the field's development as movement along seven broad dimensions: learner modelling, domain modelling, pedagogic strategies, interactive modalities, variety in users, length and breadth of interaction, and ethical/social/cultural context including human rights. It states that "Progress from Scholar to the present day has progressed along seven broad dimensions, as evidenced here largely through AIED citations", presenting each dimension with indicative citations rather than a complete review.
requirements: Evidence for each dimension is drawn from AIED citations; the framework is indicative, not an exhaustive review of the field
constraints: The author states it is "not supposed to be a complete review of the field, merely an indicative collection of citations"
target_learners: learners using AI-based educational systems across all levels of education
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI-based educational systems have developed in pedagogy, cognition, and social context
examples: Each dimension is illustrated with citations, e.g. learner modelling covering cognition, metacognition, affect, motivation and meta-affect; domain modelling covering production rules, constraints, simulations and games
key_sources: Benedict du Boulay. (2024). Pedagogy, Cognition, Human Rights, and Social Justice. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:116–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00355-0

article_title: Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue
citation: Monique Grandbastien, Rosemary Luckin, Riichiro Mizoguchi, Vincent Aleven. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0092-6
title: Seven-question reflection framework used to structure the anniversary articles
description: The editors structured each invited retrospective around seven questions: motivation, approach, core contributions, practical impact, core limitations, subsequent research, and future directions. They state: "We asked the reviewers to evaluate not only whether the article met the regular review criteria, but also whether it addressed the seven questions above." This framework turns classic papers into structured accounts of a research programme's motivation, impact, limitations and trajectory.
requirements: Reviewers evaluated whether invited articles addressed all seven questions in addition to regular review criteria
target_learners: AIED researchers writing reflective accounts of their own prior work
target_learning_goals: documenting the motivation, contributions, limitations and future directions of a research line
examples: Questions ranged from 'What was the core problem that motivated the work?' to 'What are the future needs for tackling the problem addressed in your paper?'
key_sources: Monique Grandbastien, Rosemary Luckin, Riichiro Mizoguchi, Vincent Aleven. (2016). Preface to the IJAIED 25th Anniversary Issue. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0092-6

article_title: Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Ruth Janning, Carlotta Schatten, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. (2016). Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0097-9
title: Self-labelling tutoring tool dataset: 7 students, 40 fraction/arithmetic tasks, 280 self-labelled tasks with log-file recording
description: A dataset from a study in which "7 students in the age of 21 – 28 each had to solve 40 mathematical tasks and to label at the end of a task the perceived task-difficulty themselves by means of the small offline self-labelling tutoring java tool". "Each of the 7 students has seen all 40 tasks resulting in 280 labelled tasks", distributed as 40 too hard, 20 hard, 93 appropriate, 121 easy and 6 too easy. The tool is a drill-and-practice math system that does not model student knowledge but provides only the log-file data and labels; every action was written with a time stamp into a log file.
requirements: Students self-label each task (or skipped tasks as too hard/too easy); every action such as pressing buttons, typing numbers, hint requests and answer submission must be logged with a time stamp.
constraints: The dataset is small (7 students, 280 labelled tasks); per-task recognition used only non-skipped tasks (234 examples), and the authors state larger data is needed for generalisability.
target_learners: students aged 21–28 practicing fractions and arithmetic
target_learning_goals: self-reported perceived task-difficulty labelling for adaptive tutoring research
examples: Task areas included reducing, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions, the distributivity law, finite sums of unit fractions and the rule of three.
key_sources: Ruth Janning, Carlotta Schatten, Lars Schmidt-Thieme. (2016). Perceived Task-Difficulty Recognition from Log-file Information for the Use in Adaptive Intelligent Tutoring Systems. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0097-9

article_title: Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”
citation: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8
title: SE-Coach: an ILE combining a solution-graph representation, incremental scaffolding interface tools, and a probabilistic student model to coach self-explanation
description: The SE-Coach is an intelligent learning environment designed to help students self-explain worked-out example solutions in introductory physics. It leverages "An explicit representation of what it means to understand an example solution" (the solution graph dependency network), "Interface tools to scaffold the target self-explanations" delivered via three levels of scaffolding, and "A probabilistic student model" that uses interface actions to assess which parts of the example have been correctly explained. It was designed to integrate with the Andes physics problem-solving ILE.
requirements: Requires a solution graph dependency network modeling how each solution step derives from previous steps and physics knowledge
Requires interface tools providing incremental scaffolding so as to interfere as little as possible with spontaneous student behaviors
Requires a probabilistic student model leveraging the solution graph and observed interface actions
constraints: Initially self-explanation is voluntary; more direct tutorial interventions are reserved for students with low tendency to self-explain
key_sources: Conati, C. (2016). Commentary on: “Toward Computer-Based Support of MetaCognitive Skills: a Computational Framework to Coach Self Explanation”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0074-8

article_title: ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem
citation: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8
title: Service-oriented AIED ecosystem decomposes the four-component ITS architecture into reusable, composable web services
description: The article argues AIED is reaching a juncture where systems split "into an ecosystem of reusable infrastructure and platforms" that may be "hosted across many different servers or institutions." It questions the traditional four-component ITS architecture (Domain, Pedagogy, Student, Communication modules from Woolf, 2010), stating "there is no reason to think that any given ITS must contain all these components, in the sense of building them, controlling them, or owning them." Instead, each piece could be "used as a web-service for many different learning systems," enabling deep specialization while remaining widely applicable through integration with platforms that have large sustained user bases.
requirements: Composing and coordinating specialized AIED services requires greater standardization and focus on data sharing between systems
constraints: Moving toward services carries costs: asynchronous service-oriented programming expertise, risk that a key service may fail or be discontinued, and collaboration investment to understand others' work
target_learners: learners across K-12 and higher education using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: enabling user adaptation and large-scale experimentation in education
examples: The author analogizes to web applications that integrate log-in services, cloud-based ads, and embedded media from many providers
key_sources: Nye, B. D. (2016). ITS, The End of the World as We Know It: Transitioning AIED into a Service-Oriented Ecosystem. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0098-8

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Monitor and guide collaborative skills by connecting sentence openers with sentence closers, not openers alone
description: This principle states that identifying, monitoring, guiding, and assessing collaboration should combine the sentence opener a student selects with the free-form sentence closer they write, since the closer provides context the opener lacks. Reflecting on later systems, the authors write that 'we recognize that the use of sentence openers alone for identifying, monitoring, and guiding collaborative skills is insufficient.' Israel's ICSS demonstrated that coupling openers with closer text enabled more accurate classification of skills and discussion types.
requirements: A mechanism (e.g., agents or natural language processing) that can couple each sentence opener with text from the corresponding sentence closer to classify the skill and discussion type
constraints: The ICLS itself relied on openers alone given the resources of its era; the principle emerged from the authors' retrospective assessment informed by later research
target_learners: students collaborating in networked or online group learning environments
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring, guidance and assessment of collaborative skills during group discussion
examples: Israel's ICSS coupled sentence openers with text from sentence closers using agents, achieving correct classification whenever a closer keyword was recognized
key_sources: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6

article_title: Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations
citation: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1
title: Seven curriculum-design principles operationalized as measurable properties of recommendation lists
description: The paper derives from curriculum-design literature a set of seven principles intended to be equalized in educational recommendations: familiarity, validity, learnability, variety, quality, manageability, and affordability. Instructional designers traditionally organize learning opportunities relying on "a range of principles coming from the curriculum design field, including significance, self-sufficiency, validity, interest, utility, learnability, feasibility". Each principle is operationalized as a function over a recommended list returning a value in [0,1] computed from platform data such as course categories, last-update timestamps, instructional levels, asset types, learner ratings, enrolment counts, and fees. The set is explicitly not claimed to be unique or universal.
requirements: Principles are operationalized only from data typically available on an online course platform, so not all curriculum-design principles or guidelines can be directly operationalized
constraints: The authors do not argue these are the only principles, as they depend on educational context and fairness auditing; some operationalizations are simplified (e.g., recency of updates as a proxy for validity)
target_learning_goals: equality of recommended learning opportunities consistent with platform educational principles
examples: The exploratory analysis characterized recommendations from ten algorithms against these seven principles using the COCO dataset.
key_sources: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1

article_title: Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture
citation: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y
title: The 7C's taxonomy of teamwork competencies
description: The article presents teamwork competencies summarized by Salas et al. (2015) and Sottilare et al. (2015) as the "7C's": Cooperation, Coordination, Communication, Cognition, Coaching, Conflict Resolution, and Conditions (Context, Composition, Culture). Each is defined behaviorally — for example, Coordination covers "mutual performance monitoring, back-up and support, adaptability, and task-related assertiveness". The article proposes these competencies as behavioral markers from which GIFT team models, as antecedents of learning and performance, may be derived.
requirements: Team models derived from these markers require data on team member behaviors and their interactions
target_learners: small interdependent teams in military and organizational training
target_learning_goals: teamwork competencies including communication, coordination, and shared cognition
examples: The article lists each C with its definition, e.g., Communication as "Information exchange protocols including clarity, timeliness, confirmation, and openness"
key_sources: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y

article_title: Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education
citation: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0
title: Sense of promisingness operationalized as knowing-what, knowing-how, and knowing-why
description: The article operationalizes sense of promisingness in graduate education as a student's ability to identify relevant literature (knowing-what), utilize appropriate research methods (knowing-how), and articulate study significance (knowing-why) to generate promising thesis proposals. It defines the concept as "an ability to discern or judge what may be effective in uncertain conditions", drawing on Bereiter's promisingness knowledge, and treats knowing-why as especially essential because it justifies relevance and feasibility.
requirements: Content analysis of online discourse notes coded for theoretical relevance, methodological feasibility, and study importance
key_sources: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0

article_title: Learning critical thinking skills online: can precision teaching help?
citation: Ramasamy, S. (2011). An Analysis of Informal Reasoning Fallacy and Critical Thinking Dispositions among Malaysian Undergraduates. Asia e University. https://www.aeu.edu.my
title: Seven-construct model of critical thinking disposition
description: The article presents the Facione, Facione and Giancarlo (2000) account in which "the dimension of critic al thinking disposition has seven conceptually non -discrete constructs which emphasizes on developing the habitual intention to be truth- seeking, open-minded, systematic, analytical, inquisitive, confident in reasoning, and maturity in making judgments." Dispositions are thought of as a critical spirit and probing inquisitiveness that weak critical thinkers generally lack, and a person may be positively or negatively disposed toward some dispositions but not all equally. The article defines each construct (e.g., truth-seeking as intellectual integrity and a courageous desire for best possible knowledge even against one's beliefs) and operationalises the model through the CCTDI's seven sub-scales, each scored 10-60 with interpretive bands for negative, ambivalent and positive disposition.
requirements: Measurement via the CCTDI's seven sub-scales, each scored 10-60 with interpretive guidelines
constraints: The constructs are conceptually non-discrete
A person can be positively or negatively disposed toward certain thinking skills but not toward all dispositions equally
examples: The study used the CCTDI, a 75-item attitudinal measure with 6-point Likert response format, obtaining overall Cronbach's alpha of .843
key_sources: Ramasamy, S. (2011). An Analysis of Informal Reasoning Fallacy and Critical Thinking Dispositions among Malaysian Undergraduates. Asia e University. https://www.aeu.edu.my

article_title: From sources of self-efficacy to technology integration intentions: a new social cognitive model
citation: Serkan Perkmen, Sara Dexter. (2026). From sources of self-efficacy to technology integration intentions: a new social cognitive model. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10623-0
title: Sources of Educational Technology Self-Efficacy Scale (SETSES)
description: A 29-item scale (final 23-item version) developed by the first researcher to measure preservice teachers' perceptions of the four sources of self-efficacy within educational technology coursework: Mastery Experiences (10 items), Vicarious Information (7 items), Verbal Persuasion (5 items), and Emotional Arousal (7 items). Items were drawn from mathematics self-efficacy scales, a qualitative educational technology study, and the researcher's own items. The article reports that "The Cronbach's alpha of the overall scale was found to be 0.90, indicating a high reliability" for the retained 23-item version, and suggests it "can serve as a diagnostic tool for instructors".
requirements: Administered as a 5-point Likert instrument; negative items reverse-scored before analysis
constraints: Discriminant validity only partially established: mastery experiences were not distinct from vicarious information (HTMT 0.91)
target_learners: preservice teachers in educational technology courses
target_learning_goals: measuring sources of self-efficacy for educational technology
examples: Pilot tested with 35 preservice teachers and reviewed by two experts for face validity before the main study
key_sources: Serkan Perkmen, Sara Dexter. (2026). From sources of self-efficacy to technology integration intentions: a new social cognitive model. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10623-0

article_title: Use of graphs in air force teaching materials
citation: Research Abstracts. (1953). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Seven types of graphs for instructional materials
description: Peterson's monograph organizes graphs used in instructional materials into seven types. The abstract states: "In general, there are seven types of graphs: multiple bars; divided bar; divided circle; line graph; cosmograph; composite bars; and pictograph." This taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the monograph's recommendations about matching chart types to common graphic problems in teaching materials.
requirements: The report aims "To summarize in a brief monograph the best knowledge about the use af graphs in instructional materials."
target_learners: military and general learners of instructional materials design
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate graph types for presenting information in instruction
key_sources: Research Abstracts. (1953). https://eric.ed.gov/

article_title: DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown
citation: Walter Setti, Rebecca Tarello, Erica Volta, Lucia Ferlino, Monica Gori, Gualtiero Volpe. (2025). DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown. Education Tech Research Dev 73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10407-4
title: Sequential educational escape room structure for a digital learning unit
description: The unit adopts the escape room model, relying on the EscapED theoretical framework and Nicholson's puzzle-organization typology. The authors state: "We applied the sequential structure, where players must solve the puzzles one at a time, and the final puzzle allows them to win the game." In D-UDA, solving classroom riddles yields a code linking to Scratch games, whose completion yields puzzle pieces composing a feather that unlocks the final Domus escape room. A narrative character, a cycling-traveler archaeologist, links the enigmas.
requirements: A narrative link connecting all enigmas
Puzzles organized so each solved puzzle yields access to the next stage
target_learning_goals: Logical-mathematical problem solving within a game narrative
examples: Four classroom enigmas (e.g., a Caesar's cipher puzzle about Emperor Titus) unlock a code leading to the virtual archaeological site games
key_sources: Walter Setti, Rebecca Tarello, Erica Volta, Lucia Ferlino, Monica Gori, Gualtiero Volpe. (2025). DUDA: a digital didactic learning unit based on educational escape rooms and multisensory learning activities for primary school children during COVID-19 lockdown. Education Tech Research Dev 73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10407-4

article_title: Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography
citation: Fiock, H., Meech, S., Yang, M., Long, Y., Farmer, T., Hilliard, N., Koehler, A. A., & Cheng, Z. (2022). Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10075-8
title: Use intentional self-reflection practices to strengthen theoretical understanding and expertise development
description: The article recommends that learners use intentional self-reflection practices such as "journals, blogs, informal conversations, concept maps" to strengthen skills and knowledge in developing individual expertise. Self-reflection deepens theoretical understanding and strengthens metacognitive skills and problem solving.
requirements: Learners must engage in reflective practices such as journals, blogs, informal conversations, or concept maps
constraints: Expertise development takes time, practice, and awareness of experts' thought processes
target_learning_goals: developing theoretical understanding of instructional design theory
examples: The six learners used reflexive narratives, concept visuals, and focus group discussions to reflect on their sensemaking
key_sources: Fiock, H., Meech, S., Yang, M., Long, Y., Farmer, T., Hilliard, N., Koehler, A. A., & Cheng, Z. (2022). Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10075-8

article_title: Using scenarios to design complex technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Ton de Jong, Armin Weinberger, Isabelle Girault, Anders Kluge, Ard W. Lazonder, Margus Pedaste, Sten Ludvigsen, Muriel Ney, Barbara Wasson, Astrid Wichmann, Caspar Geraedts, Adam Giemza, Tasos Hovardas, Rachel Julien, Wouter R. van Joolingen, Anne Lejeune, Constantinos C. Manoli, Yuri Matteman, Tago Sarapuu, Alex Verkade, Vibeke Vold, Zacharias C. Zacharia. (2012). Using scenarios to design complex technology-enhanced learning environments. Education Tech Research Dev, 60, 883–901. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9258-1
title: Scenario-based design pattern: select a scenario, adapt it to context, then add domain content
description: The SCY design pattern treats instructional design as selecting a reusable pedagogical scenario blueprint, adapting it, and adding domain content. The original two-step process (select scenario, instantiate with content) was extended in practice with an intermediate adaptation stage: "the initial two-step design process (select scenario, instantiate with content) was extended with an intermediate stage in which designers adapted a scenario by leaving out LASs" or specific ELOs that did not fit their context. Designers first decide target group and learning goals, select one of the 12 scenarios, then specify assignments, resources, and ELO-specific information. The scenario functions as an overall framework from which elements can be omitted while its character and structure are preserved.
requirements: A fixed collection of pedagogical scenarios available in the technical infrastructure
Domain content in the form of assignment texts, resources, and ELO-specific information
constraints: Designers did not follow a scenario unthinkingly; LASs were left out, combined, or repeated, and larger missions were divided into content-related parts each following the scenario individually
target_learners: Instructional designers of technology-enhanced learning environments
examples: ECO mission design: target group and curriculum analysis, selection of the Inquiry Learning scenario, expert interviews with six domain experts to identify content, and teacher evaluation of resources

article_title: Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment
citation: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z
title: Sequence representational challenges before introducing scientific explanations in online representation-focused units
description: The article's findings indicate that the ordering of student-generated representational work relative to expert scientific representations shapes the quality of students' uptake. In the Temperature module, students explored their own ideas first and then refined them after a video explanation, whereas in the Convection module the early video seemed to lock students into a procedural interpretation. The authors conclude that "grappling with the representational problem before being introduced to scientific ideas better prepared students for generative uptake," and recommend embedding multimodal formative representation-focused activities early in the learning sequence.
requirements: Online units must be carefully planned to embed multimodal formative representation-focused activities early in the learning sequence
Teachers need to refine the planned sequence in response to students' representations
constraints: If scientific resources are presented too late, students may not understand the principles well enough to translate them to another activity, per prior studies the article cites
target_learners: K-12 science students, exemplified by Grade 9 students
target_learning_goals: Generative uptake of scientific ideas through representation construction and refinement
Conceptual understanding of energy transfer and the particle model
examples: In the Temperature module students engaged in open-ended exploratory activities before viewing the first scientific video and showed steady uptake across modes; in the Convection module the video preceded the challenges and students copied its conventions inappropriately
key_sources: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z

title: Seven-type taxonomy of graphs for instructional materials
description: Peterson's monograph organizes instructional graphs into seven types: "multiple bars; divided bar; divided circle; line graph; cosmograph; composite bars; and pictograph." The taxonomy is presented as a summary of "the best knowledge about the use af graphs in instructional materials," and it underpins the monograph's recommendations matching chart types to common graphic problems.

article_title: BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners
citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink, Alieke M. van Dijk, Ton de Jong. (2020). BE COOL! a digital learning environment to challenge and socially include gifted learners. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09754-9
title: Seven-step learning-by-design cycle with three group-composition phases
description: BE COOL! structures the lesson series as a seven-step learning-by-design cycle: problem statement, orientation, gathering information, designing, testing and improving, developing a prototype, and reporting. These steps are organized into three phases with different group compositions: a heterogeneous prior-knowledge phase (steps 1–2), a homogeneous expert phase (step 3, containing the five inquiry-cycle phases of orientation, investigation, drawing conclusions, evaluating, and broadening), and a heterogeneous design phase (steps 4–7). The cycle is meant to engage learners in designing a solution for an authentic problem so they achieve understanding of complex systems.
requirements: A design challenge formulated at a level such that learners have the need to learn
constraints: The inquiry learning is embedded specifically in the third step of the design cycle, in which children work in homogeneous groups
target_learners: Primary school children in grades 4 to 6 of mixed ability levels
target_learning_goals: Deep and transferrable knowledge and skills through designing a solution to an authentic problem
examples: In the moon-house series, testing and improving uses four flowcharts, one per topic, to identify further improvements before building a prototype to scale

article_title: The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains
citation: Manuel Ninaus, Rodolpho Cortez, Izabel Hazin, Kristian Kiili, Silke M. Wortha, Elise Klein, Elisabeth M. Weiss, Korbinian Moeller. (2023). The added value of game elements: better training performance but comparable learning gains. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10263-8
title: Semideus game-based fraction number line estimation training
description: A digital training environment in which the number line from 0 to 1 is visualized as a walkable platform; participants control the character Semideus recovering gold coins stolen by a goblin on Mount Olympos. The article states it "was already successfully utilized in previous studies for evaluating fraction knowledge in Finnish and German schoolchildren". It includes game fiction, visual aesthetics, coins, life points, and a 3-star end-of-level rating.
requirements: Participants estimate fraction positions within 10 s and repeat trials until correct; correct answers earn coins scaled to precision
constraints: In this study it was compared against a stripped, minimalistic non-game version with identical items and task, isolating the game elements
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude estimation on a 0-to-1 number line
examples: In the study, 41 adults trained five consecutive days, 15–20 min per session, on 96 trials of fraction number line estimation

citation: Gloria Natividad Beltrán del Río. (2021). A useful framework for teacher professional development for online and blended learning to use as guidance in times of crisis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09953-y
title: Special-issue table of seven responses to Philipsen et al.'s TPD-for-OBL review
description: A table in the editorial listing the seven respondents, their perspectives (adoption and diffusion, research, critical pedagogy, international, practice, design, practice/K-12), their article titles, and each response's stated value for the Philipsen et al. framework. It organizes the special issue's contributions, noting for example that "The findings can be clearly applied to guide an appropriate TPD for the recovery as well as for a resilient education system".
requirements: Read alongside the Philipsen et al. (2019) framework it responds to
constraints: Summarizes responses at a high level; full arguments are in the response articles themselves
target_learners: educational professionals preparing teachers for online and blended learning
target_learning_goals: understanding perspectives on TPD for OBL in crisis conditions
examples: The table maps each respondent to a perspective, e.g. Gogus on adoption and diffusion and Sullivan on critical pedagogy and equity

article_title: Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
citation: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2
title: Seven design principles for chatbot-based digital tutors in long-term formal learning settings
description: From ten requirements derived from an expert workshop, the ICAP framework, and the CASA paradigm, the authors deduced seven design principles in three categories: DP1, a natural language-based conversational user interface; DP2, availability all the time on common devices; DP3, a Q&A component based on a (learning) object database; DP4, provision of a formative assessment component; DP5, provision of learning content; DP6, a learning analytics component; and DP7, functionalities for collecting input and feedback. The principles were implemented and evaluated in the field.
requirements: A natural language processing component to enable communication, access to databases or a knowledge base containing learning objects and organizational information, and storage of messages and learning actions for analytics
constraints: DP6 is not visible to students and therefore could not be evaluated by them in the survey
target_learning_goals: answering knowledge and organizational questions, formative assessment with automatic feedback, provision of learning content, and collection of student feedback
examples: The digital tutor app implemented all seven principles, including an audience response system for DP7 and a discourse storage and learning action log feeding the learning analytics component for DP6
key_sources: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2

article_title: Addressing students’ emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments
citation: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski. (2021). Addressing students' emotional needs during the COVID-19 pandemic: a perspective on text versus video feedback in online environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09897-9
title: Feedback modality should be selected with respect to situational principles rather than treated as universally superior
description: The article cautions against treating video feedback as universally appropriate: "video feedback is not panacea for any learning scenario. Instead, the type of feedback should be selected with respect to situational principles". It illustrates that video feedback may suit an assignment in a computer graphics course but may not be pertinent for feedback on a multiple-choice quiz.
requirements: Instructors must judge the fit between feedback modality and the specific assignment or learning scenario
constraints: Video feedback may not be pertinent for feedback on a multiple-choice quiz
examples: The article contrasts video feedback for a computer graphics course assignment with feedback on a multiple-choice quiz

article_title: Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms
citation: Andre L. C. Barczak, Anuradha Mathrani, Binglan Han, Napoleon H. Reyes. (2023). Automated assessment system for programming courses: a case study for teaching data structures and algorithms. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10277-2
title: Seven progressive DSA coursework activities spanning linked-list, stack, queue, list, tree, graph and heap
description: The DSA coursework was organised into seven distinct topics forming learning activities that gradually extended in complexity of programmatic concepts. "The DSA coursework was organised into seven distinct topics related to the different data structures, namely linked-list, stack, queue, list, tree, graph and heap." Table 1 details each activity's task (e.g., adding sparse matrices, evaluating RPNs, Dijkstra shortest path, heap sorting) and the automarker functionality for marking it, including stress tests, infinite-loop checks and tolerance-based verification.
requirements: Activities must be pertinent to each topic since different programming skills apply to different topics/sub-topics
Exercises need a justified pedagogical foundation formalizing skills and notions pertinent to the algorithmic field
constraints: Activities gradually extended in complexity to challenge students within one second-year course
target_learning_goals: algorithmic reasoning and programming practice across core data structures
examples: Activity 6 asks students to find the shortest path from a source node to every other node in a graph using Dijkstra's algorithm, with the automarker verifying minimum distances and using graphs with islands to stress the code

article_title: Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning
citation: Schmid, R., Pauli, C., & Petko, D. (2023). Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10167-z
title: Regular self-directed learning phases with personal learning plans as the structural core of school-wide personalized learning
description: Across the Swiss perLen schools, personalized learning was implemented through a common structural pattern: regular scheduled time slots in which students learn autonomously following individual learning plans, with teachers providing adaptive support. As the article states, "they have integrated regular time slots in the schedule in which the students learn autonomously according to a personal learning plan." During these phases students have more voice and choice about what, how, and when they learn, and digital technology use is concentrated in them (e.g., computer workstations in learning landscapes and learning studios).
requirements: Schedule slots for self-directed learning; personal learning plans per student; teachers reoriented toward adaptive support during these phases
constraints: Observed in German-speaking Swiss lower-secondary schools with explicitly implemented personalized learning concepts; implementations differed in details across schools
target_learners: lower-secondary students in heterogeneous learning groups
target_learning_goals: student self-direction, student voice and choice, adaptive individual support
examples: School A students spend one third of their time in self-directed learning phases in mixed classes, working in a learning landscape; School C runs learning studios of about 50 students
key_sources: Schmid, R., Pauli, C., & Petko, D. (2023). Examining the use of digital technology in schools with a school-wide approach to personalized learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10167-z

article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Sen's capability approach applied to university teachers' digital capabilities
description: The article adopts Sen's capability approach to broaden thinking about teachers' digital capabilities. Capabilities are connected to people's freedoms to be and to do what they value, and are "more than a person's individual abilities, or the absence of constraints, instead as encompassing the actual opportunities that help people to achieve their values". This view emphasises relational agency to make choices appropriate for oneself, other people and the environment, and requires reconciling personal, professional and societal values through teaching practices.
requirements: Recognition of the diversity of values and the complexity of contexts that teachers navigate
constraints: Requires moving beyond individually situated and profession-referenced conceptualisations of capability
target_learning_goals: exercising relational agency in teaching with digital technologies
examples: The article contrasts Sen's relational, opportunity-centred view with person-centred definitions of competence adopted in psychology
key_sources: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z

article_title: Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students
citation: Eunhye Flavin, Moon Chung, Sunghwa Flavin, Matthew T. Flavin. (2025). Augmented reality for area measurement reasoning of elementary students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10502-0
title: Sequenced AR tiling activities progressing from basic rectangles to composite shapes with increasing unit-size variety
description: The intervention used four weekly AR activities, each about 60 minutes, sequenced from measuring a rectangle with two unit sizes, to L-shapes with two and then three unit sizes, to a large rectangle with four unit sizes. The design rests on the premise that "Understanding the same area can be tiled with different shapes and measured using various unit squares is essential for developing area measurement competency", so the authors "intentionally instructed students to use different unit sizes when measuring the area of shapes". Later activities pushed students toward efficient strategies such as covering more area with fewer, larger units.
requirements: an instructor present as a social scaffolder to explain each activity and guide reasoning
constraints: activities were implemented over four weekly sessions in a summer program setting
target_learners: elementary students with weak area measurement reasoning
target_learning_goals: decomposition and recomposition of composite shapes
multiplicative reasoning with rows and columns
examples: Activity 3 asked students to measure a 700 cm2 L-shape using 10 cm × 10 cm, 10 cm × 20 cm, and 10 cm × 30 cm units

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: Seamless learning as integration of experiences across formal/informal, individual/social, and physical/cyberspace dimensions
description: The article defines seamless learning as the integration of learning experiences across several dimensions. It states that "Seamless learning refers to the seamless integration of the learning experiences across various dimensions including formal and informal learning contexts, individual and social learning, and physical world and cyberspace." The construct frames the review of mobile-assisted seamless learning and serves as the organizing idea for identifying the seams that MSL designs aim to remove.
requirements: A design must address integration across at least some of the stated dimensions (formal/informal contexts, individual/social learning, physical world/cyberspace) to count as seamless learning
target_learners: learners in settings using one or more mobile device per learner
target_learning_goals: connecting formal and informal learning experiences
examples: The review uses this definition to investigate "the meaning of seamless learning and the potential ways to put it in practice" through academic papers on MSL

article_title: Examining supervising field instructors’ reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement
citation: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753
title: Self-sustaining cycle of presentation-focused technology use in school placement
description: The article proposes that a self-sustaining cycle maintains the dominance of presentation-type technology use on school placement. Field instructors expect pre-service teachers to use technology for presentations, and the feedback they provide focuses on improving the clarity and quality of PowerPoint slides, which "maintains almost exclusive attention to this type of technology use." This cycle operates within a broader context where the dominant use of technology in host schools aligns with field instructors' expectations, leaving pre-service teachers with little impetus to experiment with alternative, more student-centred uses. The article argues this cycle cannot be addressed through tutor professional development alone, as it reflects systemic practices in schooling.
requirements: A school placement context where field instructors assess and provide feedback on pre-service teachers' technology use
constraints: The article frames this as specific to the Irish school placement model, where school-university partnerships are not formalised
target_learning_goals: developing pedagogically informed technology integration practices
key_sources: McGarr, O., & Gallchóir, C. Ó. (2020). Examining supervising field instructors' reporting and assessment of technology use by pre-service teachers on school placement. Computers & Education, 146, 103753. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103753

citation: Tsai Chia-Wen, Lin Michael Yu-Ching, Cheng Yih-Ping, Lee Lan-Yu, Chyr Wen-Li, Lin Chih-Hsien, Lin Jian-Wei, Tsai Meng-Chuan. (2023). description: The article describes a structured seven-phase peer coaching facilitator process adapted from Schaefer, Fabian and Kopp (2020) and Wolf et al. (2018) for implementing peer-facilitated learning online. The phases are: start and problem selection, problem and situation, vision and resource, collecting further resources, setting goals, solution and next step, and feedback. Each phase defines specific roles for team members and the peer facilitator in guiding collaborative system development.
requirements: A facilitator must be selected for each team based on observed programming performance and interest
constraints: Designed for first-year undergraduates without prior programming experience in teams of six

article_title: A systematic literature review on serious games evaluation: An application to software project management
citation: Calderón, A., & Ruiz, M. (2015). A systematic literature review on serious games evaluation: An application to software project management. Computers & Education, 87, 396-422. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2015.07.011
title: Six-category taxonomy of serious game application domains for evaluation studies
description: The review classifies the application domains of evaluated serious games into six categories: health & wellness, culture, professional learning & training, social, support, and education. Each category is defined by the purpose of the games it contains, e.g. health & wellness "includes serious games developed to improve people's quality life regarding their health." The taxonomy underpins the review's answer to RQ1 and its distribution analysis of evaluated games per domain.
requirements: Primary studies must report the application domain of the evaluated serious game (QA5)
constraints: Classification derived from the 102 primary studies published until March 2015
target_learners: learners across formal education, professional training, and health contexts
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge and skills addressed by serious games

article_title: Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl
title: Service-learning as a pedagogical strategy with four success criteria
description: Service-learning is defined in the article as "a pedagogical strat- egy in which students engage in community service that will enhance their understanding of course con- cepts and enable them to make contributions to their communities" (citing Rhodes & Davis, 2001). Drawing on Eyler and Giles (1999), the article states a service-learning experience needs to satisfy four criteria to be considered successful: personal and interpersonal development, understanding and applying knowledge learned in class, perspective transformation, and a developed sense of citizenship. The pattern is used across disciplines, including communication courses.
requirements: Community service must be integrated so as to enhance understanding of course concepts and enable contributions to communities
constraints: The four success criteria are attributed to Eyler and Giles (1999) as a definitional framework, not tested in this article
examples: The 11 meta-analyzed studies spanned education, English, mass communication, pharmacy, political science, psychology, rehabilitation services, and sociology disciplines
key_sources: Jami L. Warren. (2012). Does Service-Learning Increase Student Learning?: A Meta-Analysis. Michigan Journal of Community Service Learning. https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mjcsl

article_title: Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
citation: Tian Qi, Liu Yaowen, Wang Ziyu, Qin Gang. (2026). Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1905122
title: Select and implement structured physical education teaching models according to student age, learning objectives, sport content, and teaching context
description: Because the network meta-analysis found no definitive hierarchy of teaching models — rankings shifted with outcome definition, age, and study inclusion — the authors recommend that model choice be made contextually rather than by universal ranking. They state: "In practice, physical education teachers should select and implement structured teaching models according to student age, learning objectives, sport content, and teaching context." The principle treats P-score orderings as conditional effect estimates rather than proof of universal superiority.

constraints: The article states the P-score ordering should be interpreted as conditional effect estimates, not proof that one teaching model is universally superior; significant inconsistency, sparse comparisons, and risk of bias preclude a definitive hierarchy
target_learners: School-aged children and adolescents in school physical education
target_learning_goals: Motor skill development, including motor competence, sport-specific technical execution, and game performance
examples: The 13-study under-18 primary network found only Hybrid TGfU-SE, Nonlinear, and Functional games had confidence intervals excluding zero versus Control, while Game-based, Sport Education, TGfU, Traditional, and Linear estimates were imprecise

Comparative effects of physical education teaching models on motor skill development in school-aged children and adolescents: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. article_title: Analysis of research on gamification, critical thinking and academic performance: A systematic review in the context of higher education.
citation: Gamarra-Vargas NM, Cosio Borda RF, Quispe-Farfán PH, Bosmans Flores FG, Robladillo-Bravo LM. (2025). Analysis of research on gamification, critical thinking and academic performance: A systematic review in the context of higher education. F1000Research 14:913. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.164232.1
title: Self-determination theory and gamified learning as the most relevant theoretical approaches for studying gamification
description: The review identifies the theoretical structures underpinning gamification research. Its analysis of the selected literature concludes that "the most relevant approaches for the study of gamification are self-determination and gamified learning". Self-determination theory positions motivation as the center of human behavior, so a subject motivated through gamified activities can develop critical thinking; Landers' gamified learning theory highlights benefits including favored academic performance. The review also lists other theoretical bases: relevance theory, the transtheoretical model of behavior change, cognitive load theory, constructivism, the technology acceptance model and social cognitive theory.
requirements: Studies of gamification adopt an explicit theoretical approach to understand its application and benefits, as the review's analysis of theoretical structures presupposes.
constraints: The theoretical-structure analysis rests on the review's qualitative reading of thematic networks, which its own reviewer noted lacks quantitative centrality metrics.
examples: The review's WOS thematic network (Figure 12) links a motivation-centered cluster to games and critical thinking clusters, consistent with self-determination theory.
key_sources: Gamarra-Vargas NM, Cosio Borda RF, Quispe-Farfán PH, Bosmans Flores FG, Robladillo-Bravo LM. (2025). Analysis of research on gamification, critical thinking and academic performance: A systematic review in the context of higher education. citation: Jørgensen Louise Bidstrup, Jensen Jette Nygaard, Clausen Caroline Skovsbo, Kousgaard Marius Brostrøm, Arnold Sif Helene. (2026). Barriers and facilitators to implementing e-learning for infection management in primary care: a scoping review. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-026-03385-4
title: Corpus of seven included studies of e-learning for infection management in primary care (2017–2025)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of "Seven studies published between 2017 and 2025" conducted in the Netherlands, Belgium, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Nigeria. Six used quantitative designs and one used mixed methods; participants included GPs and GP trainees, nurse and pharmacist prescribers, nurse practitioners, and multidisciplinary teams. Most were pilot or feasibility evaluations, with outcomes focused on knowledge acquisition, confidence, and attitudes.
requirements: Studies described asynchronous, interactive e-learning targeting infection management in adults, delivered as CME or professional development, in primary care settings, from 2015 onwards
constraints: No grey literature sources met the eligibility criteria; the corpus is limited and heterogeneous, restricting generalizability
target_learners: primary care healthcare professionals: GPs, GP trainees, nurses, pharmacists, nurse practitioners, and multidisciplinary teams
target_learning_goals: infection management knowledge, attitudes, confidence, and prescribing behavior
examples: Included interventions ranged from a national STI consultation e-learning programme with 2192 GPs at baseline to a 5-minute animated URTI consultation scenario feasibility study
