article_title: The use of large language models in generating multiple choice questions for health professions education: A systematic review and network meta-analysis.
citation: Riehm Lauren, Nanji Keean, Lakhani Moiz, Pankiv Evelina, Hasanee Dean, Pfeifer Wesla. (2026). The use of large language models in generating multiple choice questions for health professions education: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0340277
title: Seven-outcome framework for evaluating MCQ quality in health professions education
description: The article identifies "seven pre-defined outcomes" for assessing MCQ quality: "question relevance, question clarity, distractor quality, question accuracy/correctness, item difficulty analysis, and item discrimination analysis (point biserial correlation and item discrimination index)". The item difficulty analysis assesses the proportion of examinees who respond correctly to a given item, whereas the item discrimination index reflects how well a given item distinguishes between high- and low-scoring students. This framework provides a structured approach for evaluating generated examination questions.
requirements: Expert panels to evaluate qualitative outcomes
Administered MCQs to students for quantitative outcomes
constraints: Data on different scales was transformed to a 10-point scale to facilitate statistical analysis
Certainty of evidence was very low for all outcomes
examples: The framework was applied to compare five LLMs (ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, Bard 1.0, Llama 2, ChatPDF.com) against human-generated MCQs
key_sources: Riehm Lauren, Nanji Keean, Lakhani Moiz, Pankiv Evelina, Hasanee Dean, Pfeifer Wesla. (2026). The use of large language models in generating multiple choice questions for health professions education: A systematic review and network meta-analysis. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0340277

article_title: A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals' competencies related to health literacy.
citation: Mac Olivia, Marshall Sarah, McFadden Kathleen, Ayre Julie, McCaffery Kirsten J, Billah Sk Masum, Muscat Danielle M. (2026). A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals’ competencies related to health literacy. Health Promotion International. https://doi.org/10.1093/heapro/daaf227
title: Seven-domain framework of health literacy competencies for health professionals
description: The review developed a framework of seven domains of health professional health literacy competencies, iteratively and deductively refined from the data and informed by health literacy expertise. The domains cover knowledge of health literacy (performance-based and self-reported), self-efficacy to address health literacy, direct observation of ability to address health literacy, self-reported frequency of using health literacy techniques, and perceived effectiveness and behavioural intentions to address health literacy. The authors state these expert-informed, iteratively developed domains "provide a structured framework that others can use to target specific competencies and to adapt or develop new measurement tools".
requirements: Developed through iterative, deductive refinement informed by health literacy expertise and the current literature
target_learning_goals: Health literacy competencies: knowledge, skills, practices, attitudes, self-efficacy, and behavioural intentions
key_sources: Mac Olivia, Marshall Sarah, McFadden Kathleen, Ayre Julie, McCaffery Kirsten J, Billah Sk Masum, Muscat Danielle M. (2026). A scoping review of measures to assess health professionals’ competencies related to health literacy. Health Promotion International. https://doi.org/10.1093/heapro/daaf227

article_title: Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge-a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses.
citation: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8
title: Seven-module progressive course structure with longitudinal manuscript preparation
description: The proposed course comprises seven modules, each with learning outcomes, interactive elements, and assessment methods. Preparation for the final module (Module 7, manuscript preparation) starts at the beginning of the course and continues as an ongoing thread across all modules in a 'building blocks' fashion. Successful completion of interactive elements in each module is a prerequisite for progression to the next module.
requirements: Successful completion of interactive elements in each module as prerequisite for progression
key_sources: El Ansari Walid, El-Ansari Kareem, Hany Mohamed. (2025). Healthcare research and education: actively constructed research knowledge–a model for online systematic reviews and meta-analyses courses. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07111-8

article_title: Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors.
citation: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 417–439. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.14082
title: Classification of mediators and moderators into stress, support, stimulation, child characteristics, and other contextual factors
description: The review classifies mediators and moderators of the SES-cognition/achievement association into five categories: stress, support, stimulation, child characteristics, and other contextual factors. Stressors reflect environmental experiences that are likely to require adaptation and overwhelm the coping resources of an average child. Support is defined as the provision of nurturing relationships, resources, and environments that offer emotional and practical assistance. Stimulation refers to the availability of enriching environmental inputs that facilitate learning opportunities for children. Other contextual factors include broader environmental elements such as neighborhood and school characteristics.
requirements: Factors not falling into the defined categories are classified as 'other'.
key_sources: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 417–439. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.14082

article_title: Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors.
citation: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). title: Pathway model: SES influences stress, support, and stimulation, contributing to differences in EF and language, which in turn influence academic achievement
description: The review proposes a pathway whereby SES influences stress, support, and stimulation, contributing to differences in EF and language ability, which in turn ultimately influence academic achievement. This suggests that stress, support, and stimulation mediate links of SES with EF and language ability, which then mediate the relationship between SES and academic achievement.
requirements: This model proposes a sequential pathway from SES through proximal environmental factors to cognitive and language abilities, and ultimately to academic achievement.

article_title: Strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review.
citation: Hobenu Kafui A., Adefuye Anthonio O., Naab Florence, Nyoni Champion N. (2025). Strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0305789
title: Seven-theme taxonomy of strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education
description: The review organises its findings into seven themes and 36 sub-themes: 'scaffolding the curriculum, transformative teaching and learning approaches, integrating simulation-based education, dedicated education units for clinical placement, applying technology in clinical education, developing interprofessional teamwork and collaboration, and integrating inter-country clinical experience'. The taxonomy was generated through inductive thematic analysis of 40 included articles, with initial coding by one author and co-coding with another, verified by two further authors. It maps the reported strategy space for nursing clinical education.
requirements: Peer-reviewed articles and dissertations published in English between January 2011 and September 2023 on strategies for undergraduate nursing clinical education
constraints: Included studies were undergraduate nursing populations; postgraduate and other health profession programmes were excluded
key_sources: Hobenu Kafui A., Adefuye Anthonio O., Naab Florence, Nyoni Champion N. (2025). Strategies to enhance clinical teaching and learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0305789

article_title: Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review.
citation: Ge Wei-Li, Zhu Xia-Yin, Lin Jiang-Bo, Jiang Jian-Jun, Li Tao, Lu Yi-Fei, Mi Ya-Fei, Tung Tao-Hsin. (2025). Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06951-z
title: Introduce organized learning early in the curriculum and gradually expand active, self-directed learning as students master foundational knowledge
description: The review recommends sequencing PBL against students' prior knowledge: because PBL "requires students to have a certain level of foundational knowledge and concepts", it may be limited in early teaching stages. The authors advise introducing organized learning early and expanding active, self-directed learning afterwards, and gradually increasing PBL teaching frequency as grade level rises.
requirements: Students must have mastered certain basic knowledge before PBL is expected to yield better critical thinking and skill outcomes
constraints: In fields requiring rigorous theoretical foundations, such as biostatistics, PBL may have limitations because it focuses on problem-solving rather than in-depth theoretical instruction
target_learners: undergraduate medical, nursing and dental students
examples: The review reports first-year medical students' critical thinking, problem-solving and self-direction showed no significant PBL advantage, supporting delayed rather than early PBL introduction
key_sources: Ge Wei-Li, Zhu Xia-Yin, Lin Jiang-Bo, Jiang Jian-Jun, Li Tao, Lu Yi-Fei, Mi Ya-Fei, Tung Tao-Hsin. (2025). Critical thinking and clinical skills by problem-based learning educational methods: an umbrella systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06951-z

article_title: Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses
citation: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820
title: Treat meaning-dependent items as a separate evaluation regime rather than averaging them with surface-aligned items
description: The article recommends that "Meaning-dependent items should be evaluated and monitored separately" because if an assessment mixes surface-aligned and meaning-dependent items, "a single overall QWK obscures the most consequential failures". This principle operationalizes the meta-analytic finding that the read indicator is negative across specifications: items requiring semantic integration systematically lower LLM-human agreement. Monitoring these items separately makes the regime where rubric interpretation, negation, partial credit logic, and child-specific phrasing matter visible to practitioners.
requirements: Item-level classification of assessment items as meaning-dependent versus surface-aligned; separate monitoring pipelines for each regime
constraints: The article states this applies when an assessment mixes surface-aligned and meaning-dependent items
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with mixed item types
target_learning_goals: Detecting consequential LLM scoring failures on semantic-interpretation items
examples: The article's recommendation that practitioners avoid anthropomorphizing item difficulty and use human reliability metrics as quality control for labels rather than as a proxy for expected model behavior
key_sources: Michael Hardy. (2026). Autoscoring Anticlimax: A Meta-analytic Understanding of AI's Short-answer Shortcomings and Wording Weaknesses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04820

article_title: Airway management education: simulation based training versus non-simulation based training-A systematic review and meta-analyses.
citation: Sun Yanxia, Pan Chuxiong, Li Tianzuo, Gan Tong J. (2017). Airway management education: simulation based training versus non-simulation based training-A systematic review and meta-analyses. BMC Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-017-0313-7
title: Seventeen-study comparative evidence base on simulation versus non-simulation airway management training
description: The review assembled a corpus of 17 published comparative trials evaluating SBT against NSBT for airway management training, identified from six databases from inception to May 2016. Studies covered techniques including direct laryngoscopy, flexible laryngoscopy or bronchoscopy, bag-mask-ventilation, cricoid pressure and surgical airway, with a "Median sample size of included studies was 60 (range 6–245)" and median MERSQI score 13.5 (range 9.5–16).
requirements: Comparative trials featuring SBT as the educational intervention and NSBT as the comparison group, with assessment of learner and/or patient outcomes
constraints: Data from letters, case reports, reviews or abstracts were excluded
Some studies could not be included in pooled analyses because of missing data
target_learners: Residents and physicians with limited airway management experience
target_learning_goals: Airway management techniques including laryngoscopy, intubation, bag-mask-ventilation, cricoid pressure and surgical airway
examples: Thirteen of the 17 studies were randomized controlled trials; four were non-randomized two-group designs
key_sources: Sun Yanxia, Pan Chuxiong, Li Tianzuo, Gan Tong J. (2017). Airway management education: simulation based training versus non-simulation based training-A systematic review and meta-analyses. BMC Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-017-0313-7

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. NCEE 2017-4026
citation: Kautz, T., Schochet, P., & Tilley, C. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation (NCEE 2017–4026). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.rct-yes.com
title: Select impact estimators whose assumptions best suit the study's goals, regardless of whether they are design-based or model-based
description: The report's central recommendation is that method choice should be driven by the alignment between an estimator's assumptions and the study's goals rather than by the design-based versus model-based label, since the empirical differences were small. It advises that "researchers should select estimators with assumptions that best suit the goals of their study regardless of whether they use a design- or model- based approach," and that researchers should consider how assumptions affect interpretation. A stated advantage of design-based methods is that their assumptions are explicit and must be specified by the analyst.
requirements: Researchers must consider (1) how clusters and blocks are weighted to align with the impact parameter of interest and (2) whether results are to be formally generalized outside the study sample
constraints: The recommendation is based on the nine RCT datasets considered in the report; the report notes competing estimators could have different finite-sample properties that vary by context
target_learners: education researchers conducting or supporting impact evaluations
target_learning_goals: choosing impact estimation methods whose assumptions match the study's estimand and generalization goals
examples: The report weighed equal cluster weighting against precision weighting and the finite- versus super-population choice as assumptions analysts should consciously select
key_sources: Kautz, T., Schochet, P., & Tilley, C. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation (NCEE 2017–4026). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED575021

article_title: The Impact of an Integrated Pre-K STEM Curriculum on Teachers' Engineering Content Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Teaching Practices
citation: Sibuma, B., Wunnava, S., John, M.-S., Anggoro, F., & Dubosarsky, M. (2018). The Impact of an Integrated Pre-K STEM Curriculum on Teachers' Engineering Content Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Teaching Practices. 2018 IEEE Integrated STEM Conference (ISEC). https://ieeexplore.ieee.org
title: Seeds of STEM: an 8-unit integrated Pre-K STEM curriculum built around the engineering design process
description: Seeds of STEM (SoS) is an 8-unit integrated STEM curriculum for Pre-K classrooms developed by engineers, STEM pedagogy experts, psychologists, and six Head Start classroom teachers, refined through feedback from approximately 20 teachers over a 10-week period. Each unit integrates science concepts, technology tinkering centers, mathematics activities, and engineering via the EDP: "children are taught the steps to solve design problems encountered by the curriculum's main character, Problem Panda." Units include formative and summative authentic embedded assessments.
requirements: Intervention teachers received two 2.5-hour professional development sessions on the EDP before implementing the curriculum units in sequence
constraints: Developed for and piloted in Head Start Pre-K classrooms in central Massachusetts
target_learners: Pre-K children in Head Start preschool classrooms
target_learning_goals: integrated STEM concepts (science, technology, engineering, mathematics)
examples: Unit 6 (Matter) has children explore absorbency and material groups, design a container to send cookies across a river without getting wet, and sort materials by property
key_sources: Sibuma, B., Wunnava, S., John, M.-S., Anggoro, F., & Dubosarsky, M. (2018). article_title: Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies
citation: Olu Oyinloye, Abiodun.A. Popoola. (2013). Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 1(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.1n.2p.1
title: Semantic mapping as a graphic strategy for activating prior knowledge and introducing concepts
description: Semantic mapping is a strategy for graphically representing concepts, portraying the schematic relations that compose a concept. The article states it assumes "there are multiple relations between a concept and the knowledge that is associated with the concept", organised as associations of class, of property, and of example. It can be used to activate prior knowledge, introduce key vocabulary, and introduce Mathematics concepts such as types of triangles and their properties; as a post-reading activity, words, categories and new concepts can be added to the original maps.
requirements: Teacher raises questions that make students supply answers using their prior knowledge
constraints: Illustrated in the article for triangle properties (scalene, isosceles, equilateral, obtuse, right-angled)
examples: The article presents a diagram mapping the properties of five triangle types, which students can be led to name as the diagrams are presented.

Activating Junior Secondary School Students' Prior Knowledge for the Development of Vocabulary, Concepts and Mathematics through Instructional Strategies. article_title: Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too!
citation: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164
title: Educational semiotics (Sert)
description: The article introduces Sert's educational semiotics as a bridge between semiotics and foreign language teaching. Reviewing the three kinds of signs as symbol, icon and index, it asserts that "icons (cartoons, pictures, etc.) play a vital role which may be a positive contribution if foreign language learning is considered". Reinforcing new vocabulary with relevant pictures is said to support long-term coding of target language items, and pictures related to target culture help students bridge the gap between native and target language and culture.
requirements: Icons combined with the presented content and the target language skill to be improved
constraints: Theoretical position attributed to Sert (2006); not empirically tested in this study
target_learners: Foreign language learners in ELT and ESP classes
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning and foreign language awareness
examples: The article's example is reinforcing new vocabulary with relevant pictures so the target language item is coded long term.
key_sources: Seyyed Mahdi Erfani. (2012). Pictures Speak Louder than Words in ESP, Too! English Language Teaching, 5(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n8p164

article_title: Effectiveness of Game and Poem Enhanced Instructional Strategies and Verbal Ability on Students' Interest in Mathematics Learning
citation: Frederick-Jonah, T. M. & Igbojinwaekwu, P. C. (2015). Effectiveness of Game and Poem Enhanced Instructional Strategies and Verbal Ability on Students’ Interest in Mathematics Learning. Journal of Research in Education, 25(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Research+in+Education+Volume+25+Number+2
title: Seven validated instruments for measuring interest, verbal ability, and instructional fidelity in primary mathematics
description: The study used seven instruments: instructional guides for the poem-enhanced, game-enhanced, and modified lecture strategies (IGPEIS, IGGEIS, IGMLIS), the Students’ Interest in Mathematics Inventory (PIMI), the Students’ Verbal Ability Test (PVAT), and teacher assessment sheets for poems and games (TASP, TASG). The article reports "PIMI and PVAT where Structured dichotomous (yes/no) and had reliability coefficients of 0.73 and 0.85, respectively, using Kuder-Richardson 21 (KR-21) statistic." The guides and assessment sheets used Pearson correlations (0.81, 0.74, 0.76, 0.84, 0.78) from test-retest pilot data.
requirements: Teachers required one week of training on the instructional guides and two days on the assessment instruments before teaching
constraints: PIMI was adapted from Ekine (2010) and PVAT from Komolafe (2010); reliability was piloted on 20 students outside the study schools
target_learning_goals: Measurement of interest in mathematics and verbal ability
examples: Interest data were collected with PIMI before treatment and after the two-week lesson period, with pretest scores used as covariates in the ANCOVA.
key_sources: Frederick-Jonah, T. M. & Igbojinwaekwu, P. C. (2015). Effectiveness of Game and Poem Enhanced Instructional Strategies and Verbal Ability on Students’ Interest in Mathematics Learning. Journal of Research in Education, 25(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1098014

article_title: A Benefit-Cost Analysis of a Long-Term Intervention on Social and Emotional Learning in Compulsory School
citation: Alli Klapp, Clive Belfield, Brooks Bowden, Henry Levin, Robert Shand, Sabine Zander. (2017). A benefit-cost analysis of a long-term intervention on social and emotional learning in compulsory school. International Journal of Emotional Education, 9(1), 3-19. https://www.um.edu.mt/ijee
title: SET (Social and Emotional Training): a Swedish universal SEL intervention delivered by ordinary teachers in regular classrooms
description: SET is a longitudinal universal social and emotional learning intervention launched by Kimber (2001a,b), in which two schools in one Swedish municipality participated from 2000 to 2005. It was "designed to fit into the standard school curriculum, using equivalent classroom space and replacing regular instruction time", delivered by ordinary teachers using a detailed manual and student workbooks. Teachers in Grades 1-5 delivered two 45-minute sessions weekly (400 sessions over five years) and Grades 6-9 one weekly session (200 sessions over five years).
requirements: Delivered by trained ordinary teachers within the regular school schedule; teachers received 33.5 hours of initial and ongoing training in the first year, provided by the intervention counsellor
constraints: The evaluation used a quasi-experimental design with no randomization of schools and classes; the intervention targeted students from a low socioeconomic catchment area, which the authors say may limit generalizability
target_learners: students in Grades 1-9 in Swedish compulsory school
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competencies such as self-awareness, empathy, self-regulation and relationship skills
examples: Teachers in Grades 1-5 delivered two 45 minutes sessions of SET instruction every week, for a total of 80 sessions per year and 400 sessions over the five years of the intervention
key_sources: Alli Klapp, Clive Belfield, Brooks Bowden, Henry Levin, Robert Shand, Sabine Zander. (2017). A benefit-cost analysis of a long-term intervention on social and emotional learning in compulsory school. International Journal of Emotional Education, 9(1), 3-19. https://www.um.edu.mt/ijee

article_title: The Effectiveness of Computers on Vocabulary Learning among Preschool Children: A Semiotic Approach
citation: Basoz, T. & Can, T., D. (2016). The effectiveness of computers on vocabulary learning among preschool children: A semiotic approach. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science, 11(1), 02-08. http://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/cjes/
title: Semiotic approach to preschool foreign-language vocabulary instruction
description: The study grounds both instruction types in semiotics, the study of signs and sign processes called semiosis, applied to foreign language learning as educational semiotics. In early language learning, pictures are central because "a picture represents a wide variety of meaning by the use of signs". In the experiment, semiosis was provided by the researcher's verbal and visual cues in the TVI group and by the computer itself in the CAVI group, with both groups studying the same 20 target words over four weeks.
requirements: Instruction must provide meaningful sign systems, with pictures or visual cues acting as conveyors of meaning for the target words
constraints: The article states there was no prior research on teaching vocabulary through semiosis in EFL preschool context
target_learners: preschool children (5-year-olds) learning English as a foreign language
examples: Both experimental groups learned the same 20 target words (e.g. cat, dog, lemon, to dance) with semiosis supplied either by the computer or by the researcher's verbal and visual cues.
key_sources: Basoz, T. & Can, T., D. (2016). The effectiveness of computers on vocabulary learning among preschool children: A semiotic approach. Cypriot Journal of Educational Science, 11(1), 02-08. http://sproc.org/ojs/index.php/cjes/

article_title: Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge
citation: Ajitoni, S. O., & Gbadamosi, T. V. (2015). Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge. JISTE Vol. 19, No. 2. https://www.jiste.org
title: Four-phase service learning procedure: preparation, action, reflection, demonstration/celebration
description: The article operationalises service learning as a four-phase instructional sequence in which pupils connect a curriculum concept to a local environmental issue, carry out a service project, reflect on it, and present what they learned. In Phase 2 "The teacher assists the pupils to organize the project themselves and develop a work plan and carry out the service such as making of sand bags and planting of trees to control erosion". The pattern was delivered over eight weeks by trained facilitators.
requirements: A teacher or facilitator guides pupils to link the concept with an environmental issue in the school/community, and structured time is provided for reflection
examples: Pupils made sand bags and planted trees to control erosion and washed toilets as service activities
key_sources: Ajitoni, S. O., & Gbadamosi, T. V. (2015). Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge. JISTE Vol. 19, No. 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1177058

article_title: The Effect of Project Based Learning on Seventh Grade Students' Academic Achievement
citation: Kızkapan, O. & Bektaş, O. (2017). The Effect of Project Based Learning on Seventh Grade Students' Academic Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 10(1), 37-54. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_1_3.pdf
title: Seven-step PBL lesson plan structure
description: The article's PBL lesson plans follow a seven-step sequence covering the full project cycle from topic selection to evaluation. As printed, "Lesson plan based on PBL included seven steps. These were the determination of the topics, organization of the groups, planning the project, application of the project, planning the presentation, making the presentation, and the evaluation." All curriculum objectives were placed on both PBL and traditional lesson plans to ensure equality of coverage across conditions.
requirements: All objectives placed on the lesson plans to ensure equality between conditions
Groups of four or five students for hands-on activities
constraints: In this study students missed some objectives while preparing their own projects, whereas the teacher covered all objectives in the control group
target_learning_goals: Structure and properties of matter concepts
examples: First-week activities included an electrification activity with pen, wool, balloon and paper, and a ball-and-bowl atomic model activity

article_title: Effects of a School-Based Social-Emotional and Character Development Program on Self-Esteem Levels and Processes: a Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Silverthorn, N., DuBois, D. L., Lewis, K. M., Reed, A., Bavarian, N., Day, J., Ji, P., Acock, A. C., Vuchinich, S., & Flay, B. R. (2017). Effects of a School-Based Social-Emotional and Character Development Program on Self-Esteem Levels and Processes: A Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial. SAGE Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244017713238
title: Self-Esteem Enhancement Theory (SET)
description: Self-esteem enhancement theory (SET; DuBois et al., 2009) posits that strategies for obtaining or sustaining self-esteem — cognitive, behavioral, and affective — have direct implications for outcomes such as health, well-being, and academic achievement. The outcome of these strategies forms a feedback loop: successful efforts to feel worthy reinforce the behaviors, while unsuccessful efforts are adjusted. The article evaluates Positive Action as an intervention "oriented strongly toward cultivating adaptive and healthy ways of developing and sustaining self-esteem, consistent with the SET model".
requirements: Interventions aiming to promote adaptive self-esteem processes must teach youth strategies that build a healthy foundation for self-worth and provide supports and reinforcement for using them
constraints: The study provides only initial evidence for the SET model, with effects small in magnitude
target_learners: developing children and adolescents in elementary and middle school
target_learning_goals: adaptive self-esteem formation and maintenance strategies
positive self-evaluations in school and peer domains
examples: The Positive Action curriculum's first unit teaches the Thoughts–Actions–Feelings about Self Circle, sensitizing students to the motivation to feel good about oneself and the potential to achieve such feelings through positive or negative behaviors
key_sources: Silverthorn, N., DuBois, D. L., Lewis, K. M., Reed, A., Bavarian, N., Day, J., Ji, P., Acock, A. C., Vuchinich, S., & Flay, B. R. (2017). Effects of a School-Based Social-Emotional and Character Development Program on Self-Esteem Levels and Processes: A Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial. SAGE Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2158244017713238

article_title: The Effect of Using Self-Monitoring Strategies in Social Studies Course on Self-Monitoring, Self-Regulation and Academic Achievement
citation: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905
title: Set of self-monitoring strategies for Social Studies lessons (checklists, rubrics, self-created graphics, self-evaluation)
description: The article's independent variable is a set of individual plans used to increase self-help in academic, behavioral, individual and social areas, called self-monitoring strategies. The article lists "using control lists, using rubrics and rating scales, creating his/her own graphic, writing learning outcomes, critical writing, keeping a reflective diary, creating comparison (decision making) matrices and making a self -evaluation". In the experiment, the first experimental group used checklists and rubrics during class time, while the second experimental group created their own graphics and made self-evaluations at the end of the class period.
requirements: The article states teacher competencies are vital in implementing these strategies (N=5 teachers) and that enough time must be allocated for them to contribute to improving student behaviors
constraints: The article reports these strategies cause trial and implementation difficulties within an intensive curriculum, and that students were not adequately informed about how the techniques contribute to their development
target_learners: fifth-grade primary school students in Social Studies course
examples: Experimental group 1 applied checklists and rubrics during the class period; experimental group 2 created their own graphics and made self-evaluations at the end of the class period
key_sources: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905

article_title: Text-Based Vocabulary Intervention Training Study: Supporting Fourth Graders with Low Reading Comprehension and Learning Disabilities
citation: Solís, M., Scammacca, N., Barth, A. E., & Roberts, G. J. (2017). Text-based Vocabulary Intervention Training Study: Supporting Fourth Graders with Low Reading Comprehension and Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 15(1), 103-115.
title: Self-regulation checklist with goal setting and BEST attribution statements
description: A student-facing checklist provided to each student in the intervention condition. It "consisted of sections to establish goals of vocabulary learning, monitor learning through self-monitoring statements before and after the lesson, and reflect on goal attainment." Students set a goal for how many vocabulary words to learn and self-assessed attribution statements labeled Believe, Execute, Stay with it, and Think before and after each lesson. Students completed the checklist for each of the eight lessons, and assessment of vocabulary goals was based on accurately using vocabulary in a sentence.
requirements: Completed by students at the start and end of each lesson alongside the vocabulary and text-based reading routine
target_learners: Fourth graders with low reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of reading and learning behavior
examples: Students completed the checklist each lesson, setting goals such as how many new and old words to use and self-assessing the BEST statements
key_sources: Solís, M., Scammacca, N., Barth, A. E., & Roberts, G. J. (2017). Text-based Vocabulary Intervention Training Study: Supporting Fourth Graders with Low Reading Comprehension and Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities: A Contemporary Journal, 15(1), 103-115. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1141988

article_title: Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students' Independence and Writing Competence
citation: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a
title: Three-step self-assessment process: self-monitoring, self-judgment, and learning targets with instructional correctives
description: The article describes self-assessment as a formative process in which students "reflect on and evaluate the quality of their work and learning" against explicitly stated criteria (Andrade & Du, 2007, as cited). It unfolds in three steps: self-monitoring, where students attend to external standards such as language accuracy and text organization; self-judgment, where they judge achievement against established standards and criteria, often via a teacher-provided rubric; and learning targets and instructional correctives, where students select subsequent objectives to fix misunderstandings and improve performance. The study operationalises this process with checklists and analytical scoring rubrics in EFL writing lessons.
requirements: Explicitly stated goals or criteria must be available to students, e.g. a rubric of assessing writing that guides meaningful judgment
constraints: The article frames the process for language learning contexts, specifically EFL writing of genre texts
target_learning_goals: writing competence in short and long functional genre texts
examples: In the experiment, experimental-group students used a self-assessment checklist and analytical scoring rubric across pre-writing, writing, revising, and proof-reading phases
key_sources: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a

article_title: Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students' Independence and Writing Competence
citation: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a
title: Self-assessment writing pattern: co-constructed criteria, process-and-product orientation, and peer proof-reading
description: Table 1 contrasts the self-assessment treatment with conventional assessment along five dimensions. Assessment tools, tasks and criteria are "developed and determined by the teacher in collaboration with the students", and students are involved in evaluation; scoring occurs at the end of each writing step via self-assessment checklist and analytical scoring rubric; the writing process spans pre-writing, writing, revising, and proof-reading rather than drafting-final writing; and a proof-reading phase lets students read and judge peer work and receive peer input. The control condition was teacher-structured, product-oriented, and individual.
requirements: Self-assessment checklist and analytical scoring rubric available at each writing step
Collaboration between teacher and students in determining assessment tools, tasks, and criteria
constraints: Evaluated in junior secondary EFL writing of descriptive, procedure, and short functional texts
target_learning_goals: student independence and responsibility for learning
examples: Experimental-group students proof-read with peers, gaining input on how to improve writing quality, while control students revised only from teacher comments
key_sources: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a

article_title: Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students' Independence and Writing Competence
citation: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a
title: Self-assessment checklist and analytical scoring rubric with multi-source feedback
description: The treatment instruments were a 30-item independence questionnaire-derived checklist and an analytical scoring rubric used at each writing step. Students analysed their own writing with the checklist and rubric, receiving "frequent feedback from self -realization" that was strengthened by teacher and peer feedback, so they could recognise strengths and weaknesses from several directions. The writing tests showed very high inter-rater reliability (0.97 invitation, 0.81 descriptive, 0.96 procedure), and the questionnaire showed very high reliability (0.91).
requirements: Criteria made available to students so they can compare their work against the standards by which it is judged
constraints: Content validity and reliability were established with two expert judges and try-outs in this Indonesian junior secondary setting
target_learning_goals: self-editing and revising of genre texts
examples: Students in the experimental group evaluated their writing in terms of expressing their ideas and its organization using the checklist and rubric
key_sources: Ratminingsih, N. M., Marhaeni, A. A. I. N., & Vigayanti, L. P. D. (2018). Self-Assessment: The Effect on Students’ Independence and Writing Competence. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 277-290. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11320a

article_title: Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students
citation: Subahi, N. H. (2019). Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students. World Journal of Education, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n2p90
title: Two-part sex education misconception test with dual answer and justification items
description: The misconception test measures the prevalence of misconceptions in the Family Planning and Reproduction unit. Each question has two parts: a four-choice concept answer and a second part requiring a scientific justification for the answer, with the justification mark not counted if the first part is wrong. The initial form comprised 21 items; item-total correlations ranged 0.48-0.79 and "Alpha Cronbach coefficient was calculated and got (0.97), reflecting the high reliability of the test."
requirements: Answer choices were based on students' results in the pilot study
Appropriate answering time was estimated at 35 minutes
constraints: Designed for the Family Planning and Reproduction unit and reviewed for appropriateness to female students' level
examples: The test was applied pre- and post- to both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Subahi, N. H. (2019). Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students. World Journal of Education, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n2p90

article_title: Using a Digital Planetarium for Teaching Seasons to Undergraduates
citation: Ka Chun Yu, Kamran Sahami, Victoria Sahami, Larry C. Sessions. (2015). Using A Digital Planetarium For Teaching Seasons To Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 2(1). https://www.cluteinstitute.com
title: Seasons module alternating Earth-based and space-based reference frames with discrepant evidence
description: The ALIVE seasons instructional module follows the Willard & Roseman learning progression and AAAS benchmarks, beginning with diurnal solar motion from different latitudes and times of year before introducing space-based perspectives. "The lecture on seasons intersperses Earth-bound views of the sky from different latitudes with orbital views looking back at Earth, while the instructor connects the two different sets of perspectives in the oral presentation." Discrepant information counters the distance misconception, and graphical markers (cardinal directions, meridian, altitude-azimuth grid, ecliptic line) orient the audience.
requirements: A live navigator controlling the visualization software alongside an instructor following a shared lecture outline
constraints: Because of time constraints, the sequence of visuals was usually strictly followed for each topic
target_learning_goals: apparent solar motion across the year
length of day variation by latitude
examples: The virtual camera switches between Earth-based views of the Sun in the sky and space-based views of Earth's illumination at different times of year
key_sources: Ka Chun Yu, Kamran Sahami, Victoria Sahami, Larry C. Sessions. (2015). Using A Digital Planetarium For Teaching Seasons To Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 2(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1101071

article_title: The Combined Impact of the Flipped Classroom, Collaborative Learning, on Students' Learning of Key Marketing Concepts
citation: Motameni, R. (2018). The Combined Impact of the Flipped Classroom, Collaborative Learning, on Students' Learning of key Marketing Concepts. Journal of University Teaching & Learning Practice, 15(3). https://ro.uow.edu.au/jutlp/vol15/iss3/4
title: Spread a collaborative group project across the semester with clearly delineated session tasks rather than a final-weeks report
description: The article recommends that "a collaborative comprehensive group project consist of many interrelated components and be spread across the semester, as opposed to requiring students to prepare the final report, in its entirety, during the last few weeks of the semester". In the study, students completed seven collaborative sessions with predetermined objectives, performing 19 detailed tasks guided by a seven-page blueprint integrated with the textbook. Project information, reading assignments and tutorials should be carefully prepared and communicated in advance.
requirements: All relevant information, reading assignments, tutorials and online assignments should be carefully prepared in advance and communicated effectively
Project objectives need to be unambiguous and tasks in each session delineated clearly
constraints: Scheduling meetings among students was the most important impediment, given course loads and work and family demands
target_learners: undergraduate students working in project teams
target_learning_goals: critical thinking through considering others' ideas
examples: The instructor prepared a seven-page single-spaced guideline requiring seven collaborative sessions from mid-September to early December to perform 19 detailed tasks
key_sources: Motameni, R. (2018). The Combined Impact of the Flipped Classroom, Collaborative Learning, on Students' Learning of key Marketing Concepts. Journal of University Teaching & Learning Practice, 15(3). https://ro.uow.edu.au/jutlp/vol15/iss3/4

article_title: The Relative Impact of Aligning Tier 2 Intervention Materials with Classroom Core Reading Materials in Grades K-2
citation: Foorman, B. R., Herrera, S., & Dombek, J. (2018). The relative impact of aligning Tier 2 intervention materials with classroom core reading materials in grades K–2. The Elementary School Journal, 118(3). https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/journals/esj
title: Select Tier 2 intervention materials with credible evidence of effectiveness, whether embedded in or stand-alone from the core program
description: The article argues that schools choosing Tier 2 materials should weigh empirical evidence, not just alignment or cost. Embedded materials are attractive because they are "aligned with standards and classroom instruction and do not require the purchase of additional materials", but they are "rarely evaluated empirically"; an alternative is materials outside the core program with "credible evidence of effectiveness on reading and language outcomes, such as the ratings provided by the WWC". This study tested both options head to head.
requirements: Access to WWC evidence ratings or comparable empirical evaluation evidence for candidate Tier 2 materials
Capacity to implement either option with fidelity in daily small-group sessions
constraints: In this trial the two options produced similar outcomes on average, so evidence ratings alone did not determine relative impact
target_learners: At-risk K–2 students in low-performing schools receiving Tier 2 small-group intervention
target_learning_goals: Reading and language outcomes in grades K–2
examples: The study selected Sound Partners for having the strongest WWC evidence in alphabetics, fluency, and comprehension, and compared it against the embedded Strategic Intervention materials
key_sources: Foorman, B. R., Herrera, S., & Dombek, J. (2018). The relative impact of aligning Tier 2 intervention materials with classroom core reading materials in grades K–2. The Elementary School Journal, 118(3). https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/journals/esj

article_title: The Effect of Using Vocabulary Flash Card on Iranian Pre-University Students' Vocabulary Knowledge
citation: Maryam Eslahcar Komachali, Mohammadreza Khodareza. (2012). The Effect of Using Vocabulary Flash Card on Iranian Pre-University Students' Vocabulary Knowledge. International Education Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n3p134
title: Seven-step vocabulary flash card (VFC)
description: The VFC is a two-sided card the article presents as a new vocabulary learning tool. Per the article, "This seven-step vocabulary flash card consisted of word entity, word pronunciation, different parts of speech, synonyms and antonyms, dictionary example (Oxford Dictionary), learner's example and L1 definitions." The front page carries the L2 word, pronunciation and word forms; the back page carries examples and the L1 translation. Cards were made by the researcher and used across eight sessions with about 7 to 8 new words per session.
requirements: Both sides of the flash card should be used, with letters visible and large enough for the whole classroom
constraints: The flash card used in this research was limited to vocabulary from the students' textbook
target_learners: female Iranian pre-university EFL students aged 18
target_learning_goals: vocabulary knowledge, including meaning, pronunciation, word forms and spelling
examples: In the study, new words of each lesson were presented to the experimental group through vocabulary flash cards, with a warm-up review of previous words at the start of each session
key_sources: Maryam Eslahcar Komachali, Mohammadreza Khodareza. (2012). The Effect of Using Vocabulary Flash Card on Iranian Pre-University Students' Vocabulary Knowledge. International Education Studies, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n3p134

article_title: The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills
citation: Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Self-explanation as a constructivist learning strategy in which learners explain and check their own understanding
description: The article frames self-explanation as a general learning strategy grounded in Constructivist Theory: "Self-explanation strategy occurs when learners try to explain and clarify concepts for themselves, and check their own understanding of those concepts, which in turn generates mental coherence and help achieve better learning." In this study students wrote their explanations of programming tasks and worked examples. The article presents it as a mental process engaged during reading that helps learners understand complex, new material.
requirements: Learners must actually produce explanations of the material, in this study by writing what they understood about the programming task
constraints: Studies on self-explanation in computer programming are scarce according to the article, with prior work mainly from the 1990s on Lisp
target_learning_goals: understanding programming concepts and acquiring programming skills
examples: Students in the experimental group wrote self-explanations about programming tasks and worked examples, and were told the explanations would be graded
key_sources: Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1133008

article_title: The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills
citation: Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Three modes of implementing self-explanation: silent reflection, thinking aloud, and writing thoughts
description: The article organizes self-explanation implementation into a three-branch taxonomy: "The literature shows that there are three modes or methods that can be applied to achieve the desired benefits of the self-explaining strategy". These are silent reflection, thinking aloud (which the article says enhances metacognitive awareness), and writing thoughts. The writing mode is described as more effective for science subjects and for learners who find it difficult to express thinking audibly, which is why this study used written self-explanations.
requirements: The chosen mode must be monitorable; the article notes silent reflection is hard to monitor in learning studies
constraints: Mode suitability varies: writing suits learners with difficulty in intensive reading and scientific problem solving, while speaking suits proficient readers learning theoretical topics
target_learners: high school and college learners of technical subjects
target_learning_goals: deeper understanding of new concepts through learner-generated explanations
examples: This study adopted the writing-of-thoughts mode: students wrote directly what they understood about the programming task and worked examples
key_sources: Riyadh Alhassan. (2017). The Effect of Employing Self-Explanation Strategy with Worked Examples on Acquiring Computer Programing Skills. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.6. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1133008

article_title: How Much Videos Win over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners
citation: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://tojet.net/
title: Seven listening strategies for the classroom
description: The article enumerates, citing Nihei (2002) and Andrade (2006), seven listening strategies: listening for the main idea, for specific details, to predict, to make inferences, using nonverbal cues, for taking notes, and for imitation or reproduction. Each is described with classroom behaviours, e.g. prediction via "speakers' gestures and facial expressions, plus rhetorical markers as well as keywords". The article argues foreign learners should be taught these strategies because most do not know how to listen in the foreign language.
requirements: Students who do not know how to listen to the foreign language should be taught listening strategies, per the article citing Brown (2001)
key_sources: Yasin, B., Mustafa, F., & Permatasari, R. (2018). How Much Videos Win Over Audios in Listening Instruction for EFL Learners. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165770

article_title: Mnemonic Aids during Tests: Worthless Frivolity or Effective Tool in Statistics Education?
citation: Karen H. Larwin, David A. Larwin, Jennifer Gorman. (2008). Mnemonic aids during tests: Worthless frivolity or effective tool in statistics education? Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mnemonic+aids+during+tests+statistics+education
title: If statistics instructors permit exam aids, student-generated aids are the aid of choice
description: The article concludes that when instructors allow any in-test aid in college statistics courses, self-generated aids should be preferred: students who prepared their own aids significantly outperformed those given instructor-prepared aids or an open textbook. The authors state that if aids are allowed, "the self-generated aids is the mnemonic aids of choice," while noting self-generated aids were not shown superior to allowing no aids at all.
requirements: Instructor must permit aids and give students an opportunity to prepare their own aid before the exam
constraints: The benefit over standard no-aids testing was not demonstrated conclusively in this study's data
target_learners: college students in introductory applied statistics courses
target_learning_goals: exam performance on constructed-response and application problems in statistics
examples: In the study, each of four course sections experienced all four testing conditions across four exams in a randomly determined order, with student-prepared aids on an 11 X 8.5 inch sheet of paper
key_sources: Karen H. Larwin, David A. Larwin, Jennifer Gorman. (2008). Mnemonic aids during tests: Worthless frivolity or effective tool in statistics education? Journal of Instructional Pedagogies. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Mnemonic+aids+during+tests+statistics+education

article_title: Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model
citation: Michael R. Vitale & Nancy R. Romance. (2013). Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Semantic relatedness as learning leverage: vocabulary is acquired largely inferentially through underlying semantic dimensions
description: Drawing on Latent Semantic Analysis, the article frames vocabulary acquisition as inferential: underlying semantic dimensions represent relatedness among words, phrases, and prose that provide the "learning leverage" through which words are understood. Because children acquire vocabulary too rapidly for direct teaching, the majority of vocabulary must be gained inferentially, so instruction should develop general semantic (conceptual) meaning rather than only literal word-by-word understanding.
requirements: Instruction must engage students in inferring meanings of new words from semantic context rather than pre-teaching every word
constraints: The article notes definitional variation in the literature over how words and word understanding are counted (word roots vs. root variants; recognition vs. in-depth understanding)
examples: The intervention operationalized the account by having students infer meanings of untaught target words substituted into story sentences (Part 3)
key_sources: Michael R. Vitale & Nancy R. Romance. (2013). Accelerating Vocabulary Development and Reading Comprehension in Grades 3-4-5 through an Inductive Vocabulary Model. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563063

article_title: The Impact of Computer Assisted Grammar Teaching on EFL Pupils' Performance in Jordan
citation: Abdallah M Abu Naba'h. (2012). The impact of computer assisted grammar teaching on EFL pupils’ performance in Jordan. International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology (IJEDICT), 8(1), 71-90. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu//viewarticle.php?id=1408
title: Self-paced CALL grammar program with audio-visual explanation, exercises, and immediate feedback per section
description: The article's software embodies a repeating lesson-unit design: each grammatical sub-title is divided into components comprising audio-visual explanation and examples, exercises to check understanding, and a Test Yourself section, with "An immediate feedback is received after the completion of each section." Drills support overall understanding and a comprehensive exam drawn from General Secondary Certificate examinations closes the program. Learners may move freely between components at their own pace.
requirements: Content validated by TEFL and curriculum-design specialists; exercises with model answers and a correction system
constraints: Designed for one grammatical topic (the passive voice) in the first secondary curriculum
target_learning_goals: English grammar structures, specifically the passive voice
examples: The researcher classified gathered passive-voice data into four sub-titles: present verbs, past verbs, modal auxiliaries, and problematic issues, then divided each into components.
key_sources: Abdallah M Abu Naba'h. (2012). The impact of computer assisted grammar teaching on EFL pupils’ performance in Jordan. International Journal of Education and Development using Information and Communication Technology (IJEDICT), 8(1), 71-90. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu//viewarticle.php?id=1408

article_title: The Effect of Using a Proposed Teaching Strategy Based on the Selective Thinking on Students' Acquisition Concepts in Mathematics
citation: Dr. Ahmad Hassan Qudah. (2016). The Effect of Using a Proposed Teaching Strategy Based on the Selective Thinking on Students' Acquisition Concepts in Mathematics. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.2. https://www.iiste.org
title: Selective thinking strategy: a three-stage concept-acquisition pattern using positive and negative examples, hypothesis testing, and analysis of thinking
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern for teaching concepts in which, per the article, "In a form of selective thinking exposed students to examples that make up the concept as well as al-Qaida is determined by which this concept". It proceeds through three stages: presenting data and identifying qualities (the "teacher presents examples of positive and negative examples without providing assistance"), testing or accessing the concept by giving more examples and having students give examples from their experiences and redefine the concept, and thinking strategy analysis in which students describe ideas and discuss hypotheses. The learner classifies affiliated and non-affiliated examples, receives feedback after each test, and proposes own examples.
requirements: The teacher presents examples without declaring or mentioning the concept name in advance
Students receive appropriate feedback after each test attempt and repeat attempts until reaching the concept name
constraints: The article applies the pattern to teaching basic mathematical concepts to classroom-teacher students at university level
target_learners: classroom teacher (grade-teacher specialization) students at Al al-Bayt University
target_learning_goals: classification of affiliated and non-affiliated examples of a concept
examples: In the study, the experimental group was taught according to the selective thinking strategy while the control group studied the traditional way (lecture and discussion)
key_sources: Dr. Ahmad Hassan Qudah. (2016). The Effect of Using a Proposed Teaching Strategy Based on the Selective Thinking on Students' Acquisition Concepts in Mathematics. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1089778

article_title: Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool
citation: Nilüfer Okur Akçay. (2016). Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n3p83
title: Researcher-developed sense organs achievement test with drawing, cut-and-paste, and matching components
description: A data collection tool developed by the researcher "to determine the knowledge levels of the students about organs like ear, tongue, eye and skin and senses like hearing, smelling, tasting, seeing and sensing". It was calibrated to the children's observed rather than expected levels after readiness questions showed low preparedness, and included drawing items, a cut-and-paste organ-placement test, and a matching test pairing objects with senses. Children who could not draw organs proportionally were given full grades.
requirements: Items calibrated to children's observed developmental levels rather than expected levels
Pre-cut organs and adult scissor help for the cut-and-paste component
constraints: Developed specifically for this study's sample and topic; no validity or reliability statistics are printed
target_learners: preschool children aged four to five
target_learning_goals: assessing knowledge of sense organs and their functions
examples: A pretest drawing showed a child scratching out all organs despite teacher repetition; the posttest drawing showed attempted organ drawings
key_sources: Nilüfer Okur Akçay. (2016). Implementation of Cooperative Learning Model in Preschool. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n3p83

article_title: Mind the Gap: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Dorsett, R., Rienzo, C., Rolfe, H., Burns, H., Robertson, B.-A., Thorpe, B., & Wall, K. (2014). Mind the Gap: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Mapping each session of a family learning programme to a named learning disposition with goal and reflection sheets
description: The animation course used a repeating lesson-level design in which each session carried a named metacognition focus and families completed goal and reflection sheets: "goal and reflection sheets that allowed the families to record their learning experiences". Each element of the programme (story planning, modelling, trialling equipment, exploring animation techniques, filming, editing) was matched to one of the 5Rs, and the progression was mapped so that metacognitive elements and the animation process were closely associated to maximise opportunities for transfer.
requirements: Standardised course materials (presentation, family handbook, teachers' handbook) and goal and reflection sheets for each session
constraints: Fidelity depended on consistent use of course materials when school staff changed; scheduling and staff commitment varied across schools
target_learners: Year 4 pupils and their parents or guardians working together
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of the learning process
creating learning goals and reflecting on progress
examples: Session 3 (Responsibility) was the most technical session in which families got to grips with the software, completed model making and started filming, completing goal and reflection sheets
key_sources: Dorsett, R., Rienzo, C., Rolfe, H., Burns, H., Robertson, B.-A., Thorpe, B., & Wall, K. (2014). Mind the Gap: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581160

article_title: "I Like Computers but My Favourite Is Playing outside with My Friends": Young Children's Beliefs about Computers
citation: Hatzigianni, M. (2014). 'I like computers but my favourite is playing outside with my friends': Young children's beliefs about computers. International Research in Early Childhood Education, 5(1). https://www.education.monash.edu.au/irecejournal/
title: Seven-month integrated computer intervention with 32 activities using open-ended and close-ended software
description: The intervention was a program of 32 computer activities (four software packages, eight activities each) designed by the researcher and implemented with two teachers over seven months. It followed an integration philosophy in which "the computer was 'one more centre' in the preschool class and the extension of curriculum areas was attempted". Software included open-ended programs (Paint, Kid Pix Deluxe 4) for exploring and creating, and close-ended programs (Adiboo, Putt-Putt Joins the Circus) for mouse control and curriculum-linked activities. Preschool children participated twice weekly for 20-30 minutes; preps once weekly for 45 minutes.
requirements: Teachers were given lesson plans, examples and written and electronic instructions in advance, with regular researcher contact to ensure consistency of delivery
constraints: Software selection was limited by availability, usability and teachers' prior unfamiliarity with the programs
target_learners: children aged 44-79 months in preschool and prep classes
target_learning_goals: familiarity with computers as tools integrated across curriculum areas
curriculum skills such as shapes, letters, numbers and animals
examples: An example activity had preschoolers practice drawing basic shapes with Paint ('Learn to draw with shapes') when the curriculum aim was learning shapes
key_sources: Hatzigianni, M. (2014). 'I like computers but my favourite is playing outside with my friends': Young children's beliefs about computers. International Research in Early Childhood Education, 5(1). https://www.education.monash.edu.au/irecejournal/

article_title: New Evidence on Self-Affirmation Effects and Theorized Sources of Heterogeneity from Large-Scale Replications
citation: Hanselman, P., Rozek, C. S., Grigg, J., & Borman, G. D. (2017). New evidence on self-affirmation effects and theorized sources of heterogeneity from large-scale replications. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 405-424. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000141
title: Self-affirmation theory: values-affirmation writing exercises buffer identity threat by expanding the working self-concept.
description: The article describes self-affirmation interventions as brief writing exercises asking students to reflect on meaningful personal values, designed to allow students to "reaffirm their self-integrity." The theory holds that these activities restore a sense of worth in the face of identity threats, muting detrimental stress responses. Drawing on Critcher and Dunning's "affirmation as perspective" model, the article explains that self-affirmation "expand[s] the contents of the working concept—thus narrowing the scope of any threat," so that threats to a specific aspect of identity become less salient and stress responses that impair performance are reduced.
requirements: Activities must be implemented before stressful events to short-circuit negative recursive cycles, and presented as a normal classroom activity rather than as evaluative or beneficial.
constraints: The article reports that effects are theorized to depend on subtle features of delivery, individual characteristics, and social context, and that its own large-scale replication found no benefits, highlighting potential fragility when implemented widely.
target_learners: middle school students subject to racial/ethnic identity threat (Black and Hispanic students)
target_learning_goals: reduce racial achievement gaps in academic performance (GPA)
examples: The intervention consisted of 15-20 minute classroom writing exercises administered several times per year by teachers, timed before formative and state assessments.
key_sources: Hanselman, P., Rozek, C. S., Grigg, J., & Borman, G. D. (2017). New evidence on self-affirmation effects and theorized sources of heterogeneity from large-scale replications. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 405-424. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000141

article_title: A Study on Simulation Methods in Academic Success with Reference to Teaching Biology for Education Students
citation: Sasikala, P., & Tanyong, S. (2016). A Study on Simulation Methods in Academic Success With Reference To Teaching Biology for Education Students. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105115
title: Semi-structured interview form for assessing student perceptions of simulation-supported biology education.
description: The researchers prepared a semi-structured interview form containing 10 open-ended questions administered to experimental group students to determine their ideas about simulation-supported biology education. Each interview took about 8 minutes per participant and was recorded. Qualitative data were analyzed using a coding technique based on notions received from the data, with responses "encoded upon the concepts of biology."
requirements: Administered at the end of the experimentation period
Recorded interviews with approximately 8 minutes per participant
constraints: Applied only to the experimental group students
target_learners: Education students receiving simulation-based biology instruction
target_learning_goals: Student perceptions and satisfaction with simulation-based biology education
key_sources: Sasikala, P., & Tanyong, S. (2016). A Study on Simulation Methods in Academic Success With Reference To Teaching Biology for Education Students. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099628

article_title: Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills among Middle School Students with Disabilities
citation: Espelage, D. L., Rose, C. A., & Polanin, J. R. (2016). Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills Among Middle School Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education, 37(6), 323–332. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932515627475
title: Use universal SEL programming to build protective factors against bullying among students with disabilities
description: The article argues that universal SEL programs like SS-SSTP, which include "empathy training, emotion regulation, communication skills, and problem-solving strategies," serve students with disabilities because universal supports should be embedded across the entire student population regardless of service location. The RCT found significant gains in willingness to intervene and promising GPA gains. The authors conclude that schools "should begin to incorporate interventions that are designed to increase skill development."
requirements: Universal SEL instruction delivered with fidelity, supported by teacher training in the program rationale and implementation strategies
constraints: Gains in willingness to intervene emerged only after 2 years of instruction; empathy, caring, school belonging, and standardized test scores showed no significant effects
target_learners: middle school students with disabilities receiving special education services under IDEA
target_learning_goals: willingness to intervene in bullying situations
examples: Teachers in intervention schools completed a 4-hr training covering bully prevention research, lesson walkthroughs, and fidelity strategies before delivering 15 sixth-grade and 13 seventh- and eighth-grade lessons
key_sources: Espelage, D. L., Rose, C. A., & Polanin, J. R. (2016). Social-Emotional Learning Program to Promote Prosocial and Academic Skills Among Middle School Students With Disabilities. Remedial and Special Education, 37(6), 323–332. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932515627475

article_title: Changing Perceptions of Teachers Regarding the Importance and Competence of Their Principals as Leaders
citation: Grobler, B., Bisschoff, T., & Beeka, A. (2012). Changing perceptions of teachers regarding the importance and competence of their principals as leaders. South African Journal of Education, 32(1), 40-55. https://journals.co.za/handle/10520/EJC132899
title: Seven-dimension holistic leadership model for school principals
description: The holistic leadership model comprises seven dimensions: the creation of a professionally inviting culture, effective communication, an ethical foundation, a vision of excellence, empowerment of followers, personal mastery, and authentic collaboration. The model presents causal pathways among these dimensions, with the ethical foundation directly influencing effective communication, personal mastery, and authentic collaboration. The article states that "the seven factors involved in educational leadership influence one another in a holistic way" and that the model was confirmed using structural equation modelling with suitable fit indices.
requirements: The model requires consideration of the interdependent causal pathways among all seven dimensions when designing interventions for school principals.
constraints: The model was developed and tested in the South African context and may require contextualisation to other settings.
target_learning_goals: Develop holistic leadership capabilities across seven dimensions
Transform bureaucratic leadership practices toward collaborative approaches
examples: The intervention programme used the ethical foundation as a basis and employed group work and self-reflection strategies with 20 principals.
key_sources: Grobler, B., Bisschoff, T., & Beeka, A. (2012). Changing perceptions of teachers regarding the importance and competence of their principals as leaders. South African Journal of Education, 32(1), 40-55. https://journals.co.za/handle/10520/EJC132899

article_title: Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice
citation: Lancaster, J., & Bain, A. (2019). Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 44(2). https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol44/iss2/4
title: Self-organizing systems approach to course design, with embedded design as the pivotal principle
