description: A design framework derived from Bain's work on a self-organizing K-12 school and extended to higher education, in which "Self-organizing systems theory involves the application of six principles that enable change from the ground up": simple rules, embedded design, similarity at scale, emergent feedback, dispersed control, and a schema to guide action. Embedded design is treated as "the overarching and pivotal principle that guides application of all others". In this study it was applied to a pre-service inclusive education course to build deep, coherent pedagogical content knowledge.
requirements: Course content valued as important must be embedded at all levels of the course design, not delivered once
constraints: The article tests only the embedded design principle, not the other five principles, and in a single course at one university
target_learning_goals: pedagogical content knowledge about inclusive education and differentiation
examples: The study instantiated embedded design at four levels in a 13-week inclusive education course: quizzes, lesson-plan workshops, peer feedback, and assessment consequences
key_sources: Lancaster, J., & Bain, A. (2019). Designing University Courses to Improve Pre-Service Teachers' Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Evidence-Based Inclusive Practice. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 44(2). https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol44/iss2/4

article_title: Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria
citation: Fakolade, O. A. & Adeniyi, S. A. (2010). Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria. International Journal of Special Education, Vol 25 No 1. https://www.internationaljournalofspecialeducation.com
title: Treffinger's Self-Directed Learning Model: sequential development of independent-learning skills with shifting teacher and student roles
description: Treffinger's Self-Directed Model is designed for "moving students towards independent learning" through "the sequential development of skills in managing individual learning," building on gifted children's strengths and motivation by letting them study areas of interest. It rests on two assumptions: children learn better when involved in their own learning, and are more motivated when directing learning in areas of their own choice. As students assume more responsibility, the teacher moves from director to provider of options to facilitator, while the student moves from passive learner to director of learning and self-evaluator. The model was the second treatment in the study.
requirements: Not all gifted children are independent learners, so the model provides a structured way to develop self-management skills gradually rather than assuming students already possess them
constraints: In most classrooms the four basic instructional factors (goals, entering behaviour, procedures, performance assessment) are completely under the teacher's direction and control
target_learners: gifted and talented secondary school students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in English language and Mathematics
examples: Participants experienced 13 weeks of English and Mathematics sessions structured by the stages of the Self-Directed model as part of the treatment package
key_sources: Fakolade, O. A. & Adeniyi, S. A. (2010). Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria. International Journal of Special Education, Vol 25 No 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ890561

article_title: The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment
citation: Ng Sook Han, Ho Ket Li, Lee Choy Sin, Keng Pei Sin. (2012). The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). http://www.moj-es.net
title: Reflective writing intervention with seven guided prompts after chemistry lab experiments
description: The intervention is a reflective writing task administered after about one session (roughly 3 hours) of experimental work, using seven prompts adapted from Xu and Talanquer (2012), such as "What did you learn in this lab?" and "How would you improve what you did?". Individual written reports were collected from one member of each two-person lab group; 191 reports were gathered. The format of administration, completion and submission is described as convenient, and participants reported the writing load and questions were reasonable.
requirements: Administered after experimental work once the required theory has been covered in lectures
Prompts guiding students' reflections
constraints: Tested with first-semester general chemistry students in a single experiment at one institution
target_learners: undergraduate pharmacy and health sciences students in general chemistry
examples: Students in the treatment labs (G1 and G2) completed reflective writing for the chloride-determination experiment while control labs (G3 and G4) did not.
key_sources: Ng Sook Han, Ho Ket Li, Lee Choy Sin, Keng Pei Sin. (2012). The Evaluation of Students' Written Reflection on the Learning of General Chemistry Lab Experiment. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(4). http://www.moj-es.net

article_title: Adolescents' Self-Regulation Development via the Sensory Room System
citation: Aydar M. Kalimullin, Elena A. Kuvaldina & Julia Koinova-Zoellner. (2016). Adolescents' Self-Regulation Development Via the Sensory Room System. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(5), 663-671.
title: Self-regulation as management of psycho-emotional state controllable by external impacts (Prokhorov's term)
description: The article adopts A. O. Prokhorov's (2005) term, characterizing self-regulation as management of the psycho-emotional state of a person which can be controlled by external impacts, in particular by using the system of sensory room. Self-regulation is described as "a capacity to control your psycho-emotional state which is achieved by self-influence through the power of words (affirmation), visual images (visualization), control over your muscle tonus and breathing." The study operationalizes this through the sensory-room program's affirmation, visualization and psycho-physiological regulation exercises.
requirements: Self-influence techniques: affirmation (power of words), visualization (visual images), and control over muscle tonus and breathing
constraints: The article notes psychological and pedagogical researches had failed to pay enough attention to the sensory room system, with prior works only in teaching aids and practitioners' articles
examples: The program "Find yourself" applied this account by pairing affirmation and visualization with breathing-control and muscle-tonus exercises in the sensory room
key_sources: Aydar M. Kalimullin, Elena A. Kuvaldina & Julia Koinova-Zoellner. (2016). Adolescents' Self-Regulation Development Via the Sensory Room System. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(5), 663-671. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114271

article_title: Formation of Social Tolerance among Future Teachers
citation: Roman S. Nagovitsyn, Dana K. Bartosh, Aleksandr Y. Ratsimor, Yuri G. Maksimov. (2018). Formation of Social Tolerance Among Future Teachers. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.754
title: Seven-component scheme for forming social tolerance within the holistic university educational process
description: The article's organizing framework is a seven-part scheme spanning the definition of social tolerance as "benevolent respect for differences", the formation goal (understanding of social differences with active negative attitude toward asocial behavior), content (familiarity with history, culture and social interaction of subcultures), interactive methods, a substitution mechanism redirecting group energy into socially significant creative activity, influence on the causes of asocial behavior, and criteria (moral values, tolerance index, conflict-related competence). It was embedded fragment-wise in courses, electives and teaching practice.
requirements: Implementation within the integral educational process at the university, including disciplines of choice, practical classes and teaching practice
constraints: The scheme was tested only with future teachers in pedagogical university profiles over one semester
target_learners: university students training to be teachers
target_learning_goals: social tolerance for differences within legal norms
intolerance toward violations of moral norms
examples: Content was included by fragments in various educational courses and disciplines of choice, and experimental work was carried out in practical classes in student groups and during teaching practice
key_sources: Roman S. Nagovitsyn, Dana K. Bartosh, Aleksandr Y. Ratsimor, Yuri G. Maksimov. (2018). Formation of Social Tolerance Among Future Teachers. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.754

article_title: Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills
citation: Nurhan Aktaş & Hayati Akyol. (2020). Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills. https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2020.248.20
title: Self-determination theory as an explanatory account of how digital tool choice affects task participation and motivation
description: The article uses self-determination theory, defined as individuals determining their behaviour "with their own personal beliefs and value judgements, rather than with external factors", to explain how a digital tool affects a student's participation in a task. It states that "In the self-determination theory, three basic psychological needs, named autonomy, competence and relatedness, are found" and applies each need to the workshop: autonomy via student choice of applications, competence via feedback and perceived writing ability, relatedness via the task's meaning for the student's own life.
requirements: For motivation to be supported, students should be able to choose the tasks and digital tools they use
constraints: In this study the applications were selected by the researcher, so the autonomy need was limited
examples: The authors interpret the motivation decline through limited autonomy, undermined competence feelings, and weak relatedness of the workshop to students' school lives
key_sources: Nurhan Aktaş & Hayati Akyol. (2020). Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills. https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2020.248.20

article_title: Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing
citation: Ammar, Abdullah Mahmoud Ismial. (2016). Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(5). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.247
title: Separate and connected ways of knowing as complementary epistemic stances in argumentation
description: Drawing on Belenky et al.'s epistemic development model and Schneider and Ingram, 'ways of knowing' is "how one interprets the elements in a given situation and makes sense of the relationships among them". Separate knowers "play the doubting game", seeking loopholes and contrary evidence with a critical, detached stance; connected knowers "play the believing game", learn through empathy, and build on others' ideas. The article argues the two are complementary rather than distinct: "preference of certain ways of knowing depends on the context rather than being a personal trait", and connected knowing does not require giving up one's own views.
requirements: Assessment via a ways-of-knowing scale distinguishing connected and separate factors (the study used a 12-item, two-factor revalidated form)
Classroom conditions the article says are needed for transformation: reflective blogfolios "availed suitable conditions and effective tools for transforming students' ways of knowing"
constraints: Ways of knowing are flexible and context dependent rather than stable traits, so measurement reflects context-specific preferences
target_learners: learners in virtual and connectivist learning environments
examples: In this study pre-assessment scores indicated separate-leaning preferences; after the semester-long blogfolio treatment scores shifted toward connected knowing
key_sources: Ammar, Abdullah Mahmoud Ismial. (2016). Reflective Blogfolios in the Language Classroom: Impact on EFL Tertiary Students' Argumentative Writing Skills and Ways of Knowing. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(5). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.5p.247

article_title: The Effects of Learning Strategies Instruction on Metacognitive Knowledge, Using Metacognitive Skills and Academic Achievement (Primary Education Sixth Grade Turkish Course Sample)
citation: Muhittin ÇALIŞKAN & Ali Murat SÜNBÜL. (2011). The Effects of Learning Strategies Instruction on Metacognitive Knowledge, Using Metacognitive Skills and Academic Achievement (Primary Education Sixth Grade Turkish Course Sample). Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(1), 148-153. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ930514
title: Self-instructed learners as a metacognitive cycle of planning, strategy choice, monitoring, and revision
description: The article frames self-directed learning as a cycle in which "self-instructed" students determine goals, consider what they know, plan time, choose an appropriate learning strategy, perform it, check the result, and choose a new strategy if learning has not taken place. Metacognition is defined as individuals' awareness of their own cognitive structure, and metacognitive skills as deciding what strategy to use, monitoring learning, and changing strategy when needed. The study's intervention is designed to build this cycle in sixth graders.
requirements: Students need to know learning strategies in order to decide what strategy to use in a given learning situation
constraints: The article situates the full cycle at sixth grade and above, since younger students cannot use complex strategies independently
examples: The experimental group was taught underlining, margin note-taking, mental repetition, grouping, note-taking, summarizing, and conceptual mapping over 15 weeks
key_sources: Muhittin ÇALIŞKAN & Ali Murat SÜNBÜL. (2011). The Effects of Learning Strategies Instruction on Metacognitive Knowledge, Using Metacognitive Skills and Academic Achievement (Primary Education Sixth Grade Turkish Course Sample). Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(1), 148-153. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ919894

article_title: Impact of Co-Operative Learning Strategies in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2010). Impact of Co-operative Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 4, No. 2, August-October 2010.
title: A seven-activity co-operative learning sequence for grammar lessons
description: The article organises its co-operative learning treatment as a sequence of seven named team activities: "(i).Positive interdependence.(ii).Round-Table.(iii).Face–to-Faceinteraction.(iv).Write around.(v).Jigsaw Team.(vi).Team pair solo and (vii).Think–Pair Share." These structured team formats rotate roles so students practise grammar through peer interaction rather than teacher-led drill. The pattern was the treatment administered in Phases 3–6 of the study to both groups.
requirements: Small teams with students of different ability levels, with each member responsible for helping teammates learn
constraints: Evaluated only for English grammar with standard-X students in one school
target_learners: secondary students learning English as a second language
examples: The treatment phases administered Round-Table, Write around, Jigsaw Team, Team pair solo and Think-Pair Share activities before post-testing
key_sources: G. Singaravelu. (2010). Impact of Co-operative Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 4, No. 2, August-October 2010. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102270

article_title: The Effect of 3D Virtual Learning Environment on Secondary School Third Grade Students' Attitudes toward Mathematics
citation: İrfan Şimşek. (2016). The Effect of 3D Virtual Learning Environment on Secondary School Third Grade Students' Attitudes toward Mathematics. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(3). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Three-dimensional Mathematics Robot in Second Life
description: A three-dimensional Mathematics Robot developed in the Second Life virtual world, used to teach mathematics to secondary third-grade students so they can "see the 3D objects in mathematics courses in a concrete way, access the information outside of the school and provide them with an education through games." Students logged into SL from home in sessions of 3 hours on defined days, and the environment supported student-student interaction. The article evaluates its effect on attitudes with a pretest-posttest design.
requirements: Works in the Second Life three-dimensional online virtual world with avatars representing multiple users at the same time
Requires permission from the school principal and parent permission forms before application
constraints: Evaluated only with a one-group pretest-posttest design with 28 students in a single Istanbul school; no control group was used
target_learners: Secondary school third grade (seventh grade) students
target_learning_goals: Concrete understanding of three-dimensional objects and the Cartesian coordinate system in mathematics
examples: 28 students at Fatih Secondary School used the robot during the 2014-2015 academic year; a written exam prepared by the researcher covering the objective 'Student is able to explain two dimensional Cartesian coordinate system and use it' was applied as pretest
key_sources: İrfan Şimşek. (2016). The Effect of 3D Virtual Learning Environment on Secondary School Third Grade Students' Attitudes toward Mathematics. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1106361

article_title: Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context
citation: Mehmet ALTAY. (2017). Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(1), 42-52. https://novitasroyal.org
title: Hybrid semantic-mapping vocabulary strategy with paper templates, WordNet and WebspirationPro
description: The treatment used a hybrid vocabulary learning strategy combining a paper-based semantic mapping template with web-based resources. Each student received a template in which "the lexical semantic items could be stratified", with one template used as a schema for only one new lexical item. Students completed templates outside class from the coursebook word list, then relations were extended using WordNet and collected in WebspirationPro, online software to map ideas and concepts using visual graphics, giving each learner an individual learner dictionary of templates by semester's end.
requirements: One template per new lexical item; classification of relations done in class at the end of each coursebook unit; access to web-based resources such as WordNet and WebspirationPro
constraints: Practiced over 15 coursebook units with A1-level preparatory students at one Turkish state university
examples: Students carried out paper-based mapping outside class using the coursebook word list preloaded to the school website, and all data were collected in WebspirationPro after 15 units
key_sources: Mehmet ALTAY. (2017). Raising Awareness of Lexical Semantic Relations in Undergraduate EFL Context. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 11(1), 42-52. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167230

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course
citation: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Use multimedia selectively rather than in every learning situation
description: The article argues that although multimedia in computer-based learning is expected to increase understanding, "an excessive use of multimedia may or may not improve the learning effectiveness". Following Singh (2003), it recommends multimedia be used only when students have low prior knowledge, when students have low motivation, and when the multimedia is effectively designed. Applying multimedia in every situation uses many resources without necessarily yielding desirable results.
requirements: Multimedia must be effectively designed to contribute to learning effectiveness
constraints: Applying multimedia in every situation uses a lot of resources but does not necessarily provide a desirable result
target_learning_goals: understanding of learning materials presented with multimedia
examples: The article cites Najjar (1996), who found higher achievement for multimedia-based instruction, and Asoodeh (1993), who found animated visuals produced significantly higher mental-rotation scores than static visuals.
key_sources: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057334

article_title: The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency
citation: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21
title: A set of seven Cooperative Learning activities for developing EFL oral fluency
description: The article enumerates the Cooperative Learning activities the researcher selected for fostering peer interaction and communicative language development: "(Jigsaw - Round Table and Round Robin - Three-Step Interview - Role-Play -Numbered Heads Together - Think-Pair-Share - Carousel Brainstorming)." Each structure is described: jigsaw is a special form of information gap with specific information per member; Round Robin gives each person an equal chance to contribute orally while hindering evaluative talk; Three-Step Interview requires each person to produce and receive language; Think-Pair-Share moves through individual thinking, pair discussion and whole-class sharing. The experimental group practiced all prescribed topics through these activities for a whole month.
requirements: The article states that for small group learning to be truly cooperative, teachers must ensure positive interdependence, face-to-face interaction, individual accountability, and determination of each student's mastery level so students can support one another.
constraints: The article warns that placing socially unskilled students in a learning group and telling them to cooperate will not be successful; students must be taught the social skills needed for cooperation and motivated to use them.
target_learning_goals: Oral fluency of speaking, including vocabulary use, grammatical structures, smooth speaking, effective communication, and pronunciation and intonation
examples: Think-Pair-Share is implemented in four steps: groups of four listen to a teacher-posed question, individuals think and write responses, pairs read and discuss responses, and the teacher calls some students to share with the whole class.
key_sources: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21

article_title: Exceptionality and Peer Victimization Involvement in Late Childhood: Subtypes, Stability, and Social Marginalization
citation: Chin-Chih Chen, Jill V. Hamm, & Thomas W. Farmer. (2015). Exceptionality and Peer Victimization Involvement in Late Childhood: Subtypes, Stability, and Social Marginalization. Remedial and Special Education, 36(5).
title: SEALS (Supporting Early Adolescent Learning and Social Success) teacher professional development program
description: SEALS is a professional development model delivered to all sixth-grade teachers in intervention schools over a year in a cluster randomized trial. "The SEALS program is a professional development model that focuses on supporting teachers' use of proactive strategies to foster students' productive academic engagement while managing classroom behavior and social dynamics in ways that promote a positive classroom peer culture." It does not explicitly address peer victimization involvement but centers on fostering a positive and supportive social ecology. In this study it was associated with reduced perceptions of peer encouragement of bullying among students with exceptionalities, though not with subtype placement.
requirements: Year-long professional development for all sixth-grade teachers, delivered with implementation fidelity monitoring
constraints: The program does not explicitly address involvement in peer victimization; no intervention effect on subtype placement was found
target_learners: sixth-grade students in rural middle schools
target_learning_goals: reduced perceptions of peer encouragement of bullying
examples: Matched pairs of rural schools were recruited and one of each pair randomly assigned to receive SEALS; control schools received it at project end
key_sources: Chin-Chih Chen, Jill V. Hamm, & Thomas W. Farmer. (2015). Exceptionality and Peer Victimization Involvement in Late Childhood: Subtypes, Stability, and Social Marginalization. Remedial and Special Education, 36(5). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED588091

article_title: The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning
citation: Wang, X. (2015). The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.111
title: Semantic field theory: a language's vocabulary consists of interrelating networks of word relations, so words should be studied as an integrated system
description: Semantic field theory, brought to maturity by J. Trier in the 1930s, assumes that "the vocabulary of a language consists of many interrelating networks of relations between words". Word relations include synonymy, antonymy, homonymy, hyponymy and meronymy. The article presents it as the theoretical justification for teaching words in SR sets, but reports its finding as not in line with the theory.
requirements: Vocabulary treated as an integrated lexical system rather than a random list
constraints: The study's delayed-test result did not support the theory's teaching implication for these learners
examples: The article classifies its 31 collected SR sets into five relationship types: synonymy, hyponymy, homonymy, antonymy and meronymy
key_sources: Wang, X. (2015). The Impacts of Presenting New Words in Semantically-Related Sets on Vocabulary Learning. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.111

article_title: The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32
title: Allow learners to self-select the vocabulary they study to build autonomy and motivation
description: The article argues that letting learners decide which words are worth learning fosters autonomy, confidence and motivation, which in turn supports vocabulary growth. It states: "Allowing students to self-select words is a po werful vocabulary teaching tool that builds autonomy." During treatment the self-selection group "performed more motivated in guessing the unknown words" than the enhancement group, whose members the author says did not feel confident or independent because they could not choose words freely.
requirements: Reading texts matched to learner interests
Teacher models word selection and context-clue guessing, then acts as facilitator
Collaborative group work for discussing and negotiating word meanings
constraints: The advantage was demonstrated against an Input Enhancement comparison group limited to pre-highlighted words, with pre-intermediate Iranian EFL girls aged 14-16
examples: The Vocabulary Self-Selection group freely chose any words from ten illustrated texts, while the Input Enhancement group could only choose among highlighted words, and the free-choice group outperformed on both posttests
key_sources: Golfam Masoudi. (2017). The Effect of Vocabulary Self-Selection Strategy and Input Enhancement Strategy on the Vocabulary Knowledge of Iranian EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 10(8). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n8p32

article_title: Treating of Content-Based Instruction to Teach Writing Viewed from EFL Learners' Creativity
citation: Selamet Riadi Jaelani. (2017). Treating of Content-Based Instruction to Teach Writing Viewed from EFL Learners' Creativity. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p156
title: Select writing-teaching methods according to learners' creativity level
description: The article concludes that method choice should be matched to learner creativity because method effectiveness interacted with creativity level. It states that "English teachers are expected to be able to select and use the appropriate teaching methods to teach writing for the EFL Learner having high and low creativity", i.e., CBI for high-creativity learners and PBL for low-creativity learners per its findings.
requirements: Teachers must be able to assess or identify learners' creativity level, as the study did with a 30-item creativity test
constraints: Recommendation rests on one quasi-experimental study with 80 learners in two classes; the low-creativity advantage for PBL is an author interpretation rather than a separately tested contrast
target_learning_goals: EFL writing ability (vocabulary, grammar, organization, content/meaning)
examples: The study assigned one class to Content-Based Instruction and one to Problem-Based Learning via cluster random lottery, then gave both classes the same writing test after treatment
key_sources: Selamet Riadi Jaelani. (2017). Treating of Content-Based Instruction to Teach Writing Viewed from EFL Learners' Creativity. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p156

article_title: The Effect of Second Life on Speaking Achievement
citation: Guzel, S. & Aydin, S. (2016). The effect of second life on speaking achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching. 6(4), 236-245. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1100452
title: Second Life as a virtual EFL speaking practice environment
description: Second Life is a 3D multi-user virtual environment developed by Linden Labs in 2003 in which learners create avatars and interact in virtual spaces. The article describes it as "social network software which enables sharing multimedia items in addition to its MUVE characteristics" and used it to deliver the same advanced-level speaking lessons as the control group received face-to-face. Its anonymity and risk-free features are said to lower anxiety and fear of negative evaluation, supporting self-regulated language practice.
requirements: Learners need avatar creation and access to the SL platform, plus structured lesson topics; here Q-Skills Advance Your Listening and Speaking by Oxford Press.
constraints: The study applied SL to advanced-level Turkish EFL learners in a university ELT department over four weekly 45-minute sessions.
target_learning_goals: Speaking achievement: grammar, vocabulary, intelligibility, fluency, and task achievement
examples: Experimental-group learners joined the same speaking lessons on the virtual world of SL while controls took traditional classes.
key_sources: Guzel, S. & Aydin, S. (2016). The effect of second life on speaking achievement. Global Journal of Foreign Language Teaching. 6(4), 236-245. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED573975

article_title: The Effect of Brain-Based Teaching on Young EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy
citation: Parastoo Alizadeh Oghyanous. (2017). The Effect of Brain-Based Teaching on Young EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. English Language Teaching, 10(5), 158. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n5p158
title: Self-Efficacy Questionnaire for Children (SEQ-C)
description: SEQ-C, developed by Muris (2001), is a 24-item self-report instrument measuring three dimensions of children's self-efficacy: "social self-efficacy, academic self-efficacy, and emotional self-efficacy". Respondents rate items from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very well). The article reports Muris's reliability of 0.88 for total self-efficacy and internal consistency of 0.78 in this study's Persian translation.
requirements: Translation and piloting for reliability check when used across languages
constraints: Designed for children; used here with Persian translation in Iranian EFL context
target_learning_goals: Measuring social, academic, and emotional self-efficacy
examples: Administered as pretest and posttest to both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Parastoo Alizadeh Oghyanous. (2017). The Effect of Brain-Based Teaching on Young EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. English Language Teaching, 10(5), 158. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n5p158

article_title: Effects of Second Step Curriculum on Behavioral and Academic Outcomes in 5th and 8th Grade Students: A Longitudinal Study on Character Development
citation: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47.
title: Second Step curriculum: a classroom-based SEL and character development program for preschool through 8th grade
description: Second Step is a comprehensive, classroom-based social-emotional learning and character development curriculum aimed at inculcating skills in "the areas of empathy, perspective taking, problem solving, self-control or self-regulation, and anger management or emotion regulation for preschool through 8th grade". It makes "extensive use of social learning theory" and "social information-processing models of children's social behavior". In this study, 19 schools implemented it for four consecutive school semesters while 16 schools did not.
requirements: Implementation across consecutive school semesters with school-wide adoption
constraints: Schools self-selected into treatment and control conditions rather than being randomly assigned
examples: 19 schools in an open-enrollment charter school system in Texas implemented the curriculum for four consecutive semesters (Fall 2012 through Spring 2014)
key_sources: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167262

article_title: The Effects of the Family-Involved SDLMI on Academic Engagement and Goal Attainment of Middle School Students with Disabilities Who Exhibit Problem Behavior
citation: Kim, N. H., & Park, J. (2012). The effects of the family-involved SDLMI on academic engagement and goal attainment of middle school students with disabilities who exhibit problem behavior. International Journal of Special Education, 27(1), 117-127. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ977631
title: Self-Determination Learning Model of Instruction (SDLMI)
description: The SDLMI is an instruction model that "enables teachers to achieve educational goals and students to employ self-regulated problem-solving strategies and to achieve self-selected goals." It consists of three steps: "setting a goal, taking action, and adjusting the goal and plan," operationalized through 12 questions that guide students to identify learning problems, explore solutions, and evaluate outcomes. Teachers ask questions and work with students to answer them, optimizing communication skills. In this study, the SDLMI was applied in Korean language classes with additional components added to involve families.
requirements: Teachers guide students through the three steps using 12 questions written on student worksheets
Teacher training in the SDLMI procedures is provided before implementation
constraints: The study applied the model in Korean language resource room settings with special educators, not in general classrooms
target_learners: middle school students with disabilities who exhibit problem behavior
examples: Special education teachers applied the SDLMI in Korean language classes over seven months, with students taught to set goals, take action, and adjust goal and plan using 12 questions on worksheets.
key_sources: Kim, N. H., & Park, J. (2012). The effects of the family-involved SDLMI on academic engagement and goal attainment of middle school students with disabilities who exhibit problem behavior. International Journal of Special Education, 27(1), 117-127. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ979719

article_title: The Impact of Metacognitive Strategies and Self-Regulating Processes of Solving Math Word Problems
citation: Eda Vula, Rrezarta Avdyli, Valbona Berisha, Blerim Saqipi, Shpetim Elezi. (2017). The impact of metacognitive strategies and self-regulating processes of solving math word problems. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017131886
title: Self-regulation of learning as three components: cognition, metacognition, and motivation
description: The article adopts an account in which self-regulation of learning consists of three main components: cognition, metacognition, and motivation. Cognition covers abilities for codifying, memorizing, and retrieving information; metacognition covers abilities enabling learners to understand and monitor their own cognitive processes; motivation involves beliefs and attitudes influencing the use and development of cognitive and metacognitive abilities. The article states each component is "essential, but not sufficient for self -regulation" (citing Schraw, Crippen & Hartly, 2006) and ties self-regulation to early mathematics achievement.
requirements: Learners need to set goals, select strategies to reach their goal, apply the selected strategies, and continuously monitor their own progress.
constraints: Each of the three components is essential but not sufficient on its own for self-regulation and efficient problem solving.
target_learners: elementary-school learners, especially in early mathematics
target_learning_goals: monitoring and controlling one's own cognitive processes
examples: The study's intervention targeted the metacognitive component through strategy questions and self-checking steps during collaborative problem solving.
key_sources: Eda Vula, Rrezarta Avdyli, Valbona Berisha, Blerim Saqipi, Shpetim Elezi. (2017). The impact of metacognitive strategies and self-regulating processes of solving math word problems. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2017131886

article_title: The Effect of Spanish and English Narrative Intervention on the Language Skills of Young Dual Language Learners
citation: Trina D. Spencer, Douglas B. Petersen, M. Adelaida Restrepo, Marilyn Thompson, and Maria Nelly Gutierrez Arvizu. (2019). The Effect of Spanish and English Narrative Intervention on the Language Skills of Young Dual Language Learners. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418779439
title: Seven-activity small-group narrative lesson format with story grammar icons, peer retelling, and embedded vocabulary review
description: Each lesson conformed to the same instructional format with seven activities: story reading with icons, vocabulary introduction in story context, story-part naming with Story Gestures, individual retells with progressively removed visual supports while peers played listening games (Story Bingo, Story Cubes, Story Sticks), and vocabulary review with photos or objects. Children heard the story twice and retold it as a group and individually each session.
requirements: Presentation book with scripts and illustrations
icons representing story grammar elements
photographs or classroom objects for vocabulary contexts
constraints: Lessons were semimanualized; interventionists were taught to complete each activity's primary objective and differentiate based on children's language and engagement
target_learners: preschool children in small groups of three
examples: During individual retells the first child used illustrations and icons, the second only icons, and the third no visual supports
key_sources: Trina D. Spencer, Douglas B. Petersen, M. Adelaida Restrepo, Marilyn Thompson, and Maria Nelly Gutierrez Arvizu. (2019). The Effect of Spanish and English Narrative Intervention on the Language Skills of Young Dual Language Learners. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418779439

article_title: The Development and Implementation of a Model for Teaching Astronomy to Deaf Students
citation: Bolat, M. (2016). The Development and Implementation of a Model for Teaching Astronomy to Deaf Students. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1506
title: A seven-step preparation model for teaching astronomy to deaf students
description: The article develops a teaching model whose pre-implementation preparation stage "consists of 7 steps": identifying which astronomy concepts students know in sign language, deciding how concepts will be added in sign language, selecting activities, choosing methods and media, allocating time, specifying cognitive process skills, and selecting and training teachers. The model was implemented as a 7-day project combining a basic astronomy theme and a seasons theme, using experiments, videos, modeling, a planetarium and outdoor observation. The author offers it so other researchers can use the activities and test the model.
requirements: Sign language about the subject should be developed first, and conceptual learning and teaching sign language should be simultaneous
Teachers require in-service training about the activities before the project starts
constraints: The model was tried with a single group of 30 deaf students without a control group, and the author recommends control-group studies to assess it better
target_learning_goals: astronomy concepts such as solar system, eclipses, scale and axial tilt
scientific process skills such as observing, measuring and inferring
examples: Activities included scaling the solar system on a 10-meter cardboard, modeling eclipses, and measuring shadow length, temperature and day length on 21st June, 23rd September and 21st December
key_sources: Bolat, M. (2016). The Development and Implementation of a Model for Teaching Astronomy to Deaf Students. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1506

article_title: The Effects of YouTube in Multimedia Instruction for Vocabulary Learning: Perceptions of EFL Students and Teachers
citation: Raniah Kabooha & Tariq Elyas. (2018). The Effects of YouTube in Multimedia Instruction for Vocabulary Learning: Perceptions of EFL Students and Teachers. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p72
title: Select YouTube videos for language classrooms based on student proficiency level, cultural context, and lesson objectives
description: In its conclusion, the article recommends that EFL teachers use YouTube but 'need to be selective about the videos they decide to use in their classrooms in order to achieve maximum effectiveness'. It states that videos selected for language classrooms 'should be based on certain criteria including proficiency level of the students, their cultural context, and the lesson's objectives.' This principle pairs the recommendation with the study's evidence of vocabulary gains when videos were deliberately integrated.
requirements: Teachers should be trained to use YouTube effectively, as the participating teachers unanimously agreed
constraints: The study's population was limited to female pre-intermediate EFL students at one institution, and the study ran over a short time frame
examples: The article's conclusion states video selection criteria and reports that participating teachers unanimously agreed they should be trained to use YouTube effectively in their classes
key_sources: Raniah Kabooha & Tariq Elyas. (2018). The Effects of YouTube in Multimedia Instruction for Vocabulary Learning: Perceptions of EFL Students and Teachers. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p72

article_title: Technology Facilitated PBL Pedagogy and Its Impact on Nursing Students' Academic Achievement and Critical Thinking Dispositions
citation: Yu, W.-C. W., Lin, C. C., Ho, M.-H., & Wang, J. (2015). Technology facilitated PBL pedagogy and its impact on nursing student's academic achievement and critical thinking dispositions. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075262
title: Self-regulation comprises four ingredients: standards, monitoring, willpower, and motivation
description: The article presents a framework in which self-regulation consists of four components: "standards, monitoring, will-power, and motivation." Motivation refers to a drive or impulse to act toward a goal, while willpower (disposition) is the volitional component that determines whether a student with adequate skills actually deploys them. The article emphasizes that a student can possess critical thinking skills but lack the will or motivation to use them, and that disposition plays a critical role in whether self-regulation succeeds.
requirements: Learners must have both the ability (skills) and the will (disposition) to engage in critical thinking for successful self-regulation
constraints: The framework is presented conceptually rather than tested empirically in this study
key_sources: Yu, W.-C. W., Lin, C. C., Ho, M.-H., & Wang, J. (2015). Technology facilitated PBL pedagogy and its impact on nursing student's academic achievement and critical thinking dispositions. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057343

article_title: The Efficiency of a Selective Training Program on the Development of Some Social Skills of Saudi Students with Autism
citation: Alothman, I. A. (2016). The Efficiency of a Selective Training Program on the Development of Some Social Skills of Saudi Students with Autism. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p265
title: Selective training program combining natural communication strategies and social stories
description: A researcher-designed teacher-training program in two axes: first training teachers of students with autism to use "some of the techniques found in the natural communication strategies and social stories", then having trained teachers apply a series of sessions with students. It comprised 20 teacher-training sessions over four weeks and 30 application sessions over six weeks, five weekly sessions of 60-90 minutes each.
requirements: Teachers trained in the techniques before applying them with students
Sessions delivered in the students' natural school environment
constraints: Developed and rated for students with autism at the Institute of Intellectual Education, east of Riyadh
examples: Applied to three children with autism during the first semester of the academic year 2014-2015
key_sources: Alothman, I. A. (2016). The Efficiency of a Selective Training Program on the Development of Some Social Skills of Saudi Students with Autism. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p265

article_title: The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Ahangari, S. (2014). The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.81
title: Use self-correction of pronunciation errors to promote active engagement and better pronunciation gains
description: The article recommends having learners find and learn the correct pronunciation of their own noted errors rather than receiving teacher correction. In the study, the teacher "used to take notes and write down that participant's pronunciation errors" and the participant then found the correct forms and retold the story. The self-correction group achieved the highest posttest pronunciation scores.
requirements: The teacher must indicate each learner's pronunciation errors, as the article states learners' work "should be previewed by the teachers and their errors should be indicated".
constraints: Studied with female pre-intermediate Iranian EFL learners aged fifteen to twenty in a language institute; generalization beyond this setting is not established.
target_learning_goals: pronunciation accuracy in oral narrative production
examples: Participants told picture-based stories, received notes on their pronunciation errors, found correct pronunciations themselves, and retold the same story with correct pronunciation in the following session.
key_sources: Ahangari, S. (2014). The Effect of Self, Peer and Teacher Correction on the Pronunciation Improvement of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.81

article_title: Peer Evaluation of Team Member Effectiveness as a Formative Educational Intervention
citation: Mentzer, N., Laux, D., Zissimopoulos, A., & Richards, K. A. R. (2017). Peer evaluation of team member effectiveness as a formative educational intervention. Journal of Technology Education, 28(2), 53-77. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1144255
title: Self-determination theory as a framework for explaining how learning environments influence student motivation
description: Self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 1985, 2000) provides a framework to explain how human motivation influences behavior. Central to the theory is the notion that humans have three basic psychological needs — relatedness, autonomy, and competence — that they seek to satisfy through interactions with one another and the environment. The article applies this framework to explain that student-centered learning environments satisfy basic psychological needs and foster intrinsic motivation, whereas controlling, instructor-centered environments lead to extrinsically regulated motivation.
requirements: Learning environments must be structured so that interactions foster student-centered conditions that satisfy the three basic psychological needs.
constraints: The theory is applied here specifically to university-level, team-based design coursework.
examples: The study used the Learning Climate Questionnaire and the competence/doubt subscales of the Basic Psychological Needs at Work Scale, both grounded in self-determination theory, to measure student perceptions.
key_sources: Mentzer, N., Laux, D., Zissimopoulos, A., & Richards, K. A. R. (2017). Peer evaluation of team member effectiveness as a formative educational intervention. Journal of Technology Education, 28(2), 53-77. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1164703

article_title: Research in Mathematics Educational Technology: Current Trends and Futrue Demands
citation: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. In Wiest, L. R., & Lamberg, T. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 33rd Annual Meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education (pp. 373-380). Reno, NV: University of Nevada, Reno.
title: Searchable database of mathematics educational technology studies 1968-2010
description: The review's completion will provide a searchable database of educational technology studies from 1968 to 2010, containing key information organized by three frameworks and four lenses. The database supports future research syntheses and meta-analyses, identification of over- and under-studied dissertation topics, and can be updated with newly released manuscripts once initial coding is completed.
requirements: Initial coding completion before database updates can be accomplished
target_learning_goals: Guiding future research syntheses and meta-analyses in mathematics educational technology
key_sources: Driskell, S. O., Ronau, R. N., Rakes, C. R., Bush, S. B., Niess, M. L., & Pugalee, D. (2011). Research in mathematics educational technology: Current trends and future demands. Reno, NV: University of Nevada, Reno. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED586002

article_title: Effects of Autonomy Supportive vs. Controlling Teachers' Behavior on Students' Achievements
citation: Hofferber, N., Eckes, A., & Wilde, M. (2014). Effects of Autonomy Supportive vs. Controlling Teachers' Behavior on Students' Achievements. European Journal of Educational Research, 3(4), 177-184. http://www.eurojedu.com
title: Self-determination theory: autonomy support satisfies the basic need for autonomy and promotes intrinsic motivation and deeper learning
description: The article frames its study within self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan), which posits that autonomy is one of three basic needs alongside social relatedness and competence. Teachers who promote autonomy offer choices, give informative feedback, and allow students to decide how they want to learn, which satisfies the need for autonomy and promotes intrinsic motivation. This theoretical account explains why autonomy supportive teaching led to greater conceptual knowledge: it fostered self-determined commitment, focused attention, and more active, effective learning, whereas controlling behavior shifted attention toward external incentives and superficial task completion.
requirements: The learning environment must allow students genuine opportunities to make decisions about their own learning process
constraints: The theory predicts that controlling environments impair deep understanding but does not predict impairment of rote reproduction, consistent with the study's null finding for rote learning
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation, engagement, and deep conceptual understanding of content
examples: The study operationalized autonomy support through choices, informative feedback, non-controlling symbols (green pen), absence of marks, and non-controlling language, following the characteristics developed by Reeve (2002) and Reeve and Jang (2006)
key_sources: Hofferber, N., Eckes, A., & Wilde, M. (2014). Effects of Autonomy Supportive vs. Controlling Teachers' Behavior on Students' Achievements. European Journal of Educational Research, 3(4), 177-184. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085991

article_title: Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and Its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context
citation: Mansoory, N. & Jafarpour, M. (2014). Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.2p.149
title: Semantic prosody: the positive, negative, or neutral connotative meaning a word acquires from its consistent collocates
description: The article defines semantic prosody (SP), also called semantic harmony, as a form of evaluative meaning spread over a unit of language rather than built into a single word. It is "a kind of (positive, negative, or neutral) connotative meaning which a word takes due to its consistent collocations", observable only across large numbers of concordance lines rather than from the word itself. The article traces the concept to Sinclair (1991) and Louw (1993), notes SP expresses speaker attitude, and that violating an SP can produce irony or humor only when a lexical item exhibits a very strong preference.
requirements: Corpus analysis of large numbers of KWIC concordances to observe SP reliably
constraints: Not all lexical items have an SP; the article quotes that "semantic prosodies seem to be inconstant friends"
SP is largely uncaptured by dictionary definitions and absent or poor in monolingual and English-Persian dictionaries
target_learners: EFL and ESL learners, especially those choosing among near-synonyms
target_learning_goals: Using lexical items appropriately in context
examples: The verb CAUSE is almost always associated with negative entities such as difficulty, trouble, problem, and damage, while BRING ABOUT is usually followed by positive entities such as improvement
key_sources: Mansoory, N. & Jafarpour, M. (2014). Teaching Semantic Prosody of English Verbs through the DDL Approach and its Effect on Learners' Vocabulary Choice Appropriateness in a Persian EFL Context. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.2p.149

article_title: Long-Term Effects of Social-Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence from a Randomized Trial of "INSIGHTS"
citation: McCormick, M. P., Neuhaus, R., Horn, E. P., O'Connor, E. E., White, H. S., Harding, S., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. (2019). Long-Term Effects of Social–Emotional Learning on Receipt of Special Education and Grade Retention: Evidence From a Randomized Trial of INSIGHTS. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858419867290
title: SEL programs at the transition to elementary school may prevent unnecessary SPED referrals for low-income children
description: The article concludes that "a time-limited and fairly intensive SEL intervention that supports teachers in effectively responding to and managing the behaviors of children implemented at the critical transition to elementary school can reduce receipt of SPED services through fifth grade for low-income students". It stresses that low-income children who need SPED services should continue to receive them, but SEL may prevent unnecessary referrals driven by behavioral issues.
requirements: SEL programming implemented at the kindergarten transition with teacher supports for behavior management
constraints: the effect was demonstrated for low-income students; no difference appeared for higher income students
target_learners: low-income children at the transition to elementary school
examples: INSIGHTS schools randomized in New York City between 2008 and 2012
key_sources: McCormick, M. P., Neuhaus, R., Horn, E. P., O'Connor, E. E., White, H. S., Harding, S., Cappella, E., & McClowry, S. (2019). article_title: Hybrid simulation approach enhances technical and non-technical skills in therapeutic pharmacology education.

description: The article uses Bandura's Self‐Efficacy Theory to frame ICU nurses' readiness and confidence in caring for patients with mental illness. It states that a person's confidence in their ability to complete a task—called self‐efficacy—affects their drive, effort and outcome. title: Self-efficacy and cognitive load theory as explanatory frameworks for brief skill-focused training design
description: The article interprets its findings through two frameworks. Citing Bandura's self-efficacy theory, it argues "mastery experience through low initial threshold and achievement of early success are critical for building confidence and motivation in the early stage of learning". Citing Sweller, it argues novice learners are vulnerable to cognitive overload, and that the curriculum reduced extraneous load by eliminating complex teaching contexts, while the transition from demonstration to self-practice provided scaffolding optimizing germane load.

constraints: The framework is applied to novice learners in simulation settings; the authors note real clinical unpredictability may represent a psychological barrier for undergraduates.
target_learners: Medical students on short clinical rotations
examples: The authors attribute immediate success and reinforced technical self-belief to the curriculum's key features, citing mastery experience and reduced extraneous cognitive load.

description: The authors suggest that analog serious games are a valuable and engaging educational strategy that can supplement conventional teaching, especially in reinforcing pharmacology knowledge among anesthesiology trainees. The card game format was chosen owing to its simplicity and shorter development time compared to digital games.

title: Serious games as active learning tools distinct from gamification
description: The article distinguishes serious games from gamification. Serious games are designed for an explicit and carefully thought-out educational purpose and are not intended to be played for amusement. The game-based learning approach utilized a serious game in which players actively engaged with the game to acquire knowledge, which contrasts with gamification, which incorporates gaming elements as only one part of the learning process. Serious games offer numerous benefits, including promoting active participation, enhancing problem-solving abilities, improving clinical reasoning and decision-making skills, and encouraging teamwork.
requirements: Games must be designed for an explicit educational purpose rather than amusement
constraints: Some studies define serious games as a digital-only tool, which narrows the conceptual scope of the term more than is warranted
examples: Card and board games such as Happy Family and GridlockED fall within the category of serious games when used in medical education

title: Self-regulated learning and executive function theory as upstream theoretical processes linking psychological resilience to computational thinking
description: The article proposes two complementary theoretical accounts for why psychological resilience may relate to computational thinking. Self-regulated learning conceptualizes learning as a cyclical process of strategic planning, self-monitoring, and self-reflection. Executive function theory identifies reasoning, planning, and problem solving as higher-order functions emerging from working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. The article positions these as "upstream theoretical processes that may help explain why CT can be related to psychological resilience."
requirements: The article states these upstream processes serve solely as theoretical background and were not measured or tested in the present study.
constraints: The upstream processes were not measured or tested in the present study.

title: Self-oriented learning (SOL) as a key competence for lifelong learning in medical practice
description: The article frames self-oriented learning (SOL) as a concept "emphasizing learners' responsibility for planning, monitoring, and evaluating their own learning process" and as a key competence for lifelong learning and professional development in medical practice. It distinguishes SOL from related constructs: self-oriented learning foregrounds personal meaning and orientation, self-regulated learning highlights strategic regulation of learning processes, and self-directed learning addresses responsibility for organizing and managing one's learning trajectory. The article uses SOL to justify supporting students in formulating and pursuing their own learning outcomes during clinical electives.

constraints: SOL overlaps with, but is distinguished from, self-regulated and self-directed learning as related constructs describing different dimensions of learner autonomy

examples: FamuPlus operationalized SOL by having students define SMART learning outcomes, review them with clinical teachers, and reflect weekly during electives

citation: Bentley DC, Sotto A, Lombardi P. Comparison of examination performance and test anxiety during bell‐paced and self‐paced gross anatomy laboratory examinations. Anat Sci Educ. 2026;19:732–742. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70215
title: Self-paced, fixed-total-time laboratory examination structure as an alternative to the traditional bell-ringer format.
description: This pattern is a laboratory examination design in which total test time is standardized but students progress through sequential specimen stations at their own discretion, with no bell chimes or other auditory aids. In the article's randomized crossover study, each examination consisted of 28 to 31 specimen stations with three evenly dispersed rest stations, each specimen station comprising two questions (A/B) primarily focused on identification of anatomical structures. Students progressed linearly without the option to revisit previously completed stations, and the exam set-up, questions, and overall time limit remained identical between pacing conditions.
requirements: A fixed total exam time balanced with the bell-paced condition, and linear station progression without revisiting completed stations.
constraints: Open-text feedback showed 26 of 35 students criticized self-pacing, largely due to the added responsibility of self-timing and distractions from a backlogged queue of students during the exam.
target_learning_goals: assessing anatomical structure identification without compromising academic rigor
examples: Students completed the self-paced condition with no bell chimes, progressing between specimen stations at their own discretion while total test time was standardized.

article_title: Extracurricular physical activity and academic performance among Chinese adolescents with high body mass index: a longitudinal mediation analysis.
citation: Zhang Bao Gen, Qian Xiao Fang. (2026). Extracurricular physical activity and academic performance among Chinese adolescents with high body mass index: a longitudinal mediation analysis. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-47332-w
title: Serial chain-mediation model linking physical activity, mental health, cognitive ability, and academic performance in adolescents with high BMI
description: The article proposes and tests a longitudinal chain-mediation model in which extracurricular physical activity at baseline predicts later academic performance directly and through two sequential mediators: mental health (M1) and cognitive ability (M2), measured at follow-up. The authors describe it as a "statistical serial model" in which improvements in psychological state and cognitive function form "an interconnected, continuous mechanism of multi-stage, sequential action." Mental health is positioned as a facilitator or contextual enabler of cognitive improvement rather than a direct outcome of activity.
requirements: two-wave (or more) longitudinal measurement of activity, mediators, and academic outcomes; controls for baseline academic performance and demographics
constraints: mediators measured concurrently at T2, limiting strict temporal causal inference about the M1→M2 ordering
target_learners: Chinese adolescents with high BMI (BMI ≥ 24), mean age ~13.9 years at baseline
target_learning_goals: academic performance in Chinese, mathematics, and English
examples: the model was tested with PROCESS Model 6 and 5,000 bootstrap samples in a sample of 221 adolescents with high BMI
key_sources: Zhang Bao Gen, Qian Xiao Fang. (2026). Extracurricular physical activity and academic performance among Chinese adolescents with high body mass index: a longitudinal mediation analysis. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-47332-w

article_title: The effect of segmented-interactive video demonstration on student performance in procedural skills among healthcare students.
citation: Hamzah Nurul Rimadhayanti, Mohd Fadzil Abdul Hanid & Mohamad Ikram Zakaria (2026). The effect of segmented-interactive video demonstration on student performance in procedural skills among healthcare students. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10471-2
title: Design procedural-skill videos as segmented-interactive experiences rather than continuous videos
description: The article recommends structuring procedural training videos into manageable segments with embedded interactive elements, because continuous videos risk information overload and passivity. The segmented-interactive design applies "seven multimedia principles (e.g., segmentation, redundancy, signaling)" alongside quizzes, overlays, and prompts, which the study associates with significantly better technical and communication performance than a continuous video.
requirements: Video divided into clear procedural stages (preparation, execution, closure)
Interactive elements such as quizzes and prompts embedded to reinforce understanding
constraints: Evidence limited to venipuncture training with a two-week self-practice window in a single institution
target_learners: undergraduate medical students learning procedural skills
examples: The treatment group watched a segmented-interactive video with three segments during self-directed learning, while the control group watched a continuous video
key_sources: Hamzah Nurul Rimadhayanti, Mohd Fadzil Abdul Hanid & Mohamad Ikram Zakaria (2026). The effect of segmented-interactive video demonstration on student performance in procedural skills among healthcare students. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10471-2

article_title: Application of AI-based virtual standardized patients in physician-patient communication training: a study based on the SEGUE framework.
citation: Sun Ning, Zhou Xintong, Yang Zhongqian, Zhou Yu, Ma Ruihang, Wang Zhong. (2026). Application of AI-based virtual standardized patients in physician-patient communication training: a study based on the SEGUE framework. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1768518
title: SEGUE framework as a structured checklist for teaching and assessing physician-patient communication
description: The SEGUE framework, proposed by Gregory Makoul in 2001, is used in this study as the primary evaluation tool: "a structured checklist designed to assess physician–patient communication competence and consists of five domains encompassing 25 specific behavioral items". The five domains are Set the Stage, Elicit Information, Give Information, Understand the Patient's Perspective, and End the Encounter. Content items are scored if performed at least once, while Process items require correct performance throughout the encounter. A Chinese-adapted version introduced by China Medical University in 2006 was used.
requirements: Scoring depends on trained assessors or automated semantic analysis mapping utterances to the 25 behavioral items
constraints: Assessed solely with the SEGUE framework without corresponding instructional content, which the authors state may limit comprehensiveness of evaluation
Process items require sustained correct performance, so a single omission yields no points
target_learners: Medical students and clinicians in communication training
target_learning_goals: Physician-patient communication competence across five encounter domains
examples: The study distributed the 25 items as Q1–Q5 Set the Stage, Q6–Q15 Elicit Information, Q16–Q19 Give Information, Q20–Q23 Understand the Patient's Perspective, and Q24–Q25 End the Encounter, adhering to the original categorization.
key_sources: Sun Ning, Zhou Xintong, Yang Zhongqian, Zhou Yu, Ma Ruihang, Wang Zhong. (2026). Application of AI-based virtual standardized patients in physician-patient communication training: a study based on the SEGUE framework. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1768518

article_title: Alexithymia and clinical communication competence in nursing interns in China with the mediating role of self-efficacy.
citation: Yu Jiaying, Zhu Chengyu, Ren Yuwen, Fan Mingna & Yang Lili (2026). Alexithymia and clinical communication competence in nursing interns in China with the mediating role of self-efficacy. Scientific Reports 16, 10615. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-44952-0
title: Self-efficacy as the mediating mechanism linking alexithymia to clinical communication competence
description: The article proposes an explanatory account grounded in Social Cognitive Theory in which alexithymia, particularly externally oriented thinking, undermines interns' confidence in their capabilities, and this reduced self-efficacy in turn lowers clinical communication competence. As the authors put it, "Nursing interns with alexithymia may lack self-confidence and initiative in clinical communication due to low self-efficacy, resulting in insufficient clinical communication skills." The account was operationalized as a structural equation model in which GSES carries part of the effect of EOT on each communication subdomain, with mediation confirmed by bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero.
requirements: Measurement of alexithymia (TAS-20), self-efficacy (GSES), and clinical communication competence with validated instruments
Sufficient sample for structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation testing
constraints: Established in a cross-sectional design, so causal ordering is not confirmed; the article calls for longitudinal studies
Tested among Chinese nursing interns in the early stage of internship
examples: The study built four SEM models (harmonious relationships, listening, recognizing problems, verifying feelings), each with EOT as exogenous predictor, GSES as mediator, and fit indices reported.
key_sources: Yu Jiaying, Zhu Chengyu, Ren Yuwen, Fan Mingna & Yang Lili (2026). Alexithymia and clinical communication competence in nursing interns in China with the mediating role of self-efficacy. Scientific Reports 16, 10615. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-44952-0

article_title: Characterising Forces Applied During the Simulated Management of Impacted Fetal Head: Pre-Clinical Methods Study.
citation: Parris Dawn, Xue Yang, Navaseelan Thurga, Salvadores Fernandez Carmen, Javidan Maryam, Gupta Rohit, Salaris Nikolaos, Chen Jeremy, Tiwari Manish K., Siassakos Dimitrios. (2025). Characterising Forces Applied During the Simulated Management of Impacted Fetal Head: Pre‐Clinical Methods Study. BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1471-0528.70107
title: Low-cost sensorised surgical glove with 12 piezoresistive force sensors for simulated fetal head disimpaction
description: A sensorised surgical glove developed through engineer–obstetrician collaboration, with "12 sensors placed on numerous points including the fingertips, palm and back of the hand". The piezoresistive sensors (10 mm × 8 mm × 2 mm) are individually calibrated to map voltage changes to force, worn under a third over-glove, and wired to a data acquisition system and laptop. The gloves are low-cost, approximately $1 USD, and were used with a Limbs and Things impacted-fetal-head simulator at a national course.
requirements: Worn as three layers (under-glove, sensorised glove, over-glove) with wired connection to a data acquisition system and laptop running custom calibration software
constraints: Wired design and triple gloving reduced usability; participants reported reduced tactile sensitivity and discomfort from wires, and the force benchmark derives from one expert rather than a validated safety threshold
target_learners: Obstetricians of varying seniority (ST1–2 to consultant)
target_learning_goals: Safe force application during impacted fetal head disimpaction at caesarean birth
examples: Used at the ART & CRAFT national course in May 2025 with 13 obstetricians performing abdominal–cephalic disimpaction and vaginal push-up on a Limbs and Things simulator
key_sources: Parris Dawn, Xue Yang, Navaseelan Thurga, Salvadores Fernandez Carmen, Javidan Maryam, Gupta Rohit, Salaris Nikolaos, Chen Jeremy, Tiwari Manish K., Siassakos Dimitrios. (2025). Characterising Forces Applied During the Simulated Management of Impacted Fetal Head: Pre‐Clinical Methods Study. BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1471-0528.70107

article_title: Transforming Hospital Care: Impact of an Evidence-Based Practice Course on Healthcare Professionals' Competencies in a Randomized Clinical Trial.
citation: Marqueze, E. C., Portela, H. O., Mauricio, E. C. B., Mizoi, C. S., de Sousa, M. R. G., Oliveira, S. B., & Franco, M. E. (2026). Transforming Hospital Care: Impact of an Evidence‐Based Practice Course on Healthcare Professionals' Competencies in a Randomized Clinical Trial. Worldviews on Evidence‐Based Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/wvn.70130
title: A seven-week, 21-hour personalized Evidence-Based Practice course for healthcare professionals
description: An interactive EBP course delivered weekly over seven weeks in three-hour sessions, totaling 21 hours, guided by a meta-analysis indicating that "programs with a total duration of 20–24 h, delivered over four to seven weeks, yielded the most significant improvements in EBP skills". The syllabus covers EBP definition, search strategies (PICO, Boolean operators), scientific databases, review and epidemiological study types, quality of evidence, and the PET process. Participants scoring at least 70% on assessments and attending at least 70% of sessions received a certificate.
requirements: Participants hold higher education degrees, have worked at the hospital at least six months, and have never previously participated in an EBP course; a minimum 70% attendance is required.
constraints: The intervention was conducted in a single private hospital, and the authors caution about generalizing to public or academic settings.
target_learners: healthcare professionals (nurses, physicians, pharmacists) in a hospital setting
target_learning_goals: evidence-based practice competencies: formulating clinical questions, searching literature, appraising evidence, and applying evidence to clinical practice
examples: The course was given by the study's lead author, a PhD holder in Public Health, and incorporated practical exercises and knowledge assessment tasks.
