article_title: AI in the Classroom: Observing Preclinical Students' Use of ChatGPT During Case-Based Learning at a UK Medical School.
citation: Taylor A. W. R., Patel F. Y., Smyth E. K., Gay S., and Bird T. (2026). AI in the Classroom: Observing Preclinical Students' Use of ChatGPT During Case‐Based Learning at a UK Medical School. The Clinical Teacher 23, no. 2: e70360. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70360
title: Self-determination account of chatbot use: autonomy, relatedness and competence in the learning culture predict how students interact with AI chatbots
description: The authors interpret their findings through self-determination theory, in which "Autonomy, relatedness and competence underpin the internal drive to learn for personal satisfaction, known as intrinsic motivation". Structured workbooks limited autonomy and fostered efficient answer-finding, while collaborative cultures strengthened relatedness and competence, reducing passive chatbot use. They propose that "the degree to which a learning culture supports autonomy, relatedness and competence could predict how students are likely to interact with chatbots".
requirements: Learning contexts whose structure, collaboration and challenge levels can be described in terms of autonomy, relatedness and competence support
constraints: An interpretive account drawn post-analysis from qualitative ethnographic data, not a quantitatively tested prediction
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation for engaging, challenging learning
examples: In the studied CBL curriculum, workbook structure reduced autonomy while socially constructing solutions in collaborative groups enhanced perceived relatedness and competence
key_sources: Taylor A. W. R., Patel F. Y., Smyth E. K., Gay S., and Bird T. (2026). AI in the Classroom: Observing Preclinical Students' Use of ChatGPT During Case‐Based Learning at a UK Medical School. The Clinical Teacher 23, no. 2: e70360. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70360

article_title: Prevention and Management of Percutaneous Coronary Intervention-Related Complications: Assessing the Impact of Simulation-Based Learning and Human Factors Training.
citation: Fukamizu Junichi et al. (2025). Prevention and Management of Percutaneous Coronary Intervention‐Related Complications: Assessing the Impact of Simulation‐Based Learning and Human Factors Training. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. https://doi.org/10.1002/ccd.70418
title: Three-pattern typology of adverse-event severity distributions across PCI complication scenarios
description: The article proposes reading the distribution of adverse-event severity grades for each complication scenario as one of three visual patterns: "a linear descending pattern indicates a foreseeable case scenario, a mountain pattern implies imminent danger, and a horizontal pattern suggests unavoidable situations that result in life-threatening or disabling events and procedure-related deaths". It uses this typology to organize operator-reported severity data (Figure 4) and to prioritize which complications receive dedicated SBL scenarios.
requirements: Requires adverse-event severity data reported per complication scenario on a graded scale, such as the Society of International Radiology Adverse Event Severity Scale used here
constraints: Pattern interpretation is presented by the authors as descriptive, based on survey-reported distributions rather than tested as a predictive instrument
target_learning_goals: Recognition of which PCI complications carry the greatest injury and mortality risk
Prioritization of complications for simulation-based training
examples: Applied to six complication scenarios reported by survey respondents; type 3 and 5 perforations showed the heaviest severity distributions
key_sources: Fukamizu Junichi et al. (2025). Prevention and Management of Percutaneous Coronary Intervention‐Related Complications: Assessing the Impact of Simulation‐Based Learning and Human Factors Training. Catheterization and Cardiovascular Interventions. https://doi.org/10.1002/ccd.70418

article_title: The effectiveness of multilingual AI-based simulator for suicide risk assessment training in improving self-efficacy among young psychiatrists: a pilot study across twenty languages.
citation: Elyoseph Zohar, Levi-Belz Yossi, Levkovich Inbar, Haber Yuval, Gramaglia Carla Maria, Castroman Jorge López, Cecile Hanon, Olie Emilie. (2026). The effectiveness of multilingual AI-based simulator for suicide risk assessment training in improving self-efficacy among young psychiatrists: a pilot study across twenty languages. BMC Psychiatry, 26, 98. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-025-07737-9
title: SEE THE PAIN: a multilingual GenAI simulator for suicide risk assessment training
description: SEE THE PAIN is a GenAI-based suicide risk assessment training simulator built on Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet and deployed via the PMFM platform. Interaction comprises three stages: an introduction to the simulation's objective and structure, a chat-based conversation with a virtual patient named "Sarah", a 17 year old woman with a defined case story and risk factor profile, and detailed constructive written feedback on rapport, risk and protective factors, suicidal-thought exploration, and reflection on risk level. Behaviour is governed by multi-layered prompt engineering with role definitions, few-shot examples, and consistency rules, and the system conducts the entire interaction, including feedback, in the user's preferred language.
requirements: Requires a large language model with persona consistency, instruction adherence and low latency, selected after extensive testing
Requires iterative validation including stress testing with a wide range of user inputs and qualitative expert review of realism and feedback accuracy
constraints: The pilot focused on linguistic adaptation feasibility rather than deep cultural adaptation; the vignette uses stressors broadly relatable across many Western cultures, and subtle cultural nuances in expressing distress may not be fully captured
No formal validation of clinical accuracy and cultural nuances across all 20 languages was performed
target_learning_goals: establishing rapport and exploring risk and protective factors
examples: In the pilot, 27 psychiatrists at the European Psychiatric Association Summer School each completed a 20-minute assessment of the virtual character in their preferred language with immediate feedback
key_sources: Elyoseph Zohar, Levi-Belz Yossi, Levkovich Inbar, Haber Yuval, Gramaglia Carla Maria, Castroman Jorge López, Cecile Hanon, Olie Emilie. (2026). The effectiveness of multilingual AI-based simulator for suicide risk assessment training in improving self-efficacy among young psychiatrists: a pilot study across twenty languages. BMC Psychiatry, 26, 98. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-025-07737-9

article_title: Surgeon perceptions of essential skills and simulation for percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic discectomy training.
citation: Cai Bohong, Wang Zihan, Lyu Xi, Qiao Yiran, Liu Yuhan, Wu Danting, Li Sihang, Yao Qi, Chen Baixiang, Fu Fujian, Jiang Wei. (2025). Surgeon perceptions of essential skills and simulation for percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic discectomy training. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34397-2
title: Select simulation modality by the training program's key learning objectives rather than technological sophistication alone
description: Drawing on the survey's modality ratings, the article concludes that "the selection of simulation modality should be driven by the key learning objectives of the training program rather than by technological sophistication alone." High-fidelity physical models and VR simulators are viable alternatives to cadaveric specimens, while low-fidelity bench-top models, though rated least favorable, remain beneficial for practicing foundational clinical steps and familiarizing trainees with essential surgical instruments.
requirements: Training programs must define their key learning objectives before choosing a simulation modality
constraints: Cadaveric training, the preferred modality, is significantly constrained by cultural, ethical, legal, and financial hurdles
target_learners: Surgeons in training for minimally invasive endoscopic spine procedures
target_learning_goals: Develop anatomical knowledge, spatial orientation, and procedural skills for PTED
examples: The survey rated cadaveric specimens most beneficial, high-fidelity physical models and VR simulators as favorable alternatives, and low-fidelity bench-top models least favorable but useful for foundational steps
key_sources: Cai Bohong, Wang Zihan, Lyu Xi, Qiao Yiran, Liu Yuhan, Wu Danting, Li Sihang, Yao Qi, Chen Baixiang, Fu Fujian, Jiang Wei. (2025). Surgeon perceptions of essential skills and simulation for percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic discectomy training. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34397-2

article_title: Medical trainees' emotions and their effects on perceptions of performance and team mood in team-based simulations.
citation: Grewal, K., Azher, S., Moreno, M., Pekrun, R., Wiseman, J., Flake, J., Lajoie, S., Sun, N.‐Z., Fried, G. M., Khalil, E., & Harley, J. M. (2026). Medical trainees' emotions and their effects on perceptions of performance and team mood in team‐based simulations. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 306–336. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70017
title: Situated Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (SERQ)
description: The SERQ is a novel self-report instrument for team-based medical simulations that measures current emotional states, perceptions of individual and team performance, and team mood in one measure. It draws on a modified Medical Emotion Scale with added stress and nervousness items, and "provides a narrative‐style summary of participants' responses" that is automatically emailed to participants to encourage reflection. The article reports first validity evidence based on content, internal structure, response processes and relations to other variables.
requirements: Completed immediately before and after the simulation; item reduction to 7 emotion variables was needed due to limited sample size and power constraints
constraints: Emotion regulation strategy items were not used in the presented analyses; discrete-emotion validity evidence was weaker than quadrant-level evidence
target_learning_goals: awareness and self-report of current emotional states
reflection on individual and team performance and team mood
examples: Administered pre- and post-simulation to 106 residents across 69 teams and 69 simulations, yielding 242 datapoints

Medical trainees' emotions and their effects on perceptions of performance and team mood in team‐based simulations. article_title: The role of academic self-concepts, parent expectations and teacher-student interactions in socio-economic gaps in educational attainment.
citation: Dempsey, C., & McCoy, S. (2026). The role of academic self‐concepts, parent expectations and teacher–student interactions in socio‐economic gaps in educational attainment. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 422–442. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70025
title: Situated expectancy-value theory combined with a developmental systems lens for socio-economic attainment gaps
description: The article draws on situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT), which "posits that academic performance and achievement‐related choices are influenced by one's expectations for success and self‐concept of ability" and that socializers' perceptions shape children's self-concepts. Because SEVT does not account for interacting parent and teacher influences, the authors add a developmental systems lens: "Developmental systems theory emphasizes how multiple important adults influence long‐term development for children through both spillover and compensatory pathways". This combined framework structures the study's tests of bidirectional change and teacher moderation across SES groups.
requirements: Longitudinal data on child self-concepts and parent expectations across the primary–secondary transition, plus a later attainment measure
constraints: SEVT does not account for the interacting influence of parent and teacher factors, which motivated the wider developmental systems lens
target_learners: Children transitioning from primary to secondary school
examples: The study tested SEVT-based hypotheses using GUI cohort data at ages 9, 13 and 20, comparing economically vulnerable and non-vulnerable families
key_sources: Dempsey, C., & McCoy, S. (2026). The role of academic self‐concepts, parent expectations and teacher–student interactions in socio‐economic gaps in educational attainment. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 422–442. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70025

article_title: Comparison study of LANJA, UE, and VDO video laryngoscopes for simulated endotracheal intubation in beginners.
citation: Wang M, Ruan W, Li H, Yuan W, Song J, Wang J. (2025). Comparison study of LANJA, UE, and VDO video laryngoscopes for simulated endotracheal intubation in beginners. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000045803
title: Seven-day structured simulation training program preparing novices for video-laryngoscope intubation
description: A training program in which volunteers with no prior endotracheal intubation experience received theoretical instruction on airway anatomy, indications, contraindications, and video-laryngoscopy principles, then watched demonstrations by anesthesiologists with "at least 10 years of clinical practice in airway management" and engaged in hands-on manikin practice. It ran "over a period of 7 days, with each training session lasting approximately 4 hours per day," chosen to let participants absorb theory and become familiar with equipment before the timed comparison.
requirements: Participants with no prior endotracheal intubation experience
Theoretical instruction followed by expert demonstration and hands-on practice
A simulated airway manikin with adjustable difficulty settings
constraints: The study simulated only normal airways and did not simulate difficult airway scenarios
Simulated patients cannot replicate real physiological conditions such as secretions, bleeding, or mist
target_learners: Medical students and resident physicians with no prior intubation experience
target_learning_goals: Performing endotracheal intubation with video laryngoscopes
examples: Twenty-nine volunteers were randomly assigned laryngoscope use order via random.org and intubated a PLHX1002 manikin whose tongue position and pharyngeal compliance are adjustable

article_title: A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education.
citation: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7
title: Seven mega-opportunities taxonomy of AI in medical student assessment
description: From a systematic review of 71 studies, the article extracts 22 distinct AI opportunities for medical student assessment and groups them into seven overarching categories called mega-opportunities. As the article states, these are Personalised Learning and Adaptive Assessment, Automated Feedback and Evaluation, Simulation-Based Assessment, Competency-Based and Skills Assessment, Data-Driven Analytics and Curriculum Improvement, Enhancing Focus Efficiency and Time Management, and Longitudinal Assessment and Development. The taxonomy is offered to bring conceptual clarity to a fragmented literature, noting that some opportunities such as AI-assisted standardised patient encounters appear under multiple mega-opportunities.
requirements: Derived from a systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and ERIC covering 2010-2025, with thematic synthesis of peer-reviewed studies on AI in student assessment in medical or health professions education
constraints: Based on the included literature, which the authors note is fragmented and often descriptive
target_learners: undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing medical education students
target_learning_goals: student assessment practice design in medical education
examples: Table 2 of the article lists each mega-opportunity with its definition, corresponding opportunities, and supporting references
key_sources: Rezaei-Zadeh M, Cerbin-Koczorowska M. (2025). A research roadmap for AI opportunities in student assessment for medical education. BMC Medical Education 25:1653. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08078-7

article_title: Use of two virtual dissection tables in a postgraduate oral anatomy course: feedback from the students.
citation: Gerardi Davide, Torge Diana, Bernardi Sara, Bianchi Serena, Macchiarelli Guido. (2025). Use of two virtual dissection tables in a postgraduate oral anatomy course: feedback from the students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07840-1
title: SECTRA virtual dissection table with IDS7 medical imaging case database
description: The SECTRA table is the second virtual dissection table used in the postgraduate oral anatomy course. The article describes it as "an anatomical table in the IDS7® database of medical imaging cases, 3D cadaveric dissections, including histology, embryology and radiology, based on real cases of clinical interest". Students rated it comparably to the Anatomage table on usefulness, user-friendliness and image quality, though the discussion notes they found the application challenging and asked for interface improvements and more maxillofacial and oral cases.
requirements: Requires access to the IDS7 database of medical imaging cases and 3D cadaveric dissections, including histology, embryology and radiology content
constraints: Students found the application challenging and reported the need to enrich the library of cases from maxillofacial and oral regions
A few students requested interface improvements for the SECTRA table
target_learners: postgraduate dental residents in oral surgery and orthodontics
target_learning_goals: working with real clinical imaging cases
examples: Residents completed a 2-hour SECTRA session per week following general training on the software and hardware
key_sources: Gerardi Davide, Torge Diana, Bernardi Sara, Bianchi Serena, Macchiarelli Guido. (2025). Use of two virtual dissection tables in a postgraduate oral anatomy course: feedback from the students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07840-1

article_title: [Acting as a change agent: longitudinal effects of a tailored training program aimed at developing the competencies of health and social service professionals].
citation: Carrier A, Beaudoin M, Éthier A, Bédard D. (2025). Acting as a change agent: longitudinal effects of a tailored training program aimed at developing the competencies of health and social service professionals. Canadian Medical Education Journal 16(4). https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.80292
title: Seven-hour online change-agent training built on a co-development pedagogical approach covering four themes
description: The article evaluates a tailored training program for the change-agent role: "une formation en ligne d'une durée de sept heures, divisée en deux demi-journées", "Reposant sur une approche pédagogique de type co-développement". It covered "quatre thèmes principaux : l'analyse du contexte de réalisation du projet de changement (organisationnel ou sociétal), le développement de partenariat, les stratégies de communication (p. ex., cibler le message) et la planification des actions." Its specific content is described elsewhere by the authors.
requirements: Participants had to master French and attend the full seven-hour online training delivered in two half-days
constraints: The specific content of the training and its pedagogical approach are described in another publication by the authors, not in this article
target_learners: Health and social service professionals in Quebec, unionized with the APTS
target_learning_goals: Competence to act as a change agent, including context analysis, partnership development, communication strategies, and action planning
examples: Delivered 5–6 April 2022 to 40 participants recruited through the APTS union across seven of its 19 unionized establishments

Acting as a change agent: longitudinal effects of a tailored training program aimed at developing the competencies of health and social service professionals. article_title: Assessing Best Practices in a Simulated Lumbar Puncture Workshop With Medical Students.
citation: Dugan L, Rei KM, Ueno A, Mahutga J, Varma M. (2025). Assessing Best Practices in a Simulated Lumbar Puncture Workshop With Medical Students. The Permanente Journal. https://doi.org/10.7812/TPP/24.155
title: For teaching complex procedural skills, institutions may prefer the less time-intensive "see one, do one" approach when time is limited
description: The article's conclusion recommends that, because Peyton's 4-step method did not yield higher checklist scores or greater confidence for the complex simulated lumbar puncture, "the simple and less time-intensive approach, 'see one, do one,' may be preferred by institutions for teaching complex skills." The actual facilitation time for "see one, do one" was approximately one-half that of Peyton's method in this study, with time parity maintained by supplementary discussion.
requirements: The skill must meet the article's criterion of a complex procedure (more than 7 skill elements; the studied sLP required 16 individual steps).
Instruction time must be held comparable across methods, as the study did by supplementing "see one, do one" with additional anatomy, physiology, pathology, and indications discussion.
constraints: The recommendation rests on immediate skill acquisition only; the article states future research should investigate long-term skill retention.
The study may have been underpowered to detect smaller effect sizes between methods.

target_learning_goals: performing a lumbar puncture safely and competently in a simulated setting
examples: In the study, both methods received exactly 30 minutes of instruction and practice, with the "see one, do one" method supplemented by additional discussion for time parity.

description: The article uses Bandura's self-efficacy theory to interpret CALD students' emotional trajectories in SBL: beliefs about one's ability to succeed influence emotion regulation and performance. The authors argue "supporting the development of self‐efficacy is critical" and frame the fear-to-growth progression through the occupational therapy concept of becoming.

article_title: Planting the seed: how parental negative conditional regard boosts vulnerability to excessive study behaviour and burnout.
citation: Brueckmann M, Wild E, Wolff F. (2025). Planting the seed: how parental negative conditional regard boosts vulnerability to excessive study behaviour and burnout. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03354-z
title: Self-esteem model of burnout
description: Hallsten's self-esteem model of burnout holds that people who define their self-esteem primarily in terms of academic achievement are at greater risk of burning out through excessive compensatory engagement. The article quotes the script "I am what I achieve" and describes an initial phase of "anxiety-driven engagement", in which high behavioural engagement coexists with worries and anxieties, chronic stress and constant worry in the pursuit of high self-esteem, ultimately producing exhaustion, reduced self-efficacy and cynicism. The present study's serial mediation results are presented as empirical support for this model.
requirements: A self-esteem that is contingent upon academic performance, which creates vulnerability to excessive compensatory engagement
constraints: The article notes the model's mediation pathways were tested cross-sectionally, so causal interpretations are inadmissible
target_learning_goals: understanding and preventing academic burnout and excessive study behaviour
examples: The study tested a serial mediation model in which academic self-esteem contingency predicted excessive study behaviour, which in turn predicted exhaustion and reduced self-efficacy in 624 university students.

article_title: SEE+ computerized classroom-based training enhances 7- to 10-year-olds' socio-emotional cognition through observation and inference.
citation: Mayer Sveta, Dumontheil Iroise, Wilkinson Hannah R., Porayska-Pomsta Kaska, Farran Emily K., Tolmie Andrew K., Mareschal Denis, the UnLocke Team. (2025). SEE+ computerized classroom-based training enhances 7- to 10-year-olds' socio-emotional cognition through observation and inference. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0330934
title: SEE+ computerized whole-class socio-emotional learning activity
description: SEE+ (Socio-emotional engagement through observation) is a computerized, classroom-based learning activity in which children observe "four virtual characters' interactions in social scenarios involving social dilemmas or conflict" and infer their mental states. It comprises 30 activities of 12 minutes each, delivered three times weekly over 10 weeks during PSHE lesson time, built from eight archetypical activities derived from developmental paradigms (emotion recognition, Reading the Mind in the Eyes, action observation, Faux Pas, Cyberball, Director, Sandbox, Strange Stories) presented in increasing complexity. Activities have four phases interleaving observation, reflective questions, prediction and feedback animations.
requirements: Delivered by the regular class teacher or teaching assistant with animations projected whole-class, with answers entered into the computerized interface via class consensus or individual responses
constraints: Activities were designed so task structure and duration matched the Stop & Think mathematics/science condition without requiring mathematics or science reasoning
target_learners: Year 3 (7–8 years old) and Year 5 (9–10 years old) primary school pupils in England
target_learning_goals: Emotion recognition from faces and body cues
examples: In the RCT, SEE+ was delivered as an active control condition for the Stop & Think intervention, allocated to 25% of classes by an independent external evaluator

article_title: Student motivation and instructional clarity: Linking experience sampling method data to objective behavioural observations.
citation: Oschwald, A., Moeller, J., Kracke, B., Viljaranta, J., & Dietrich, J. (2025). Student motivation and instructional clarity: Linking experience sampling method data to objective behavioural observations. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S281–S299. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12775
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) as a framework for situational motivation
description: Situated expectancy-value theory describes why and how students make achievement-related decisions, show persistence, and achieve performance in educational situations influenced by contextual, cultural, and situated determinants. Its core components are "task‐specific expectancies to succeed" and "task values", with task values comprising four facets: intrinsic value, utility, attainment, and perceived cost (with effort, emotional, and opportunity sub-facets). The study applies SEVT at the situation level, measuring momentary expectancies, values, and costs three times per lecture via ESM.
requirements: Assessment instruments distinguishing expectancies, competence beliefs, and the value and cost facets, as adapted from Eccles and Wigfield and Gaspard et al.
constraints: Most empirical SEVT studies have focused on inter-individual differences; situational modelling requires intensive longitudinal data.
target_learning_goals: situational achievement motivation (expectancies, task values, costs)
examples: The study measured situational expectancies with two items, task values with six items adapted to educational psychology, and separate effort, emotional, and opportunity cost items on a four-point Likert scale.

description: The article distils two takeaways for educators: PLE should be carefully selected and supported so they can contribute meaningfully, and simulation design should create structured opportunities for every learner to receive personalised PLE feedback. The authors write that 'simulation design should maximise opportunities for students to receive personalised feedback from PLE—whether through rotating facilitators or structured debriefs'. This follows from findings that PLE communication skills and psychological safety were key to learning.

citation: Aja Lucy, Odhine Innocent Sunday, Muhammad Tukur, Lubega Mohammad. (2025). Students' psychological patterns and academic performance in public secondary schools in Kazo District, Uganda: a quantitative analysis. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03187-w
title: Bandura's self-efficacy theory and Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory as the framework for interpreting students' psychological patterns
description: The study grounds its analysis in two frameworks. Bandura's social cognitive theory is used to interpret self-efficacy: "supporting Bandura's (1997) theory that higher self-efficacy fosters setting challenging goals and persistence." Self-determination theory is invoked for motivation: the article states "The results about motivation are in line with Ryan and Deci's [44] Self-Determination Theory. They show that intrinsic motivation, enjoyment, and personal relevance have a greater and longer-lasting influence on academic performance than external influences." The article also draws on Vygotsky's theory emphasizing social interaction and cultural context in learning.
requirements: Interpreting student self-report data as evidence of self-efficacy and motivation patterns
constraints: The article presents these theories as interpretive lenses for descriptive findings, not as experimentally tested predictions
examples: The discussion links the self-efficacy item means (4.43 for believing in good grades) to Bandura's claim that higher self-efficacy fosters challenging goals and persistence

title: Three-theme, three-direction taxonomy of SET bias causes in undergraduate medical education
description: The article organizes the causes of bias in medical students' teaching evaluations into three overarching themes arising from thematic analysis: teacher-student interaction, factors related to medical students, and evaluation-system factors. Bias direction is classified in three ways: "Positive Bias: Indicates that the evaluation scores are higher than the teacher's actual teaching performance," "Negative Bias: Indicates that the evaluation scores are lower than the teacher's actual teaching performance," and "Arbitrary Bias: Indicates that the evaluation scores are inconsistent or lack reliability." Subthemes include personal affinity, management style, informal score agreements, in-group and authority bias, course attributes and interest, group influence, default high scoring, anonymity doubts, feedback shortfalls, timing and workload, and indicator comprehension.
requirements: Undergraduate medical students with prior experience of student evaluations of teaching, recruited purposively across years and majors
constraints: Derived from a single medical university in northern China; the authors state this may restrict generalizability and that the Chinese cultural context may limit applicability to other countries
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students across academic years and majors at a Chinese public medical university
target_learning_goals: Objective, reliable student evaluations of teaching quality in medical education
examples: Semi-structured interviews with 22 participants (7 males, 15 females), analyzed via Braun and Clarke thematic analysis with member checking; thematic saturation reached after 24 interviews

description: A lesson-level instructional pattern designed according to Merrill's first principle of instruction, whose principles are "problem-centered" and comprise a cycle of activation, demonstration, application, and integration. In the current study, the instructional procedures of the in-class flipped classroom comprised seven steps during a 160-minute skills lab course: distributing videos and materials via Rain Classroom, group self-directed learning, targeted live demonstrations, guided re-practice, scenario simulation with peer and instructor evaluation and guided reflection, and post-class review materials and experiment reports.

title: Semantic qualifiers as higher-level abstractions of patient complaints that structure diagnostic reasoning
description: Semantic qualifiers (SQs) are keyword inputs that abstract a patient's complaints into medical terms. The article defines them as "medical terms that categorize and replace specific medical history details based on higher-level concepts" that are "often dichotomous in their logic (e.g., acute vs. chronic, local vs. radiating)". SQ selection depends on clinical ability and supports recalling diseases, narrowing differential lists, and literature searches; in this trial, three expert-defined appropriate SQs per case vignette served as the benchmark for scoring participants' free-text SQ answers.

citation: Roselló Atanet Iván, Tomova Mihaela, Sieg Miriam, Sehy Victoria, Mäder Patrick, März Maren. (2025). Generating learning guides for medical education with LLMs and statistical analysis of test results. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06978-2
title: Seven-step LLM-plus-statistics pipeline for generating personalized PTM learning guides
description: A pipeline combining large language models, the MeSH thesaurus, and statistical analysis of test results to automate personalized feedback. "We propose in this manuscript a seven-step approach to automate the construction of personalized feedback": ChatGPT 4.0 extracts MeSH terms from question vignettes and correct answers (distractors excluded); outputs are lemmatized, compared via cosine similarity, and validated against the MeSH thesaurus; ancestor terms are added; tf-idf allocates terms to 14 organ systems; precursor questions are identified; graphs of question paths are generated; and cluster-based visual and textual feedback is composed with five topic-recommendation groups. Implemented in Python with scikit-learn and Plotly.
requirements: A controlled vocabulary (MeSH) and a pre-existing curricular framework (organ systems) to group extracted terms.
Sufficiently large and heterogeneous test data: 200 questions and 2,932 participations enabled the precursor-question web.
constraints: The LLM is used only for keyword extraction; feedback generation avoids LLMs because "data protection regulations prevent feeding it with real test results".
Feedback cannot be constructed for drop-out clusters 2 and 4, and is data-scarce for cluster 3.
target_learners: medical students across all semesters in a progress-testing programme
target_learning_goals: identifying knowledge gaps and prioritizing topics to study
examples: Tested retrospectively on PT46 data, producing simulated guides for 1,401 participants with topics ranging from 34 to 243.

title: Semistructured interview protocol with MIIM-guided thematic analysis and member checking
description: This study's data-collection and analysis protocol: approximately 30-minute semistructured interviews with PCCM faculty, conducted by both authors, with a protocol modified through constant comparative analysis. title: SET-CPR booster workshop: a 3-hour simulation workshop on resuscitation and teamwork added one week before the mid-test
description: The SET-CPR (Simulation-Enhanced Team Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) intervention is an additional 3-hour workshop focused on resuscitation and teamwork training delivered one week before the 6th-month mid-test scenario. It has two content parts: resuscitation care patient management (airway, breathing, circulation and resuscitation) and teamwork including leadership behavior. Small groups of seven to eight residents practiced with three to four acting as the primary response team, one leading as doctor and two as nurses, with debriefing guided by the Gather, Analyze, Summarize (G.A.S.) debriefing model.

title: Self-determination theory account of why criterion-referenced honors/pass/fail grading supports motivation and performance
description: The article interprets its findings through self-determination theory, "an established framework for understanding motivation," which "emphasizes that fulfilling basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) is fundamental to building intrinsic motivation." The authors propose that removing rank-based grades increased autonomy, meeting specific criteria inspired competence, and alleviating competition fostered relatedness and a collaborative climate. constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of a cross-sectional, single-center study rather than a directly tested mechanism

target_learning_goals: academic performance in basic medical sciences
examples: The authors propose that removal of relative rank-based grades allowed students to pursue learning for curiosity and interest, and that criterion-based assessment inspired a sense of competence

description: The study scored every simulated case with a matrix allocating points across "7 skill elements considered important for effective ventilation": proportion of valid ventilations, ventilation rate, ventilation fraction, time to baby cry, proportion of too low pressure ventilations, avoiding dangerously high inflating pressures (≥45 cm H2O), and proportion of ventilations with no head tilt. The elements were summed to a global competence score of maximum 30 points, with a score higher than 28 defined as maintained high competence.

constraints: The scoring matrix allocates points according to percentage bands, which can weight skill elements differently to the simulator's algorithm

citation: Stieha Vicki, Earl Brittnee, Hagens Harrisen, Haynes Meagan, Ulappa Amy, Bond Laura, Oxford Julia Thom. (2024). An exploration of the relationship between active learning and student motivation in STEM: a mixed methods study. Advances in Physiology Education. https://doi.org/10.1152/advan.00247.2022
title: Self-determination theory: competence, autonomy, and relatedness as supports for motivation quality
description: The study is framed by self-determination theory, which "posits that an individual’s quality of motivation is partially dependent on the social and contextual supports for the three motivational components" of competence, autonomy, and relatedness. Competence is the need to experience the self as capable; autonomy is having choice rather than acting only on demands and is relational, not independence; relatedness is connection with others and the subject matter. The authors used SDT constructs both to build their survey instrument and as a priori codes for observed teaching practices.
requirements: Instructors establish conditions for motivation through instructional practices, curricular design, and classroom culture
constraints: Effort was measured alongside the three components but was not coded as an observable practice because it is not one of the basic needs
examples: Survey items were contextualized with phrases such as "in this course" and drawn from the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory and Learning Climate Questionnaire

title: Seven clusters of SDT-supportive instructional practices observed in active learning classrooms
description: From COPUS codes and descriptive notes, the authors clustered observed practices into seven groups: "We clustered the specific practices into categories, based on the descriptive notes and COPUS results into seven groups." The clusters are questioning during lecture/minilecture, discussion approaches, course design, formative/summative assessment, presentation-related practices, individual/paired/group practices, and general interactions. Each practice was coded against the SDT constructs it has been shown to support in prior literature (Table 6), and practices aligning with both theory and higher survey scores are highlighted in Figure 2.
requirements: Practices must be implemented with fidelity to the evidence-based methods described in prior literature
constraints: The quality or nature of questioning is not captured by COPUS codes alone and required supplemental descriptive notes
examples: Practices aligning with theory and higher survey scores included Q&A (extended/applied), small group and paired discussions, explicitly stated learning outcomes, transparent course design, think-pair-share, minute paper/muddiest point, in-class group worksheets, professor demonstrating humility, peer instruction, group work time, moving and guiding, one-on-one interactions, using students' names, and connections to student interests

title: Set simulation-based mastery pass/fail standards at the experts' average performance rather than the contrasting-groups intersection
description: The article recommends raising the pass/fail standard above the statistically derived contrasting-groups cutoff when the goal is mastery: "we decided to raise the pass/fail standard to the level of the experts’ average score of 96% to gain a real mastery competence standard". The authors argue the purpose is not to find the score that lets most experts pass, but to train trainees to the highest competence they can achieve within a reasonable timeframe, and that the standard's consequences for trainees must be explored for feasibility.
requirements: Expert plateau performance data must be collected to define the standard
The consequences of the standard on the intended target group must be explored to confirm it is obtainable
constraints: The authors caution the study setup should not be interpreted as optimal for learning: 65 minutes of training "can hardly ensure optimal learning of a complex procedure", and performance during acquisition can be an imperfect indicator of retention or transfer
target_learners: Novice orthopedic trainees prior to supervised operating-room training
target_learning_goals: Reaching mastery-level procedural competence in simulation before clinical performance
examples: In this study the raised 96% standard was met by all 10 mastery-group novices without increased hands-on training time

article_title: A sequential model of the contribution of preschool fluid and crystallized cognitive abilities to later school achievement.
citation: Carpentier Philippe, Morneau-Vaillancourt Geneviève, Aubé Sophie, Matte-Gagné Célia, Denault Anne-Sophie, Brendgen Mara, Larose Simon, Petitclerc Amélie, Ouellet-Morin Isabelle, Carbonneau René, Feng Bei, Séguin Jean, Côté Sylvana, Vitaro Frank, Tremblay Richard E., Dionne Ginette, Boivin Michel. title: A sequential model in which preschool fluid abilities contribute to school achievement through the mediation of crystallized abilities
description: The article proposes and tests a sequential developmental model in which preschool fluid abilities (cognitive visual-spatial skills, cognitive flexibility, short-term memory) contribute to the acquisition of crystallized abilities (knowledge of numbers, letters, colors and shapes), which in turn predict school achievement. The authors frame this as "a special case of asymmetrical mutualism, whereby crystallized abilities stem from the interaction (or investment) of fluid intelligence and experience, ultimately leading to achievement in school". The model includes autoregressive paths capturing the strong stability of school achievement across primary school.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of school achievement and autoregressive paths to model the stability of achievement over time
constraints: The findings are correlational, as the article itself states
The mediation is time-limited: crystallized abilities did not add or added modestly to prediction beyond grade 3
target_learners: children in primary school grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: school achievement in mathematics, writing and reading
acquisition of early numeracy and literacy knowledge
examples: Path analyses in the QNTS and QLSCD samples supported the mediation hypothesis, with the crystallized latent factor predicted by fluid skills (R2 = .45 and .44) and predicting early-grade achievement

citation: Betti, A., Biderbost, P., & García Domonte, A. (2022). Can active learning techniques simultaneously develop students’ hard and soft skills? Evidence from an international relations class. PLoS ONE 17(4): e0265408. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265408
title: Prefer semi-traditional formats combining face-to-face lectures with active learning techniques over fully flipped formats when aiming to develop content knowledge and soft skills together
description: This principle holds that when the goal is to develop content knowledge and soft skills jointly, a semi-traditional format mixing frontal lectures with active learning techniques may serve better than a fully flipped format. The article reaches it from its single marginally significant canonical correlation, found only in the semi-traditional control group after the experiment, writing that "semi-traditional teaching formats, based on face-to-face lectures integrated with active learning techniques, are more effective than fully active learning formats, such as FCs". It is framed as a possibility, not a tested result.
requirements: Requires measuring both hard skills and soft skills when comparing a fully flipped format against a semi-traditional format that integrates frontal lectures with active learning techniques.
constraints: The article frames this as a possibility suggested by one marginally significant canonical correlation, not a tested result; it also cites concerns about training and investment problems of active learning formats.
target_learners: University students in social and political sciences, such as the third-year Dual Degree in International Relations and Business students in the experiment
target_learning_goals: Development of content knowledge (hard skills) together with soft skills such as self-efficacy, teamwork, critical thinking, and perception of learning
examples: The experiment taught a control group of 32 students through two weekly hours of frontal lectures plus two hours of active learning activities, while a 31-student experimental group received a fully flipped format; only the control group after the experiment showed the marginally significant canonical correlation.
key_sources: Betti, A., Biderbost, P., & García Domonte, A. (2022). Can active learning techniques simultaneously develop students’ hard and soft skills? Evidence from an international relations class. PLoS ONE 17(4): e0265408. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265408

article_title: The Association Between Temperament and Characteristics, Smartphone App Use Patterns and Academic Performance of University Students.
citation: Lee Jea Woog, Park Sung Je, Kim Soyeon, Chung Un Sun, Han Doug Hyun. (2022). The Association Between Temperament and Characteristics, Smartphone App Use Patterns and Academic Performance of University Students. Journal of Korean Medical Science. https://doi.org/10.3346/jkms.2022.37.e143
title: Support sports-major students' academic excellence by encouraging productive serious app use rather than restricting total smartphone time
description: The article concludes that "High usage time of serious apps can help sports majors to excel academically," defining serious apps as Internet browser, schedule, e-books, creativity, education, and diary apps used "to support their studies." Because elite and general students did not differ in total smartphone time, the recommendation targets app type rather than screen-time reduction. The authors caution that the design cannot establish that app use had a direct effect on grades.
requirements: Students must use smartphones with log-monitoring activated so serious app use can be identified; the four app categories (social networking, entertainment, serious, others) must be distinguished
constraints: The study was observational: the previous year's grades preceded the four-week app-use window, so "it was difficult to conclude that the use of app had a direct effect on grades"; the elite group was small (n = 37), limiting generalization; app classification was arbitrary
target_learners: university students majoring in sports/physical education
target_learning_goals: self-management and study support through smartphone apps
examples: Elite students used serious apps 7:30 versus 3:51 hours:minutes on average over four weeks, and serious app use time predicted elite group membership in the logistic regression and both performance outcomes in the path analysis
key_sources: Lee Jea Woog, Park Sung Je, Kim Soyeon, Chung Un Sun, Han Doug Hyun. (2022). The Association Between Temperament and Characteristics, Smartphone App Use Patterns and Academic Performance of University Students. Journal of Korean Medical Science. https://doi.org/10.3346/jkms.2022.37.e143

article_title: Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement.
citation: Pardosi J and Utari TI. (2021). Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement. F1000Research, Volume 10, 465. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.51549.1
title: Seven-ability teacher performance construct used for teacher appraisal in Indonesian senior high schools
description: The article operationalizes teacher performance as seven abilities measured by questionnaire and appraisal: formulating lesson plans (RPP), planning learning activities, choosing learning sources and media, applying learning approaches and strategies, encouraging and maintaining student involvement, ending learning effectively, and designing assessment methods and evaluation tools. It reports that these seven factors "possessed a significant effect on teacher performance", with loadings ranging from 0.46 to 0.73 in the measurement model. The construct derives from the Teacher Ability Assessment Tools modified from the Georgia Department of Education instrument by the Indonesian Ministry of National Education.
requirements: Measured via 5-level Likert questionnaire items and teacher performance appraisals across the seven ability indicators
constraints: The article states this form of teacher performance in the learning process is assumed to be an assessing factor for becoming a future teacher
target_learning_goals: planning, implementing, and evaluating learning activities
examples: The Teacher Ability Assessment Tools consist of teaching plans and materials (RPP), classroom procedures, and interpersonal skills
key_sources: Pardosi J and Utari TI. (2021). Effective principal leadership behaviors to improve the teacher performance and the student achievement. F1000Research, Volume 10, 465. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.51549.1

article_title: The Integration of Gender Perspective into Young People's Sexuality Education in Spain and Portugal: Legislation and Educational Models.
citation: Cunha-Oliveira, A., Camarneiro, A. P., Gómez-Cantarino, S., Cipriano-Crespo, C., Queirós, P. J. P., Cardoso, D., Santos, D. G., & Ugarte-Gurrutxaga, M. I. (2021). The Integration of Gender Perspective into Young People's Sexuality Education in Spain and Portugal: Legislation and Educational Models. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182211921
title: Evolution of sexuality education models: from the moralizing and biologicist models to the Comprehensive Sexuality Education model incorporating the gender approach
description: The review describes a historical trajectory of sexuality education models in formal education: "from the moralizing model" focused on abstinence and control, "to the so-called biologicist model" limited to reproduction, prevention, and knowledge transmission, "until reaching the current model, that is, the CSE model". The CSE model incorporates the gender approach, which the review, citing Morgade, calls the most relevant for work on sexuality issues. The review uses this trajectory to frame its analysis of Spanish and Portuguese educational models.
requirements: Delivery based on a written, comprehensive curriculum focusing on human rights and gender equality, as the review describes for CSE
constraints: The biologicist approach is still present in educators' practices in traditional schools, per the review
target_learners: adolescents aged 10–19 in non-higher education in Spain and Portugal
target_learning_goals: comprehensive understanding of sexuality including cognitive, emotional, physical, and social aspects
gender equality and prevention of gender-based violence
examples: The review maps Spanish and Portuguese studies and legislation against this model trajectory, concluding current practice remains largely risk-prevention oriented

article_title: Impact of video quality when evaluating video-assisted cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomized, controlled simulation trial.
citation: Plata Christopher, Nellessen Martin, Roth Rebecca, Ecker Hannes, Böttiger Bernd W., Löser Johannes, Wetsch Wolfgang A. (2021). Impact of video quality when evaluating video-assisted cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomized, controlled simulation trial. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-021-00486-4
title: Seven standardized 12-second CPR video sequences at three artificial quality levels (high 1920x1080, medium 320x240, low 128x96 ppi)
description: A stimulus set of seven 12-second high-quality video clips recorded on a standardized CPR training manikin, showing either guideline-conformant compression-only CPR or one of six typical errors: "Low compression rate", "High compression rate", "Increased compression depth", "Superficial compression depth", "Wrong hand position", and "Incomplete thorax release" (Table 1). Resolution was artificially reduced with software to three quality levels, all at 30 fps, and sequences were randomly assigned to evaluators in a randomized, double-blinded evaluation with a standardized multiple-choice questionnaire.
requirements: Videos recorded with a metronome set to 110 bpm and the manikin's internal compression depth indicator used during recording, with neither visible nor audible in the final sequences
constraints: Videotaping was performed in a closed environment with sufficient light, constant weather, no disturbances and perfect technical facilities
Only one video position was used; different positions may positively or negatively influence the ability to recognize and correct certain mistakes
target_learning_goals: accurate evaluation of CPR performance quality in video sequences
examples: Each evaluator judged seven video sequences, six containing one error each and one showing correct CPR, with the possibility to indicate each category as not evaluable
key_sources: Plata Christopher, Nellessen Martin, Roth Rebecca, Ecker Hannes, Böttiger Bernd W., Löser Johannes, Wetsch Wolfgang A. (2021). Impact of video quality when evaluating video-assisted cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a randomized, controlled simulation trial. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-021-00486-4

article_title: Serving Children and Adolescents in Need during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evaluation of Service-Learning Subjects with and without Face-to-Face Interaction.
citation: Lin Li and Shek Daniel T. L. (2021). Serving Children and Adolescents in Need during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evaluation of Service-Learning Subjects with and without Face-to-Face Interaction. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18042114
title: Service Leadership Theory: three determinants of effective service leadership in service economies
description: The Service Leadership Theory, proposed by Chung and Bell, holds that in the transition from manufacturing to service economies, a leader prioritizes service over personal interests. Central to this model are "three determinants of effective service leadership: moral character, caring disposition, and leadership competences." The theory adopts a broad definition of leadership in which everyone can be a leader regardless of position, and self-leadership is an important part of effective leadership. The service-learning subject under study was designed based on this theory.
requirements: The theory assumes a service economy context where leadership is about satisfying needs through quality personal service.
target_learning_goals: service leadership knowledge, attitudes, and skills
examples: The credit-bearing subject 'Service Leadership Through Serving Children and Families with Special Needs' was based on this theory.
key_sources: Lin Li and Shek Daniel T. L. (2021). Serving Children and Adolescents in Need during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Evaluation of Service-Learning Subjects with and without Face-to-Face Interaction. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18042114

article_title: Feedback in the clinical setting.
citation: Burgess A, van Diggele C, Roberts C, Mellis C. (2020). Feedback in the clinical setting. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02280-5
title: Self-regulated learning empowers students to direct their own learning, with feedback on SRL use encouraging self-monitored strategies
description: The article describes self-regulated learning (SRL) as a process that "empowers students to actively engage in and direct their own learning". SRL helps students set goals, actively engage in learning activities, and monitor their own progress and actions in achievement of their goals. Feedback can be given to students on their use of SRL to encourage learning strategies that are clear and specific, self-monitored, and reflected upon. The article links this to learning environments where students see themselves as agents of their own change.
requirements: Educators systematically build self-analysis as an expectation within the curriculum
Learning environments where students see themselves as agents of their own change
constraints: The article frames this as a challenge for educators, without reporting empirical tests of SRL-based feedback in this paper
target_learners: health professional students on clinical placements
examples: The article states regular self-analysis helps build habits that promote comparison between self-analysis and external analysis
key_sources: Burgess A, van Diggele C, Roberts C, Mellis C. (2020). Feedback in the clinical setting. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02280-5

article_title: Video-based, student tutor- versus faculty staff-led ultrasound course for medical students - a prospective randomized study.
citation: Eimer Christine, Duschek Max, Jung Andreas Emanuel, Zick Günther, Caliebe Amke, Lindner Matthias, Weiler Norbert, Elke Gunnar. (2020). Video-based, student tutor- versus faculty staff-led ultrasound course for medical students – a prospective randomized study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02431-8
title: Ultrasound teaching videos segmented step by step and designed around Mayer's multimedia learning principles
description: The article's video design pattern segments each tutorial into learning objectives, basic skills (physics, image interpretation, probe handling), advanced standard-view examination, and a final summary, following the segmenting principle. Signaling colors, synchronous text/spoken words/visuals, dual coding, spatial and temporal contiguity, and modality, personalization and voice principles were applied; raw footage was repeatedly student-tested and externally reviewed before use.
requirements: Cooperation with multimedia production expertise for graphical visualization and video-technical implementation
Student feedback iterations and external a-priori product-level evaluation before first use
constraints: The pre-training principle was excluded from implementation
target_learners: undergraduate medical students inexperienced in ultrasound
target_learning_goals: ultrasound probe handling, standard view acquisition, anatomical identification and physiological measurement
examples: The two-picture design placed the ultrasound monitor image on the left and the examiner's hand position on the right of the video image
key_sources: Eimer Christine, Duschek Max, Jung Andreas Emanuel, Zick Günther, Caliebe Amke, Lindner Matthias, Weiler Norbert, Elke Gunnar. (2020). article_title: Assessing palliative care education in undergraduate medical students: translation and validation of the Self-Efficacy in Palliative Care and Thanatophobia Scales for Brazilian Portuguese.
citation: Gryschek Guilherme, Cecilio-Fernandes Dario, Mason Stephen, de Carvalho-Filho Marco Antonio. (2020). Assessing palliative care education in undergraduate medical students: translation and validation of the Self-Efficacy in Palliative Care and Thanatophobia Scales for Brazilian Portuguese. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-034567
title: SEPC-Br and TS-Br: validated Brazilian Portuguese versions of the Self-Efficacy in Palliative Care and Thanatophobia Scales
description: SEPC-Br is a 23-item scale on which students rate confidence in palliative care practice on a 100 mm Visual Analogue Scale scored 0–100, with three factors: communication, patient management, and multidisciplinary teamwork. TS-Br is a 7-item scale rating statements such as 'Dying patients make me feel uneasy' on a 7-point Likert Scale, scored 7–49 with higher scores indicating higher thanatophobia. Both were translated via the EORTC procedure with back-translation and developer consultation, then pilot-tested with 10 sixth-year students.
requirements: Translation followed the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer's recommendations, including independent forward translations, reconciliation, and back-translation reviewed with the original scale developers
constraints: The authors state self-assessment instruments alone are not enough for a final evaluation of learning outcomes and recommend OSCEs, mini-CEX or other external methods in addition
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in Brazilian and Portuguese-speaking contexts
target_learning_goals: thanatophobia / outcome expectancy towards dying patients
examples: Administered to 111 third-year students (response rate 93.2%) during final exams on clinical semiology in July 2017
key_sources: Gryschek Guilherme, Cecilio-Fernandes Dario, Mason Stephen, de Carvalho-Filho Marco Antonio. (2020). article_title: Effect of the Flipped Classroom and Gamification Methods in the Development of a Didactic Unit on Healthy Habits and Diet in Primary Education.
citation: Gómez-García, G.; Marín-Marín, J.A.; Romero-Rodríguez, J.M.; Ramos Navas-Parejo, M.; Rodríguez Jiménez, C. (2020). Effect of the Flipped Classroom and Gamification Methods in the Development of a Didactic Unit on Healthy Habits and Diet in Primary Education. Nutrients 12(8), 2210. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu12082210
title: Self-determination theory framing of motivation, autonomy and self-regulation
description: The study takes as its reference the theory of self-determination proposed by Deci and Ryan, which organises the outcome variables of the intervention. The article states it "is composed of variables associated with motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic), the autonomy of the individual when deciding what type of behaviour to perform and self-regulation in order to make decisions." The three constructs were operationalised as the questionnaire dimensions MOT, AUT and SER and used to evaluate the flipped/gamified nutrition unit's effects.
requirements: Measurement instruments capturing motivation, autonomy and self-regulation as distinct but related constructs
constraints: Applied here to primary students in a nutrition education context
examples: The ad hoc questionnaire's MOT, AUT and SER subscales operationalised the framework's three variables

article_title: Computer-based video training is effective in teaching basic surgical skills to novices without faculty involvement using a self-directed, sequential and incremental program.
citation: Kumins Norman H., Qin Vivian L., Driscoll Erin C., Morrow Katherine L., Kashyap Vikram S., Ning Anne Y., Tucker Nicholas J., King Alexander H., Quereshy Humzah A., Dash Siddhartha, Grobaty Lauren, Zhou George. (2021). Computer-based video training is effective in teaching basic surgical skills to novices without faculty involvement using a self-directed, sequential and incremental program. American Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjsurg.2020.08.011
title: Break each skill into its simplest elements, release videos sequentially with practice-gated progression, and reinforce prior content in each new video
description: The authors attribute their CBVT course's success to a design principle: decompose a complex skill into its simplest components, teach "simple hand movements one at a time in a progressive manner", release videos over time, and require students to demonstrate watching and practice before receiving new videos. Each video "reinforced what was learned in previous videos to build upon skills already learned", so mastery of earlier steps supports later ones and students progress without pressure at their own pace.
requirements: A video library decomposing the target skill into sequentially ordered, incrementally新增 steps
A mechanism (e.g., practice-sample submission) gating access to the next video set
constraints: The stepwise introduction of material was not directly tested against other paradigms
It is unclear whether sequential release over time helped students absorb the material
examples: In the Self-Directed Surgical Skills elective, two videos were released every two weeks and students provided practice samples, ungraded, to unlock the next set.

article_title: New doctor-patient communication learning software to help interns succeed in communication skills.
citation: Sun Chao, Zou Junkai, Zhao Lanbo, Wang Qing, Zhang Shaozhi, Ulain Qurat, Song Qing, Li Qiling. (2020). New doctor-patient communication learning software to help interns succeed in communication skills. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1917-z
title: SEGUE framework as the organizing rubric for teaching and assessing doctor-patient communication
description: The Set Elicit Give Understand End (SEGUE) framework structures doctor-patient communication into five stages: "the preparation stage, information collection, information given, patient understanding, and inquisition ending". This study adopted it as the "doctor-patient communication scale", testing 25 communication skills (e.g., courtesy title, asking about psychological factors, informing physical condition, expressing concern) before and after software training. It serves here both as the training content organizer and as the outcome measure.
requirements: Requires an instrument of scored skill items across the five stages to produce pre/post comparisons
examples: The study tested 25 SEGUE skills by t test / chi-square before and after learning and found seven results significant

article_title: Serious games, a game changer in teaching neonatal resuscitation? A review.
citation: Ghoman SK, Patel SD, Cutumisu M, von Hauff P, Jeffery T, Brown MRG, Schmölzer GM. (2020). Serious games, a game changer in teaching neonatal resuscitation? A review. Archives of Disease in Childhood. Fetal and Neonatal Edition. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2019-317011
title: Taxonomy of serious games for neonatal resuscitation training by game type
description: The review organises the serious-game literature for neonatal resuscitation into three game types: board games, computer/video games and virtual reality games. It reports that "A total of 12 games (four board games, five video games and three VR games, as indicated in tables 1 and 2) were identified using our search strategy". Each game is characterised by learning objective, how to play, availability, feedback, learners' attitudes and educational outcomes, and the review defines serious games as "games with a primary purpose other than just entertainment (eg, with an educational or training goal)".
requirements: Games must address neonatology teaching for healthcare professionals and fulfil the serious-game criteria of an engaging experience with a challenging goal teaching relevant knowledge and skills
constraints: Games used for reasons other than teaching HCPs' neonatology (eg, parental teaching) were excluded
Design and development was variable or unreported, and some games have not been scientifically evaluated or assessed for validity
examples: The review's tables summarise games including RETAIN board game, The Neonatology Game, Neonatal Emergency Trivia Game, Neonopoly, NRP eSim, RETAIN video game, Scottish and Singaporean Neonatal Resuscitation Games, eBaby, eHBB, LIFE and the Compromised Neonate Program
key_sources: Ghoman SK, Patel SD, Cutumisu M, von Hauff P, Jeffery T, Brown MRG, Schmölzer GM. (2020). Serious games, a game changer in teaching neonatal resuscitation? A review. Archives of Disease in Childhood. Fetal and Neonatal Edition. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2019-317011
